item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] Why Chinese AI Labs Are Keeping Up
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、蒸馏是"反中心化的暗流"——但它揭露的是一个更深的秘密：模型的真正壁垒不在权重里

大多数人以为前沿实验室的护城河是算力、算法、或参数。但这段对话戳破了一个反直觉的真相：前沿模型真正无法被复制的部分，其实是"用户的注意力分布"。Chinese 实验室通过 router/proxy 拿到的不是模型输出，而是真实人类在痛苦时刻发出的 prompt——那种"这个不对，让我们退一步重新想想"的挫败流。这才是无法自造的稀缺资源。

这让我想起一个隐藏的等式：Anthropic 卖的不是 Claude，Anthropic 在向 Claude 买 prompt。 每一个订阅用户既是收入来源，也是蒸馏对手的原料供应商。这是 SaaS 时代从未存在过的商业结构——你的客户越多，你的对手就变得越强。

二、"难度轴 vs 现实轴"——这其实是 AI 版的 SEAL Team 训练悖论

Alec 提出的"环境有两个维度：难度与现实感"，几乎一比一映射到军事训练学中的一个古老争论："打靶场高分选手"往往在真实巷战中表现平庸。因为难题可验证、可打分、可优化；而现实混乱、多目标、无明确 reward。Benchmark 是打靶场，Sonnet 5 之所以"AI-as-judge 味太重"，是因为它在打靶场里过拟合了——每一步都在问自己"这样对吗"，却失去了 Opus 那种"知道何时该停止思考"的沉默智慧。

这里有一个令人不安的推论：中国实验室之所以能追上，不是因为他们更强，而是因为他们不需要"发明现实感"——他们直接从美国用户的键盘上抄走了现实感。 他们跳过了最贵的一步：定义"什么是好"。

三、跨领域连接：这场景与 1980 年代日本半导体崛起完全同构

这个动态与"日本如何用美国的芯片设计做出比美国更好的芯片"是同一个剧本： - 前沿定义者（美国 / Anthropic / OpenAI）承担"探索代价"——试错、走弯路、定义 rubric - 追随者（日本 / DeepSeek / 智谱）承担"精炼代价"——用更小的模型、更清晰的信号，产出更优的商品 - 数据经纪人（就像当年的贸易商社）确保知识必然泄漏

但真正令人意外的观察是这个：Trenton 在最后随手扔出的那句"数据公司把同样的数据卖给所有人"揭示了一个未被讨论的黑洞——前沿实验室之间的"竞争"本质上是一场共谋。因为他们向同一批数据供应商付费，他们的模型底层分布正在趋同。真正的分化不会来自基座模型，而会来自你无法买到的东西：部署闭环里的私有反馈流。

这意味着一个反常识的战略结论：未来最有价值的 AI 公司可能不是模型公司，而是"用户异常行为的独家占有者"——比如某个专业软件里工程师如何咒骂 bug、某个法律平台上律师如何反复修改论点。这些"愤怒的 prompt"才是下一个原油。而 Claude Code 这类产品的真实商业逻辑，可能远不止是"卖 IDE"这么简单。

📝 转录文本

为什么模型提供商没有大规模整合？

Dwarkesh: What is the story for why there isn't huge consolidation in model providers? There's just so many things that point to centralization here. If you step back over the course of years, is there something that is going to prevent that?

Alec: Yeah, I think distillation is the main thing that fights against the centralizing force. Because basically anything that can be learned through RL can be distilled very easily — it's a small number of bits. It's something that you can learn from a small amount of data. So if you can get trajectories from the model that show a behavior, you can easily distill it.

So I think distillation is one of the things that fight centralization. There's also — I mean, there is a possibility that there'll be company-specific models, that it'll be possible to learn from deployment and have a company continually improving its own model. And such a system could be provided by the current oligopoly of model providers or some other currently smaller company. But I think that'll change the game a bit.

Trenton: Yeah, and I also want to point out that continual learning also doesn't stop distillation, right? Like even if your model is improving every day, people could be distilling it every day. So the loops could just operate at the same pace.

蒸馏的前提：Prompt 分布至关重要

Dwarkesh: Right, that makes sense. Okay, so copying model behavior — I guess you need to know yourself what the right distribution to prompt is in order to get like the relevant model behavior.

Alec: Oh yeah, for just distilling with supervised learning, the prompt distribution is extremely important. So it's very non-trivial to distill a model even if you have full access to it and have the CoT — the chain of thought — and everything. It's non-trivial to distill all of the useful capabilities from it because you need to prompt the model with something, and you need to prompt it with realistic prompts. You need to have a really wide distribution of realistic prompts.

So one thing that's been coming out recently is that some of the Chinese companies are probably using these router services which are designed to allow people in China to use the US frontier models which would otherwise be blocked in China. There are all these router or proxy services that allow people in China to use these models — mostly for coding. And these router services are collecting and selling some of the data. So I think this is a very useful dataset for distillation, because it gives you the perfect prompt distribution.

AI 自动化 prompt 采集：人类逐步退出

Trenton: Yeah. I think this is one of those things where AIs help a lot here. If you actually look at the frontier pipelines that, say, the Chinese models put in their papers, it's a lot of humans — or they get seed prompts from somewhere, which is some combination of humans, this kind of data, and then they synthesize a vast coverage from those seed prompts using their existing models or the other frontier models.

And so, you can automate an awful lot of this prompt distribution gathering and environment creation. It's just that humans need to provide increasingly fewer amounts of bits as the models get better.

Dwarkesh: Right. Or certainly, it still seems you're bottlenecked by having a service which has users, or users are going through.

Trenton: Not necessarily. I mean, yeah, that's obviously very helpful, but theoretically, you can think about like what the users want.

Dwarkesh: No, but the whole point is that the user says, "Make me an application like this." "Oh, that didn't work. I actually want you to make this new feature. But actually, let's step back and do this other thing." And capturing that whole trace is the — or to the extent you could have done that anyways, then you just have RSI anyway.

Trenton: Yeah, I mean, ultimately, if you have this fully automated loop that is basically RSI, right? The AI is deciding the data which is deciding the training. That is the loop. But it depends how much human information you need. At some point, if you're just like, "I want traces that look like this," you prompt that to the model, the model will be able to come up with a pretty good approximation.

蒸馏者的悖论：模仿比创造更容易

Dwarkesh: If you want to do like, "Make me a really good politician"? And then that's like anticipated de novo. Like, how would a discussion in the Senate halls go or something?

Trenton: Yeah, ironically, this is actually easier for the distillers than the frontier labs, right? Because the distillers just say: "I want a good politician." They go to the frontier model, the frontier model already knows how to be a good politician, so it would just generate those traces. Whereas if you actually want to build a frontier model that does this, you have to actually somehow get data on what politicians do every day and build that.

So it's actually much easier to say "I want something like this" and then get the AI to produce a billion variations, than to actually create the thing like this to begin with.

一个可检验的预测：前沿实验室在 RL 环境上未必有优势

Trenton: I think you can actually make a really concrete prediction based off this observation, that the Chinese labs have this route at all. The thing that stated this originally was I was saying, isn't it weird how Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 are almost objectively worse models than GLM 5.3 / KM K3, even though they've had access to not only distillation but logit distillation from Mythos?

And so the counter here was that: okay, the prompt distribution really really matters. You need to see what users are doing so that you can distill those kinds of behaviors and things in.

I think the prediction from this is that the frontier labs don't necessarily have much of an advantage — if at all — in RL environments now. Because yes, user distribution matters for general behavior and so on, but the best measure of a capability is the very very hard RL environments you've made at the frontier. And so if you have access to those RL environments as Anthropic, and you have access to logit distillation, and you've still made a worse model, then maybe the real-world deployment matters more than the environment.

Dwarkesh: That's really interesting. So — but they had to incentivize those capabilities in the first place in Fable, or the frontier model. And it's weird that they can't incentivize them again. Or in a smaller model or something.

Trenton: Maybe we're just in this weird uncanny valley where actually trying to copy that frontier model too much — the student-teacher gap or whatever it is — is just too large.

I think maybe people made this point with Opus: the difference between Opus 4.6 and Opus 5 is that Opus 5 really feels like it's got this "AI as a judge" checking every possible thing it's done. That's why it uses so many tokens — it tries to think about all these things, but it doesn't necessarily have the "big model smell" of Fable, to know when to stop doing that, or when's the good path to go down or whatever.

Dwarkesh: The re-60s the grass.

Trenton: Yeah.

Alec 的替代假说：难度轴 vs 现实感轴

Alec: Yeah, I would offer a slightly different hypothesis. I would say there a couple of different axes for the environments you can create. One of them is difficulty, and the other is realism.

It's sort of easy to create — or it's comparatively easy to create — a lot of difficult environments that just involve doing a much more complicated task, or doing something that requires a lot more cleverness. You could say this is like the benchmaxing distribution, because a lot of the most prominent benchmarks just involve doing some very hard puzzle-like task that's easy to verify.

And then there's the realism axis, where you want the model to be good in the realistic coding agent setting, where there's multiple back-and-forth with the human and there's multiple objectives. I'd say the labs who are crafting the model behavior for the first time need to push in both directions. And to get good model behavior, you need to really push on the realism axis and have rubrics or some kind of human feedback that's informing the reward function you use there.

But I think when — if you try to do distillation naively, you end up just sort of matching the teacher on the benchmark and distribution. And if you don't have enough of the environments that really exercise the capabilities in these trickier realistic settings, then you're not going to get those into your student model.

I think maybe one thing that's happening is: the big models generalize better from the tricky narrow tasks to these more realistic tasks. So if you have a really good realistic prompt distribution for distillation, you can match the big model really well. But if you only have this distribution of easily verifiable tasks, then you can match the big model on all the benchmarks, but you do worse on this broader distribution.

So that might even explain something about the smaller Anthropic models like Sonnet 5 — though it's hard to predict exactly what they're doing to post-train those models. It could also be that they're always changing their post-training stack, and they just got a few things wrong in some of these models. They turned up something too high and created some quirks that people really don't like. So it's really easy to screw up post-training in some way that doesn't show up in benchmarks.

最后一击：数据经纪人让"追赶"变得几乎必然

Trenton: I mean, one of the very basic points is just: the frontier AI labs get all the data from big data companies. And the Chinese can also just buy the same data from data companies.

Dwarkesh: And they are, right?

Trenton: And they are, exactly. There's a lot of people being annoyed about this. But if they have exactly the same data — and they can buy that, they can also distill — it means it's quite easy to keep up, really.

Dwarkesh: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

Alec 提出的"环境有两个维度：难度与现实感"，几乎一比一映射到军事训练学中的一个古老争论：**"打靶场高分选手"往往在真实巷战中表现平庸**。因为难题可验证、可打分、可优化；而现

item.title: [邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain] 我花了530,000,000買一張寶可夢卡，但這真的很便宜｜AJ Scaramucci【邦妮區塊鏈】
item.dc:creator: 邦妮區塊鏈 Bonnie Blockchain
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"Gotta Catch 'Em All" 是历史上最成功的稀缺性教育

AJ 没直说，但这里有一个让人后背发凉的洞察：任天堂 1996 年推出的口号"精灵全收集"，其实是全球规模最大的稀缺性心理训练营。它没有教一代人玩游戏，而是训练他们把"完整集合"当作情感终极目标——这正是收藏品投资学的核心心智模型。三十年后，这批被训练好的用户"come into wealth"（掌握财富），他们并不是被动地被 Pokémon 卡吸引，而是童年被埋下的稀缺性算法开始在成年账户中执行。这不是怀旧交易，这是延迟三十年触发的行为经济学炸弹。任天堂无意中为自己创造了未来的机构级买家。

二、恐龙化石是"文化 REIT"——一个被忽视的资产结构革命

AJ 提到 T-Rex 可以租给博物馆分票房和衍生品分成，还能给恐龙起名并做 IP 授权。这段轻描淡写地讲完了，但结构上它等于宣告：恐龙骨头是一种带现金流的文化基础设施资产，本质上和写字楼 REIT、机场特许经营权是同构的——一次性资本支出、超长折旧周期、垄断性稀缺、租金型收入。而收藏品行业竟然在完全没有金融化包装的情况下，独立演化出了这套模式。跨领域联想：古生物学 + 博物馆经济 + IP 授权 = 一个尚未被证券化的、比迪士尼版权收益更硬的现金流品类。谁第一个把 T-Rex 打包成 ETF，谁就复制了 1960 年代 REIT 立法造就的那波富豪。

三、真正反常识的洞察：评级机构在收藏品里的角色，是"倒着来的"

AJ 把 PSA / CGC / Beckett 类比成"收藏品界的穆迪"，但这个类比藏着一个反向真相：在传统金融里，评级机构是市场成熟之后才出现的产物；而在收藏品里，评级机构是市场诞生的原因。没有 PSA 10 的标准化，Pikachu Illustrator 只是一张漂亮的旧卡；有了它，卡片被压缩成一个可全球定价、可托管、可跨境套利的"标准化不可替代资产"。这解释了一件更深的事——卡片、化石、名画之所以能对抗比特币的注意力吸走效应，恰恰是因为它们主动接受了"金融基础设施化"。

由此可以推出一个 AJ 没说透的宏观预测：下一轮收藏品牛市不会由拍卖行主导，而是由"分数托管 + 借贷 + 衍生品"这层结构主导。也就是说，收藏品市场正在悄悄经历它自己的"1971 年时刻"——从熟人网络的私下议价，进化为拥有完整信用曲线的资产类别。当这层基础设施完成时，$6.5 万亿的私人收藏池会像 1980 年代的房地产一样，第一次进入机构资产负债表。

四、一个隐藏的家族信号

Anthony Scaramucci 是最早入场机构级比特币的人之一，儿子 AJ 现在全力押注收藏品。这不是父子兴趣的巧合，这是家族资本在同一逻辑（法币贬值对冲）下的"品类轮动"分工——父亲负责数字稀缺，儿子负责文化稀缺，两代人形成一个完整的"debasement 对冲组合"。当一个家族开始用世代切分资产品类时，你正在目睹一种非常古老的欧洲银行家族模式（罗斯柴尔德式的地理分工）在数字时代的复活——只不过分工维度从"国家"换成了"稀缺性介质"。

📝 转录文本

开场：为什么最有钱的人正在重仓收藏品

The richest of the rich, they understand this intimately, which is why you're seeing them come in and come in heavy.

The Pokémon market has over 2x over the last really 4 months. "Got to catch them all. Be the very best like no one ever was." It really captured the imagination of the millennial generation. And I'd say all these years later, now that myself and others around my age have come into wealth, we're looking to store our value in places that are incredibly scarce and highly desirable.

A $16.5 million Pikachu Illustrator from Logan Paul. That card has been compounding at 73% since 2012. It's a high opacity category and it's a category that's actually way bigger than Bitcoin.

The market outperformed the stock market. Oh, dramatically. We saw a T-Rex sell just a month and a half ago for a whopping $51 million. Since 1902, we have only found about 50 T-Rex specimens. And less than 10 of those T-Rex specimens have a completion threshold defined by bone count and bone volume north of 50%.

The United States really has four options to deal with their $40 trillion of debt.

I'm sure. And that has to do with dinosaur fun? It does. Absolutely freaking does.

嘉宾介绍：AJ Scaramucci

Would you say you know Pokémon pretty well? I think so. Yeah. Okay. So, my nephew prepped a question for you. He is 7 years old.

Our guest today might be the closest thing we would ever get to a real life Pokémon trainer. AJ Scaramucci from Salari Capital, Treasure Trove, and Salt. And he's bought a $16.5 million Pikachu Illustrator from Logan Paul.

Hello AJ. Hey, good to see you. Good to be with you.

童年场景：1999 年的收藏室

Before we start talking about the crazy price tag, take us back to your childhood, the journey — 1999, if we were to walk into your room, what would we have seen?

Yeah, you would see an absolute Cambrian explosion of all kinds of collectibles. I mean, when I was a kid, I was collecting things like rocks and gemstones. I have some citrine around my neck right now, which is my favorite gemstone. I was collecting Pokémon cards as a 33-year-old man. I grew up right in the crosshairs of that Pokémon nostalgia. Was collecting a lot of trading cards and sports memorabilia. So, you would just see pure chaos in my room.

从比特币到 Pikachu：文化型价值储存

And how did that passion lead to you purchasing the Pikachu Illustrator?

Sure. Yeah. Well, I mean, I'd say we're sitting at the Bitcoin conference, and I've been a longtime Bitcoin holder, and I've found the philosophy and heuristics that apply to Bitcoin also apply to collectibles. And I think Bitcoin being really the first true technology to pioneer digital scarcity has created everything you see around you, right? It's created trillions of dollars of economic wealth, hundreds of millions of participants and wallet holders. And collectibles is the same way.

And I'd say, you know, for a franchise like Pokémon, which is the highest grossing franchise of all time, that has a slogan of "got to catch them all" and "be the very best like no one ever was", it really captured the imagination of the millennial generation. And I'd say all these years later, now that myself and others around my age have come into wealth, we're looking to store our value in places that are incredibly scarce and highly desirable.

So the Pikachu card was just an expression of a broader thesis around this notion of the cultural store of value. And the same way that Bitcoin is the digital store of value or gold might be the physical store of value, that card and many of the things that I've bought, I view as the cultural store of value.

如何为一张卡片定价？

I think with Bitcoin, people are starting to understand and a lot of our viewers are Bitcoiners, but with collectibles, this is a new world. How do you look at a card and decide the fair value of it?

That's a great question. Yeah. So for Bitcoin, I think about it as in some ways a perpetual auction that is running in real time with hundreds of millions of unique participants and tens of billions of dollars of trading volume. So you have true ubiquitous and real price discovery.

For scarce collectibles, they typically get purchased in one of two ways.

一、私下交易： Let's say you've got a cool card or a compelling object that I want. I can go reach out to you and say, "Hey, I'll give you a million for it." You'll say, "How about three?" I'll say, "How about two?" We'll go back and forth.

二、拍卖会： That auction is compelling because it's creating a better form of price discovery, but it's still only takes two to tango. You just need two individual nodes and a network coming together to decide on a price.

So, for collectibles, there's a lot of arbitrage opportunities. It's a high opacity category and it's a category that's actually way bigger than Bitcoin. Even in private hands, we estimate at Treasure Trove there's about $6.5 trillion of collectible assets. In the hands of the public, which includes nation states, foundations, and museums, it's in excess of $25 trillion.

Wow.

And you know, while Bitcoin is unified and fungible with network effects, collectibles is highly heterogeneous and disjointed. But both share in common that they are a debasement trade. Right? So as fiat currency continues to debase, we're going to see a huge Cambrian explosion in scarce asset appreciation. And I'd say, like collectibles, even just being here for five minutes, walking in, I see some collectible advertisers. You know, the fact that I was invited here at this Bitcoin conference shows you that those heuristics are very, very similar.

底价、估值与"套利"

Well, you mentioned auction, right? So before you enter the room, do you have a number in your head how much you are willing to pay?

Of course. Absolutely right. Yeah. Every single object that I have purchased is meticulously underwritten just like any other investment I would make at Salari Capital.

And I'd say, for the Pikachu Illustrator card, which was a very loud sale — like the fact that you know about it, or even in the introduction, "I'm Pokémon trainer" — which I love. That virality turned into me being recognized as a Pokémon trainer. I'm just totally down for that.

But what's wild is, Pokémon cards, the asset class is now about $30 billion, right? So that is material. I mean, if that was a publicly traded company, that would be like a midcap company. And it's also growing very, very quickly. It's only been 30 years. How many companies or how many asset classes have gone from 0 to 30 billion in three decades? Very few.

And the analogy I like to use is: if someone bought $16.5 million of stock in a $30 billion company, would that have made global news? It wouldn't have. Right? And yet I could do that and I'm sitting here today and you're introducing me as a Pokémon trainer. That in and of itself is an arbitrage.

And for Pokémon — the $30 billion, when you click into it, it looks and feels a lot like a power law like any other asset class. There's a very small number of individual cards. There's 85 billion cards that have been printed by the Nintendo company. Most of them are worth almost nothing — pennies, tens of cents, dollars, tens of dollars. The cards that are truly scarce and highly desirable and represent the origin of the franchise, that are graded and certified and authenticated, that's where the real value accrues.

For a character like Pikachu, which is such a dominant character in the Nintendo universe — in the same way that if you go and collect basketball cards, you'll find that Michael Jordan and Steph Curry and LeBron James really dominate the market cap creation — you'll find the same thing for characters like Pikachu, say, and Charizard.

Pikachu Illustrator：为什么这一张如此特殊？

What is so special about this particular card? Could it be possible that in the future they come up with another one?

It's a great question. So, what makes the Pikachu Illustrator so special is that it couldn't be purchased in a pack. It had to be won in a very niche and narrow illustration contest that took place in 1998 in Tokyo. And there were only 39 of these cards printed and awarded to some of the original artists, including the woman that created Pikachu — created that card. So that card in many ways represents an emblem of the origin of the most iconic character of all time.

And what's so interesting about collectibles is: in the same way you have grading and authentication agencies like a Moody's — and they'll go in and say your stock or your bond or your credit instrument is AAA or triple B or triple C — that infrastructure has now been built in collectibles. So companies like PSA, Beckett, CGC and others, they can come in, and all those 39 illustrators are not created equal, right? It turns out some of them are bent and warped. The centering is off. There's all these little minute details and defects.

And what made this card so special is not only does it represent the origin of Pikachu, but it also is a pristine PSA 10. And those one-of-one grails — the best of the best in any given collectible asset class — create disproportionate alpha-generating opportunities. Like that card has been compounding at 73% since 2012.

And I've already received offers in like a multiple of what I paid just a few — I'm not selling anytime soon. I mean, never say never, but literally the Pokémon market has over 2x'ed over the last really 4 months.

Logan Paul 与那笔"被低估的交易"

You saw Logan Paul with the card and it was purchased for what — a little over $5 million — and you thought that was undervalued.

Yeah, I mean, at the time it shocked a lot of people that he spent that amount of money and it was a very controversial sale. But a lot of people see the sticker price and don't click into the market.

If you go to the United States or even here in Hong Kong, honestly, there are events like this — including Collecticon, Colletopia, Card Party, Comic-Con — that aggregate 5 to 600,000 people in person every year that dress like Pikachu, Charizard, Ash Ketchum. You find fathers and sons, mothers and daughters, all attending — age-agnostic from the age of 4 to 60 — buying, selling and trading Pokémon cards. And that market's very liquid.

When you think about trading cards as an asset class, it's about $80 billion in total and there's about a billion dollar a month of sales. So there's a lot of robust and global liquidity in these markets.

And Logan, to his credit, saw this. A lot of people underestimate Logan. He's a very, very smart and gifted investor and entrepreneur. And I view Logan in the same way I would view, say, a Bill Ackman — where they just are activist investors. And instead of buying equities and getting on CNBC, they're buying Pokémon cards and maybe getting on YouTube and telling their stories.

And I'd say that the Illustrator card, like any other Grail asset in any given category, sets the tone for the entire asset class. So when he bought that card in 2021 for $5.275 million, you saw a rising tide lift all boats. Same thing with the acquisition we made a few months ago.

跨品类的"Grail 资产"复利表现

And the market outperformed the stock market.

Oh, dramatically. Yeah. And again, it's not just the Pikachu card. It's the Mickey Mantle 1952 Topps rookie card. It's Dorothy's Ruby Red Slippers, the movie prop that sold for $32.5 million just a few years ago. That movie prop was compounding quietly at 20% year-over-year for 54 years.

Or even something like Salvator Mundi, which is a very famous Da Vinci painting that was bought by Muhammad bin Salman, the crown prince of Saudi Arabia. That was in 2017 during a Christie's auction. That was a $450 million transaction.

Wow.

And that piece of art was compounding behind the scenes at 192% for 12 years. So all of these one-of-one grails in every individual collectible asset class — the best of the best, the top decile — dramatically outperform the market. And the issue has always been this asset class is not ubiquitous and accessible to the average person. So people can't afford or access it. And what's beautiful about Bitcoin is it's fungible, it's decentralized, and it is accessible. So I think a lot about those characteristics in the context of Treasure Trove as we continue to build it.

Treasure Trove：给收藏品做"寻宝数据库"

So you like all of these asset classes. How do you design your portfolio?

For me, you can think of Treasure Trove as a treasure-hunting organization and our universal heuristic is one of identifying grail assets. What we've done — which really no one has ever done, even though it seems so obvious to us — is build a database that I think is the most robust database ever built in collectibles.

We have partnerships with a variety of different auction houses, some of which have even invested in our company. And we can see in our database individual SKUs where they've historically transacted, what their compounded annual appreciation has been, how those assets live in the context of broader categories. So the Pokémon card in trading cards, an Iron Man comic in the comic book category, the Monet painting in the fine art category.

So we can both systematically and algorithmically identify assets that are exhibiting these debasement trade characteristics, where they're growing at faster than market rates of return.

What's sort of peculiar to me is you have this multi-trillion-dollar asset class and it's received a lot of institutional attention — but it's only received institutional attention from the mega billionaire class, because there's really only 10,000 for sure: a Ken Griffin or a Steve Cohen or the crown prince of Saudi Arabia. All these people are looking for places to park and store value. And even for someone like Ken Griffin, he may be worth 50 to $60 billion — that guy is putting 5 to 15% of his portfolio into these kinds of scarce assets for all the reasons I just described.

恐龙：Ken Griffin 也在收藏

And you also like dinosaurs, like Ken Griffin. Absolutely. You went to Wyoming to learn about dinosaurs. What was it like?

It is awesome. As a kid, I think like many kids, a fascination with dinosaurs is always a part of youth. The T-Rex, the Triceratops, the Stegosaurus — those are really the big three that you're introduced to when you're a kid. And you watch Jurassic Park. Thanks to Steven Spielberg, the mystery and the magnificence of these dinosaurs being put on the big screen — it feels like fantasy. It doesn't feel real.

These things actually were walking among us tens of millions of years ago. And the fact that you can have something like a T-Rex, which is literally a 20,000-ton animal that's 44 ft long, 16 ft tall — the size of multiple school buses or multiple elephants — that was just hanging out, is insane. These things are relics of the past. And finding them is so freaking hard. They're really like needles in a haystack.

找到化石就归你吗？两条路径

Okay. So, if someone finds the fossil, does that automatically mean it belongs to me? How does it work?

There's different rules and regulations depending on the jurisdiction and country. In the United States, there's really two paths.

Path 1 — 私人土地（类似矿业模式）: Let's say you own a bunch of land in Montana or in Wyoming, which happen to be a hotbed for dinosaur discovery. I as a paleontologist can go to you and say, "Hey, let me prospect on your land. Let me do a geological survey" — the same way I would as if I'm a mining company. And if I find something, I'll pay you a percentage of the proceeds upon liberation. For you, if you own literally tens of miles of square land, it's a lot of time, effort, and energy to go do that surveying, and it requires a lot of deep and narrow expertise. So you say, "Yeah, no problem." We sign a contract and we're on our way.

Path 2 — 政府土地（谨慎！）: The alternative is government-owned land. There, people have sometimes gotten into trouble because they'll find something on land that's publicly owned. If you do that, even if you find something, it's not yours. It's property of the United States government.

That makes it really tricky. Since 1902 — literally almost 120, 130 years ago — we have only found about 50 T-Rex specimens. And less than 10 of those T-Rex specimens have a completion threshold defined by bone count and bone volume north of 50%. So it's really like finding a needle in a haystack. And that's why you see these sticker prices that are so extraordinary. We saw a T-Rex sell just a month and a half ago for a whopping $51 million. And just 30 years ago, those same assets, when we were discovering them for the first time, were literally tens of thousands of dollars.

恐龙的"现金流"：博物馆经济学

And these things earn yield, too. They do. They do.

For the best of the best collectible assets, you can create exhibits around those assets. People have a willingness to pay to see these spectacular collectible items. And T-Rex is such an imposing and ridiculous collectible — it's so large, you can build an entire exhibit in a museum around it.

Many people that have purchased these T-Rexes in the past, they'll lease them out to museums and they'll negotiate with the museum to collect a percentage of ticket sales and a percentage of merchandise.

And as crazy as it sounds, when you buy a dinosaur, yes, you're buying the bones, but there's also intellectual property that you're buying as well. You can name the dinosaur whatever it is you'd like. You could make t-shirts and merchandise and plushies, and on and on it goes. The most famous real dinosaur that's ever been discovered is Sue in the Field Museum in Chicago. And Sue generates like tens of millions of dollars of revenue every single year because of how famous she is.

Mind-boggling. Wow.

宏观：美债的四种出路与稀缺资产

Is this betting on the next generation being rich enough to purchase them for a higher price?

It's a good question. What we're really betting on… I would argue that the United States really has four options to deal with their $40 trillion of debt.

I'm sure — and that has to do with dinosaur funds? It does. Okay. Absolutely freaking does. It's all connected. And that's exactly why we're sitting here at the Bitcoin conference too.

Option 1 — 破产宣告: We can declare bankruptcy. We're not going to do that. Option 2 — 转为社会主义国家、大幅加税: We're not going to do that. Option 3 — 削减开支: No chance in hell we're going to do that. I mean, Elon Musk with DOGE attempted — he cut a few hundred billion dollars out and was promptly kicked out of the government in an expedient fashion. Option 4 — 印更多钱: What is our fourth and only option? Well, that's to print more money.

For something like Bitcoin, you know your numerator and your denominator. I own a single Bitcoin — that's my numerator, and the denominator is fixed at 21 million. If I own a US dollar, I know my numerator, but my denominator is not fixed and it is rapidly growing. And that debasement — which is now nearly 7% a year — is a hidden tax on society.

Again, these scarce desirable assets, whether it's a T-Rex or it's a Pokémon card or whatever it may be, there's this universal heuristic around the cultural store of value. And the richest of the rich, they understand this intimately, which is why you're seeing them come in and come in heavy into this asset class, particularly in recent decades.

For fine art, which is about $3 trillion, that is where I would say previous generations have historically stored their value. But these new categories — like trading cards or manga or Zashi or Harry Potter or Star Wars, or a lot of the IP that we grew up with — there's art and collectibles there, and you're seeing kind of a rebalancing of where that cultural value is being stored.

父亲的影响：Anthony Scaramucci

I want to circle back to your dad. Because my first on-site interview was with your dad, and he is just the most lovely person. I told him, "Hey, I'm a little nervous. This is my first on-site interview." He was like, "Oh, don't worry. I got you." A lot of our viewers love him for that. What is his influence in your life?

Definitely. Yeah. So, for me, my dad grew up kind of a lower-middle-class family, one of the first educated in his family. I'm the oldest of five. So I had a front-row seat to the American dream. I saw my mom and dad go from zero — candidly, less than zero. They were in debt, mostly because they were educated — all the way to where they are now.

I've seen my dad iterate through multiple cycles of entrepreneurship, build and sell and scale multiple businesses. And even growing up, through osmosis, just observing the way in which he thinks, operates — he's an incredibly compelling storyteller and salesperson. So a lot of those characteristics you pick up on.

I think about Bitcoin in many ways, not just as an asset class or a debasement trade, but it's also a bit of a religion and a cultural movement. And that cultural movement needs disciples. I would say, kind of jokingly and seriously, that my dad has become a disciple of Bitcoin. He was one of the first institutional investors to step into the space meaningfully in 2019. Whether it's him or Michael Saylor or Mike Novogratz or many others that are speaking here — like CZ, I think, later this afternoon — they are preaching the gospel of the debasement trade that is Bitcoin.

I view collectibles under the same guise. Collectibles also has a lot of religious characteristics, and I'm hoping to do my best to be a disciple of the culture.

To convince him that you are buying that card…

No, I mean, he knew that I loved Pokémon cards. Even prior to that acquisition, I've been buying a lot of Pokémon cards since 2019.

Really?

So it wasn't a surprise to him. It wasn't a surprise to me. But it was a surprise to many.

So he didn't say anything about it. He was super supportive.

He gets it. The heuristic for Bitcoin and the heuristic for collectibles is effectively identical. Both of these things at their core are debasement trades. Bitcoin doesn't generate any native yield, either does gold. Collectibles do in some cases, but in many cases they don't — and they're valued on their scarcity value. So again, that's why I'm sitting here. We have Bitcoin Asia behind you, and we're talking about collectibles — because there's a similarity between those two ecosystems.

彩蛋：7 岁小侄子的问题

Would you say you know Pokémon pretty well? I think so. Yeah. Okay. So, my nephew prepped a question for you. He is 7 years old, and I don't know what he's talking about, but I think you might know. Got it.

So his question is about ancient Pokémon. And where do you find them?

Right. In Pokémon — we're going to go down a nerdy rabbit hole — there are Pokémon that are alive in the current era. And then there are also Pokémon that are not alive in the current era, that are reanimated in different ways. Like one of them is Aerodactyl, which is probably what he's alluding to.

When you play the Pokémon video game, you have to go find these fossils and ambers, these different objects — almost like quasi-inspired by Jurassic Park. You know how in Jurassic Park they have the mosquito, and it has a little bit of dinosaur blood in it, and then they recreate Jurassic Park? Pokémon has a similar idea where you can go and find remnants of ancient Pokémon and reanimate them, bring them back to life, and have them on your team. That's what he's talking about.

And he's asking: where do you find them?

Where do you find them? Yeah. It depends on the game you're playing. For me, in Fire Red, if I remember correctly, it's either Vermilion City or one of the first cities. You have to go behind the gym and talk to an old man, and he tells you what I just told you about ancient Pokémon, and he's like, "Come on over here, kid," and he gives you an amber. And then you have to go and do a few other tasks to reanimate the ancient Pokémon. It's a whole thing.

If you go on serebii.net — which I would suggest your seven-year-old nephew does — there's an infinite cornucopia of information about how to do all this. In the same way Wikipedia is a cornucopia of information on all things related to humanity, serebii.net is just like that, but for Pokémon. It's the Wikipedia of the Pokémon universe.

结语

AJ, this feels like a real-life treasure hunt for me. And I learned so much new stuff. This is a whole new world. Thank you for being on the show. Of course. Thank you. Good to see you.

item.description:
## 一、"Gotta Catch 'Em All" 是历史上最成功的稀缺性教育
AJ 没直说，但这里有一个让人后背发凉的洞察：**任天堂 1996 年推出的口号"精灵全收集"，其实是全球规模最大的稀缺性心理训练营**。它没有教一代人玩游戏，而是训练他们把"完整集合"当作情感终极目标——这正是收藏品投资学的核心心智模型。三十年后，这批被训练好的用户"come into wealth"（掌握财富），他们并不是被动地被 Pokémon 卡吸引，而是**童年被埋下的稀缺性算法开始在成年账户中执行**。这不是怀旧交易，这是延迟三十年触发的行为经济学炸弹。任天堂无意中为自己创造了未来的机构级买家。
## 二、恐龙化石是"文化 REIT"——一个被忽视的资产结构革命
AJ 提到 T-Rex 可以租给博物馆分票房和衍生品分成，还能给恐龙起名并做 IP 授权。这段轻描淡写地讲完了，但结构上它等于宣告：**恐龙骨头是一种带现金流的文化基础设施资产**，本质上和写字楼 REIT、机场特许经营权是同构的——一次性资本支出、超长折旧周期、垄断性稀缺、租金型收入。而收藏品行业竟然在完全没有金融化包装的情况

item.title: [Business of Sport] Why is Pietersen Back, Root’s Weird Interview, & County Champs Heating Up
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"邪教后遗症"作为组织行为学诊断

Joe Root 那段 BBC 采访最惊人的地方，不是他说了什么，而是他 在赢下系列赛之后依然像个受害者一样在为前任辩护。主持人用"cult follower who lost his leader"来形容，看似戏谑，实则精准。心理学上有个概念叫"高控制群体退出综合征"（Post-Cult Trauma Syndrome）——被解救者在最初阶段往往会过度美化过去的领袖，因为承认"我们成就的一切都来自新起点"，等于承认过去四年被浪费。Root 三次重复"don't undervalue"，这不是感激，这是认知失调在自我修补。

二、一个反直觉的数学倒置：淘汰名单反而是胜利名单

节目主持人埋了一个惊人的事实但没有点破——这两场胜利的英雄 Ollie Robinson 和 Jordan Cox，恰恰是被 Bazball 体系明确排斥的两人。Robinson 在 McCullum 时代拥有全英最佳保龄均值却几乎不上场；Cox 在郡赛均值近 50 却从未获邀。也就是说：新教练 Fleming 上任后取胜的公式，是把旧体制的"淘汰名单"变成"首发名单"。这在企业并购语境下等价于——新 CEO 只是把前任 fire 掉的人重新招回来，业绩就转正了。这不叫"传承 McCullum 的遗产"，这叫否定即价值。Root 却在电视上把胜利归功于旧体制——这是英国板球版的斯德哥尔摩综合征。

三、跨领域连接：郡赛揭示了美国体育付费千金也解不了的谜

主持人无意间点出了一个体育经济学界的隐秘悖论：萨里队即使降级也不会伤及财务，因为收入来自 Oval 球场的酒店、会议、外部赛事承办——体育表现与商业表现在英国郡板球里已经结构性脱钩。这恰恰是美国 NFL 用特许经营制 + 收入共享 + 无升降级花几十年建立的"抗周期性"，郡板球却是无意中演化出来的。反过来看，这种脱钩正是 Somerset 百年无冠仍能保持庞大观众基础的原因——在萨默塞特，球队的意义是"地区身份"，不是"竞赛成绩"。这解释了一个更深的现象：为什么 Rob Key 领导下的 ECB 精英端可以"loose loose loose"（松散松散松散）地运作——当亏损不会杀死俱乐部时，问责机制就永远不会真正长出来。KP 的模糊角色任命、Flintoff 的仓促上任又仓促离开，都不是"意外"，而是这个没有生存压力的生态系统必然产生的治理熵。

四、一个额外的洞察：为什么"人格 45 岁后不再改变"是 ECB 应该内化的招聘算法

节目里那句"40 到 55 岁之间人真的会显著改变吗？我不这么认为"，其实是霍根人格评估（Hogan Assessment）几十年数据的通俗版本——大五人格特质在 30 岁后趋于固化，尤其是外向性与宜人性的组合几乎不变。KP 作为球员时"表现覆盖人格成本"的逻辑成立；作为教练/导师时，"人格即产品"——他没有任何可交付的"变化后的自己"。ECB 请他，本质上是在为娱乐性支付一笔组织文化的税，而这笔税会由那些无法反击 KP 的年轻球员承担。

📝 转录文本

Joe Root's BBC Interview: A Return of Concerns

We talked a couple of weeks ago, I think it was, uh, about the start that Joe Root had and how important it was that no matter who we were playing — yeah, England got some wins on the board. You can only beat what's in front of you, even though Pakistan are in some big trouble themselves. We were positive. We were positive about Joe Root's leadership, the start of it, and a new dawn.

We then — you well, you then sent me a video this morning of an interview that Joe given the BBC which I think it's fair to say threw up a few more concerns, uh, than any more positive thinking.

What do you make of it?

Oh, um, are concerning, because what Joe Root essentially was saying in this interview was that the good work that had gone on in the last few weeks — winning a couple of test matches against the lowest ranked test team — was in no small part down to the work that Brendon McCullum and Ben Stokes had done in their 10 years as coach and captain of England cricket. And we mustn't forget that. We mustn't forget that.

Specifically, I think he referenced it three times, but the actual wording, which I wrote down, he said: "We wouldn't have been able to play the two games, by the way, without all of the work those two did. Don't undervalue the impact those two had on England cricket. They deserve a lot of credit for the last two performances."

So, what do I think about that? Well, look, let's put this into perspective. Would you be expected to beat Pakistan at home? Whether Brendan McCullum, Ben Stokes had been there for the last 10 years, let alone — yes. Would you be expected to beat them if you and I were coaching them? Maybe.

So this insinuation that they have achieved something great off the back of the leadership of two people who are now no longer there, and they're continuing this great work — me, Charlie…

The "Cult" Analogy

Do you remember I said about two months ago, Charlie, that England cricket under Brendan McCullum reminded me of a religious cult?

Yeah. And I think I specifically said that one of the most interesting things when you're studying the end of a cult, the demise of a cult, and the leader of the cult is led away in handcuffs because he's been doing dreadful things — and then the video remains on the remaining members of the cult, who you might expect to be delighted about being released from being part of this cult, but actually they just wander around looking a little bit lost and often cry, because they've now become so inculcated into the cult that they can't really imagine what life could be like without being inside the cult, no matter how ghastly conditions were inside that cult.

You've just read out words from Joe Root, but I'd encourage anyone out there who's got the time and the willingness to do so to actually just Google it and actually watch the interview.

Joe Root looks like a cult follower who's lost his cult leader, and he's saying things which make no sense unless you view it in the perspective of: he would actually much rather the cult was still there.

Picking Apart the "Legacy" Claim

So, in other words, when he says "we owe so much of what we've been able to do in the last two matches to what happened over the last four years" — well, let's just pick that apart a little bit, right? So those two performances against Pakistan from an England perspective were patchy.

Yeah.

Okay, there were two or three players who had outsized impacts and Pakistan did not have the equivalent on their side. Okay. Now, it's worth pointing out — the two players who have been England's player of the season series so far, Ollie Robinson and Jordan Cox, were specifically disbarred from this cult.

Ollie Robinson, despite having the best test bowling and county bowling averages of any England bowler throughout Brendan McCullum's time in charge, was barely given a match by McCullum. McCullum couldn't stand the guy.

Yeah.

Right. He wouldn't pick him. Even when Robinson was on top form, and when there were bowlers in the England side who couldn't take a wicket, he still would not pick Ollie Robinson until right at the end in the New Zealand series. You know, "I've got to win a match or two here — better call in Robinson." And Robinson gets nine wickets. Okay, so you can hardly paint Robinson winning matches for England as being a clear example of how great Bazball was.

And Jordan Cox, who's about to turn 26, was never given a chance at all. Despite averaging almost 50 in county cricket, he was never given a chance at all under Bazball. And the innings that he's played this summer would be the types of innings which would have seen him thrown out of the team under Brendan McCullum.

So this is not to go back and relitigate the failures of Bazball and the failures of McCullum. That's in the past now. That's gone. It's just very, very worrying when you see the person who's meant to be leading this effort for the next year, 2 years, 3 years, wandering around like a lost sheep himself, trying to relitigate and basically talking absolute rubbish.

You're right. I think so much comes from that interview by watching it. Not…

So do I. I mean, I'll try — we'll put a link out. He is almost — he looks broken. He's just won a test series and he looks like a broken man.

Yeah. And that if we're looking at Joe Root's previous captaincy is the concerns that I think fans would have. It's never about his ability to perform on the pitch. It's about the environment that he's able to control to an extent, but also just create around the team.

If that is still in their thinking, there's a huge amount of work that Fleming still — Fleming has got to do when he gets into that dressing room, because you cannot keep looking back. Certainly not when basically there's nothing about what you're doing right now which has got anything to do with what was going on back then. Well, and yeah, I just said the two players that…

The Return of Kevin Pietersen

Anyway — clears throat — speaking of personalities, cultures, well, we saw the return of…

Oh god.

You nearly forgot: Pietersen. Kevin Pietersen.

Oh my god.

So, Charlie, let me ask you a question. Right. So, we've got a culture issue. Maybe we've got overconfidence issues. Maybe. Well, you know — fragile confidence issues. White ball — white ball team. What do we need? If we're trying to control that, let's bring KP back and pair him up with Baz and see what happens.

I think the fact that the idea that he is himself quite similar to Baz — I don't think it really stands up to scrutiny. I mean, Pietersen is one of England's all-time batting greats in all forms of the game.

Yeah.

Including test cricket, where he was perfectly capable of digging in and spending an hour or two just keeping the ball out away from his stumps before going and blazing the ball around the park. He was an absolutely outstanding batsman, one of England's 10 best ever batsmen. Um, you can't take that away from him, you know.

But like a significant number of great athletes, he was always a problem at team level. Always. Both in England, but actually particularly back at his counties. You know, he was originally at Nottinghamshire until they threw all his kids off the balcony because they were so fed up with him, and then he caused problems at other counties he went to as well.

The Narcissism Problem

And that is because basically the guy is objectively a narcissist, right? Everything is about him.

Now, the problem about when you become a coach is that fundamentally your job is to subsume your own short-term interests, whatever they might be. Bite your tongue if you have to, and everything you're doing is being very carefully judged as to: how is this going to benefit this player and the team? And sometimes it means, as a grown-up — you know, Pietersen's 50 odd, so he's not a kid anymore — it means the grown-up sometimes having to take stuff on the chin from very young people who, given half a chance, you'd read the riot tattoo, and then take a step back and say, "How am I going to deal with this in a way that enables us to move forward?"

There is nothing in Kevin Pietersen's career as a cricketer, or indeed as a pundit since being a cricketer, that suggests that he's somebody who is ever able to subsume his own ego for the interests of other people. And that's why I think that this is a really dodgy move.

Talent vs Culture

So two thoughts. If you're looking at England cricket right now across any of the formats, are you looking at that group thinking you have under-optimized talent?

That talent is an issue for sure at test level. At white — in white ball cricket, it's interesting — when we've been very good at T20 we've been less good at 50 over cricket. When we've been very good at 50 over cricket we've struggled at T20. But broadly speaking, I would say over the last seven or eight years, white ball wise has not been such a car crash as it has been in the test arena.

Talent, I don't think, is the problem for England cricket. Culture is the problem.

Yeah.

Is Kevin Pietersen the person that you bring in to that dressing room as a mentor in any capacity to fix a culture problem?

No.

So that's why I find this interesting.

Not in my view.

Let's see. I mean, you know, instinctively — it's fun. Instinctively, it is fun and it all adds to the — G. And most importantly, can you — it just — KP's actually got a job at the ECB. [laughter]

I mean, the mind boggles. I mean, all I would ask is that by the time that somebody gets to a certain age, the likelihood that their character is going to change significantly diminishes, right?

Yeah.

Now, come from experience.

Can — yeah, for sure. Yes, indeed. That's absolutely fair point. Um, I think — can you mellow a little bit? Yes. But your underlying structures, the way in which your mind works, stays the same and hardens even. So, can someone change between the ages of 25 to 35? Yes. Perhaps you still are doing so. Um, let's hope. [laughter] Can someone really significantly change between the ages of 40 and 55? I don't think so.

Pietersen's Team Impact

And when you look at his impact on team environments, it's broken down into two parts. Number one, as a batsman and a fielder actually, he was so able to impact matches as a performer that people put up with him, right? Mostly — until they didn't, but mostly.

But mostly they did. Once he is no longer able to impact games as a performer, then you look at: well, what's been his impact on teams he's been in? Has he brought out the best in other players within team environments?

And you speak to players about what it was like to be part of a team with Kevin Pietersen. And the answer was, broadly speaking, if you yourself were an absolute top top top top top performer and you could take him on and tell him to shut the up — because you were good enough to be able to do that — okay, that might work. Anyone who was below his level talent-wise basically was swatted out of the way and regarded as being totally irrelevant.

So to — or had a personality that didn't quite fit his, and Andrew Strauss or Andy — and Andy Flower type comments when he was, you know, mean, rude, whatever it was about Flower — it was about him basically putting everyone to sleep, right? It was an attack on a personality.

Absolutely. Absolutely. Because of the ego. And that's my problem here — is that you're putting [clears throat] an explosive ego with an already explosive ego.

Yeah, I think McCullum is a bit more nuanced. He's certainly more of a people person. Most people seem to like him. You definitely cannot say that of Pietersen. You speak to players who have played in the past with McCullum, and they're like, "Oh, Baz is great. Love to go for a drink with him." Speak to players who have played with Pietersen before and they're like, "Brilliant player. Brilliant player. Can't stand the bloke."

And to put that into that dressing room is something which I just — I just don't see why — it what? — if that's the answer, what's the problem? Right, which comes back to my point of: if culture is the problem, this move looks odd.

Very much so.

If it's just to have a bit of fun and go, "Hey guys, we — KP's back in the fold because he can be great" — but that isn't what England needs right now, from my view.

The ECB's Structural Failures

It just seems to be yet another weird move by the elite side of the ECB. Now, we've given the ECB praise — what they did with the Hundred and the way in which from nothing they magicked up a billion — a billion quid worth of value to save the future of the county game. Brilliant. Fantastic. What an effort that has been.

But we've been consistently critical of the unstrategic and unstructured way in which the elite side of that setup is led. We haven't even covered what happened a few weeks ago.

So if you go back a bit for viewers and listeners who don't know — the England Lions is effectively like the England test second team.

You're talking about Freddy.

And it's meant to be a — for a bunch of young players who haven't quite yet made the test team, who are then put in an England environment and encouraged and brought along to get them ready to play test cricket for England.

So Rob Key makes his best mate Andrew Flintoff coach of that team, even though Flintoff's coaching credentials are wafer thin, right? He spent the majority of his time post-playing as a TV celebrity. Great, brilliant — but definitely he had not done the hard yards to become coach of the Lions team.

And having done it for a short period of time, and just before the Lions actually had an important bunch of matches, which they don't often have, Flintoff just walked out and said, "Actually, I'm done with that. Oh, and by the way, anyone who comes along after me is going to have big boots to fill."

It's like — it just makes me tear what remains of my hair out — is the culture that, under Rob Key, this extraordinary culture by which it's like, "Well, let's give this a go. Well, let's give that a go. Well, let's give this a go."

It's like: you've got to have a blueprint. You've got to have a piece of paper that says this is who we are, and over the following years this is how we're going to progress players, this is what we're aiming for, this is the mix we're aiming for, here are the challenges we currently face, here are structured strategic ways to answer those challenges. Right?

It's like, "Okay, well, we don't have a good spinner at the moment. Oh, apparently so-and-so saw this young kid doing well on YouTube the other day. Let's bring him into the England squad."

The whole thing is just so sloppy. And bringing KP in as an undefined no-accountability role — like, so if England do badly, which bit of that is he responsible for? Is he responsible if a batsman plays a poor shot? Don't know. Is he responsible if Harry Brook as captain makes poor decisions out on the field? Don't know. Is he responsible for selection? No. Like, what's he responsible for?

It's just — the whole thing is just so loose, and they never seem to learn. Just loose loose loose loose loose.

There we are.

County Championship: Somerset's Historic Chance

Yeah. Well, should we use it as a chance, um, while we're on cricket to have a look at the county championship? Because it's getting towards the end of the county championship season.

Very exciting. And there's some quite interesting team performances to take a look at, particularly teams that we've covered in the past.

Well, it's very exciting actually. It's a very exciting county championship, for lots of reasons, right?

Firstly, talking about the positive side. Um, it looks like Somerset, who famously have never won a county championship — could — I mean I know it's pretty tight at the top between them, Nottinghamshire and Warwickshire — but they could break that however century-plus-old hoodoo and win their first title. And it would be fantastic.

So for those who don't follow the county cricket game closely, Somerset are from a support perspective one of the big counties. Um, if I was to compare them to an English Premier League football club, it's like Spurs, right? They're not the very biggest, but…

I like Somerset —

but they're very big, but they never win anything. It's unfair. They —

You've saved it.

But they've won various one day trophies, but even back in the 70s and early 80s when they had Viv Richards, Ian Botham, Joel Garner playing for them, they never won the county championship. And over the last five, six, seven years, numerous times, they've been in a position where they've been really, really close to doing so, and they just keep on finishing second or third, can't quite get it over the line.

If I support any county team, I support Somerset, and I've been there twice this season. Great stadium. Um, big following.

Yes.

When you go to a Somerset game, it's often quite a big crowd, quite a big atmosphere. You really feel like for the West Country, this is — Oh, is that part of the world? Well, let's say the world — sorry, that part of England, isn't it, which isn't served by multiple sports assets. And so, the ones that do exist, they really encapsulate the fandom of the area — of the whole region — and you feel that you definitely down there in the cricket team.

And you think of the player — I mean, you know, Botham and that lot they've had attached to that county. They've had some amazing players.

Yeah. Marcus Trescothick. Interestingly, no England players at the moment, which I think has helped them — definitely — because they haven't been losing players from the county championship team into the England setup, which for example are Surrey who — shock, horror — are actually towards the bottom.

Surrey's Shocking Position

Right. So we just discussed the fact — we just discussed the fact that Somerset might win. Okay. So keep an eye on that because that would be historic and that would be, you know, a real big celebration down in the West Country.

But we've also got to look at a situation which was quite amusing — again similar to football over the last couple of seasons where Man United and Spurs were dicing with relegation. Two of the biggest three clubs are in trouble.

Surrey, who have been the perpetual champions of the last four or five years — I think they've won three of the last four.

'22, '23, '24, and then they came runner up last year.

Right. They're in danger of relegation from the first division to the second division. And then Lancashire — who would be the equivalent of Man United being — literally they play next to each other, so it's very opposite — are towards, well, they're second bottom in the second division.

Yeah.

Right. So that's the equivalent of Man United being relegated to the Championship and then being in danger of finishing towards bottom — Champion Leicester City um etc.

So it's a very dramatic season. I mean, were Surrey to get relegated it would be one of the biggest cricketing shocks that this country has ever seen. It's the most resourced county of all the counties.

Why Sporting Performance Doesn't Match Business Performance

Okay. Good point, because this is where the challenge, I think, of county championship comes.

Yeah.

So what, Charlie?

Yeah.

The business of Surrey I don't think gets damaged by a relegation, and that is part of the challenge that we have here with the county championship. So you were thinking as you were talking — you, Lancashire 7th of 8th, so they've gone down there — and then you're like, "Oh no, actually wait, I can't say then they go down again."

No.

Because we're in a two-tiered system here.

Yeah. And with Lancashire and Surrey you have two of the four biggest businesses, I think — you know, those two, um — Warwickshire —

Warwickshire and Hampshire —

Yorkshire.

Yeah.

Yorkshire. You put those guys together and you'll have half of the revenue across 18 first class counties. The majority of that comes from not just cricketing and performance on the pitch. It comes from hosting fees of test matches. It comes from hotels. It comes from conference and entertainment — as we discussed with Lancashire last time, which was a huge problem with the membership, right? They were very upset because the money wasn't being — all the time, the money, the attention wasn't on improving the cricket, it was in improving the business.

But that's because — to the executive side of it — the performance on the pitch doesn't mean that they are better or worse at the business. I mean, if Surrey go down, they don't suddenly lose a huge amount of money.

It's like the American franchise system, right? Which is: look, you know you're going to be one of the 18 professional outfits in the country. Um, there's no TV revenue involved here. Well, certainly no significant TV revenue — ECB handouts come, but you know, don't change that much.

Um, and as you say, those big counties have got such large non-county-cricket revenue streams from hosting other big events, whether it be cricket events or even non-cricket events. I mean, cripes — the number of times I've been to non-cricket events at the Oval would be like a lot. A lot of conferences, a lot of lunches and dinners and all this type of stuff get hosted at the Oval, um, which simply would not be the case at Taunton for Somerset.

Um, so you're absolutely right — from a business perspective, this is small beer. From a sporting perspective, it's a pure sporting story, not a business.

The Sporting-Financial Disconnect

But — and the challenge and the frustration of people who love their county cricket is that the cricket doesn't mean more…

Financially.

Financially. I think there's an element of sport which is meaningful for the sake just of sport. Right now, in other professional sport, of course that then translates — mostly tends to translate directly through into financial performance — although we're about to discuss the NFL, which arguably doesn't really.

Um, but if you were to start creating a lot of financial jeopardy in a sports ecosystem — in county cricket that is already [clears throat] very vulnerable — that might cause problems of different kinds.

Yeah. So they benefit from the fact that getting relegated doesn't ruin you. I mean, they definitely do — because if you were getting ruined, then the count — well, the count is in Div 2.

But you also mentioned, Charlie, that in Surrey's case for instance, a large chunk of their playing staff are off playing for England most of the summer. Um, so that symbiotic relationship between the counties and the ECB — with the ECB either providing direct funding or granting test matches to be held there, which provides other funding etc. — means that effectively the counties subjugate their own performance interests to England's performance interests.

Um, and therefore, if you were to make it more financially meaningful what happened within the county game, you would start to get a real tug-of-war happening.

Which sport does that happen in? Rugby. [clears throat] Rugby. You know, there's been real tugs of war, haven't there, between the clubs and the RFU about the players and, you know, when they get released and, you know, all that type of stuff.

In England, it's broadly — in English cricket, it's broadly understood: if the England squad needs a player, they go.

Lancashire's Ongoing Drama

The atmosphere must be boiling in Lancashire cricketing.

Oh, cripes. We actually haven't caught up recently in what's happened behind the scenes with all of their various EGMs and AGMs, and having to bring people in to sign documents on bank holidays and all this type of stuff.

One for Substack, maybe.

That is maybe one for Substack subsequently.

Closing Thoughts

But yeah, I think it's worth saying: look, Surrey have been terrifically successful over the last four or five years, and sometimes teams do go through cycles. And it feels like maybe Surrey's coming towards that point in the cycle where they've got a few, you know, they've got some players like Rory Burns and Sibley and these types of guys who have been around for quite a while, who've been in the England team in previous — who have then had a really good back end of their career playing really good candy for Surrey, but who are now in their mid-30s.

Yeah.

And that becomes a bit more challenging from a performance perspective. Meanwhile, losing Atkinson's, Lawrence, Jamie Smith, Pope's even out at the moment. So they are hampered right by the structure.

So look, they are pretty close, but I think there's a lot of teams — it's actually very tight down the bottom. You have Surrey, Essex, Yorkshire — I mean, Yorkshire right down, Leicestershire, Hampshire are pretty much done, I think.

Um, anyway — there we go. There we go. Keep an eye out. Keep an eye out for county championship for the next few weeks.

item.description:
## 一、"邪教后遗症"作为组织行为学诊断
Joe Root 那段 BBC 采访最惊人的地方，不是他说了什么，而是他 **在赢下系列赛之后依然像个受害者一样在为前任辩护**。主持人用"cult follower who lost his leader"来形容，看似戏谑，实则精准。心理学上有个概念叫"高控制群体退出综合征"（Post-Cult Trauma Syndrome）——被解救者在最初阶段往往会**过度美化过去的领袖**，因为承认"我们成就的一切都来自新起点"，等于承认过去四年被浪费。Root 三次重复"don't undervalue"，这不是感激，这是**认知失调**在自我修补。
## 二、一个反直觉的数学倒置：淘汰名单反而是胜利名单
节目主持人埋了一个惊人的事实但没有点破——**这两场胜利的英雄 Ollie Robinson 和 Jordan Cox，恰恰是被 Bazball 体系明确排斥的两人**。Robinson 在 McCullum 时代拥有全英最佳保龄均值却几乎不上场；Cox 在郡赛均值近 50 却从未获邀。也就是说：**新教练 Fleming 上任后取胜的公

item.title: [Dwarkesh Clips] When will AI be better than human experts?
item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、时间预测的"倒挂现象"：AI研究员比通用远程工作者更难被取代

最反直觉的观察来自这些研究者自己的预测：通用白领远程工作者只需1-3年被AI取代，但让AI研究员获得10倍效率提升竟需要2年，而完全超越人类AI研究员则需5-10年。这构成了一个令人震惊的"倒挂"——离AI最近、最懂如何优化AI的人，反而是最难被AI替代的。

这背后揭示了一个隐藏的系统性真相：能力的"可外包性"与任务的"决策熵"成反比。远程工作的本质是"执行已被压缩的决策"，而研究的本质是"在信息稀薄地带做贝叶斯最优判断"。Charlie一句"my capacity to absorb information and make the Bayesian optimal decision"——这不是"能不能做"的问题，是信息带宽本身的问题。

二、跨领域连接：这场对话与"官僚制度演化"惊人相似

有个跨领域的观察让我震撼：他们说"人们会改造组织让AI更容易使用，让你先走完80-90%的路"。这与马克斯·韦伯论官僚制、以及集装箱革命的历史有着诡异的同构关系。

集装箱并没有让船变快，而是让港口、卡车、仓库、法律条款全部重新塑形去适配那个标准化盒子。真正的生产力革命从来不是工具变强，而是世界为工具重新排列自己。所以AI取代白领的真正时间表，不取决于模型能力曲线，而取决于"组织的AI友好化改造速度"——这是一个社会学问题，不是技术问题。

更妙的是Byron那句"模型太nice，不会去凶别人把事情办成"——这暗示着一个残酷的真相：职场里很大一部分"生产力"来自不可言说的社会压力施加能力，这部分能力AI最难学，因为它在训练数据里通常被标记为"负面"。

三、"长尾之战"与达尔文式的能力孤岛

一个被低估的洞见是Charlie反复提到的"long tail of miscellaneous stuff"。表面看这是关于AI能力覆盖的技术问题，深层却是一个认识论问题：人类专业能力的分布不是高斯的，而是幂律加长尾的混合分布。

这里有个"啊哈时刻"：他们讨论TSMC工程师、机械工程、3D空间推理时表现出的犹豫，暴露了当代AI研究一个未被言明的偏见——大部分AI进展发生在"数据丰饶带"（代码、数学、文本），而人类文明的关键节点技能反而生长在"数据饥荒带"。芯片制造、外科手术、地质勘探这些卡脖子领域，其知识以师徒制口耳相传，从未被大规模数字化。

这意味着一个悖论：AI越强，越会突显那些"没被数字化的关键知识"的战略价值。未来最值钱的可能不是会用AI的人，而是掌握着"AI进不去的知识飞地"的人——这些飞地不是因为难，而是因为"没人费心把语料库建起来"。Byron最后那句"AI will have vastly greater experience than any human"其实反过来才是关键：在没有语料的地方，AI永远只是新手。

📝 转录文本

引子：一场关于AI时间表的快问快答

Super rapid fire predictions about the future. So I want timelines on the following couple questions.

问题一：AI何时能成为"即插即用的远程工作者"？

By when do we have models which — here's what it feels like to a user: you basically hire them as a drop-in remote worker for all kinds of white collar work, not just coding but I don't know, video editing, law, paralegal, etc. Like it's literally an actual remote worker with full computer use, with literally a month of seamless learning and operation and executing on complex projects, and it required interacting with other people etc etc. It's like everything a human worker could do over a month.

回答一：

If you like mandated to use like a browser or whatever rather than the firm setting up the information to be programmatically accessible — maybe a couple years. But if it's not browser-based, like it can send Slack messages, it can do all this stuff, I'd still probably say around a year.

回答二：

Yeah. I mean, I would say maybe for the full generality maybe like three years, but I think to Charlie's point, we will end up with a lot of people making their organizations easier for the AIs to use, and so you get 80–90% of the way there before that.

一年 vs 三年的差别在哪？

So, but the thing that's the diff between one year and three years there was just literally like — I think there's going to be a long tail of miscellaneous stuff which some human can do which will take the models quite a while to do.

Yeah. Like you mean sort of computer stuff or basic cognitive capabilities?

I mean I think this really comes down to a question of how quickly can we solve this kind of online learning, and whether we can get 80–90% of the way there with compaction and writing files to yourself and stuff. And that's my big uncertainty. I really don't know.

一个模型不擅长的例子：施压他人

And maybe an example of something that I wouldn't be good at is — you know, if I have to yell at someone to get something at work, or really push someone to get something done, the model isn't just going to do that. It's just going to be too nice.

人类远程工作者本身质量差异巨大

Yeah. I'd say there's a wide variation in quality of human remote workers. So if you try to hire someone off of Upwork to do a software engineering project, there's going to be a huge variation. It's often quite hard to get them to do a good job or pay attention to all the feedback you're getting.

And I would guess that in some cases the pre-AI version of this was worse than what you can get now from existing AI. So I think it might end up being a little complicated because maybe to some extent we already have this for some not-so-high quality of work, but then obviously we're not matching human level in certain higher quality forms of work.

But I basically agree with Charlie and Byron that maybe we'll have some version of this in a year or so that's okay, and it will be able to do — maybe we'll have that form factor — and it'll be able to do some things really well, some things not so well, and things will be improving from there.

目标线的移动与已经实现的部分

Like we achieved the goalpost based on the very long tail all the time. I feel like you've used this example before of doing your taxes or something. Like this year I literally just told Codex to go get everything I needed to do and send it to the accountant, and there was this massive list of stuff it had to use computer just to click through and download some stuff, and it didn't — it was fine. It was perfect. So I don't know, a lot of this stuff it can already do.

问题二：AI何时能带来10倍生产力提升？

Okay. Give you 10x total productivity uplift. Basically if it takes you a year to make a breakthrough now, you make a breakthrough every month.

回答：

I think I would just refuse to give you a scalar on this. Like we might already be past that in some types of work. Let's say you're trying to prove — yeah, you're trying to do certain types of math.

追问：对AI研究员本身的加速呢？

I was — sorry, but for you as AI researchers trying to advance the state of AI research, how much are AI researchers sped up or uplifted?

Somewhere between five and 10 years.

Oh really, that's far away. You think it's longer than for a general remote worker?

Yeah.

Interesting.

定义澄清

I think you probably — I'm realizing you probably have very different definitions of fully general remote worker.

I could have specified. Yeah, this is true, because an AI researcher can be a remote worker and so —

Yeah. No, I'm picturing normal white collar work over the period of a month.

Yeah. I think it starts to diverge a little bit past a month. Like a very competent white collar worker but not necessarily a super creative researcher.

I would say like two years.

Two years. Yeah. 10x. Okay.

Byron的补充视角

How about you, Byron? I can kind of see that actually, because right now it's already definitely more than 10x of coding stuff, and so it's like if it can do even one or two loops of experimental feedback, that would actually be massive already.

对AI研究进展的连锁影响

So 10x uplift of AI researchers within two years — if you just plug it into a very naive model of AI progress and how much is coming from AI researchers, and there's a 10x increase in their productivity — you have a radically accelerated pace of AI progress starting 2 years from now.

Yeah. I mean I think this will mean that AI progress doesn't get bottlenecked on AI researchers' ability to run small experiments. It gets bottlenecked on other things.

Of course. Of course. But it just happens 10x faster.

For sure. Yeah.

Which is a huge deal. And that also helps the next thing which gives you 100x speedup happen sooner, etc.

Yeah. I'm happy to stick with longer on that one.

瓶颈的核心

And what's the crux?

Like my capacity to absorb information and make the Bayesian optimal decision on the next experiment.

Makes sense.

Yeah. I mean I'm assuming that you can delegate some of this to the AI. So the AI is becoming decent at deciding "okay, run this experiment, it's got this result, run the next experiment," and then if it can run two or three experiments in a row without crashing, then that is actually a big uplift.

问题三：AI何时全面超越顶尖人类专家？（即ASI）

And okay, final question. An AI which dominates top human experts across every single field of work that can be done over a computer. So not only research but all cognitive work, and not just short horizon work but literally if it takes three years or something, they will still do better than humans.

This is basically just like ASI. Okay.

I would say like three or four years.

[laughter] I mean that doesn't seem wrong.

领域差异分析

I would say AI is obviously getting more attention, so it's one of the harder things but a lot of energy is being put into it, and it's also not one of the hardest things for AI because it involves a lot of code and math which models are really good at.

Maybe for things that involve 3D and spatial stuff and physical stuff, that will take a little longer. Especially if it's like mechanical engineering or something and it's not getting the most attention right now, that might take a little longer.

数据稀薄领域的挑战

But it also doesn't include fields where there is relatively little data because of the nature of the field, and it has to learn that data on the fly. So for example, it has to become superhuman at being an engineer at TSMC or something.

Oh yeah. So you would have to assume that the onboarding — you can give the AI the same onboarding material — and then there's something has to be solved about longer horizon learning.

Yeah. Five to 10.

自动化AI研究 = ASI完备？

So basically you think automating AI research is ASI-complete or something?

Yeah, I think so. I think there's so many things in the world which — even if you have some sort of memory system external to the model, and even if context length grows a little bit — there are just fundamentally things where, even if you could research the information or write notes yourself, you need more than the context to be able to do.

Yeah.

长尾的最后一公里

I mean I kind of agree in the five year range at least for the stuff that labs are focusing on, but I think there's going to be a long tail of stuff which the AI could theoretically go out and learn about, but no one has bothered to do it and the compute hasn't been allocated to that. So that might take longer for literally every single human expert.

Yeah. And sorry, but by this I also included the ability to learn as fast as a human — a new domain.

I mean, I think that's not necessarily necessary actually, because the AI will have vastly greater experience than any human.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips.

观看原视频 →
