item.description:
## 一个诡异的自指循环：股市自己在制造促使加息的通胀
这期视频最值得停下来盯着看的一个数据点，是被主持人一笔带过的：**Portfolio Management（资产管理服务）同比通胀 20%+**，是核心 PCE 里增速最高的三项之一。
这意味着什么？**股市涨得越好，资产管理费收入越高，这一分项的服务通胀就越高，就越可能倒逼美联储加息，然后加息又要来打压股市。** 这是一个漂亮的索罗斯式"反身性回路"——股市把自己的涨势变成了对自己的绞索。华尔街分析师们习惯把 CPI/PCE 当外生变量分析，但其实核心通胀里嵌了一根反馈线，通向标普500自己。
更进一步的讽刺：**AI 资本开支推涨 memory / computer accessory 通胀，AI 又推涨股价，股价又通过 portfolio management 推涨通胀。** 现在的核心通胀里，三大高增速分项——机票（战争）、存储（AI 资本开支）、资产管理（股市自身）——全部与美联储的加息工具"绝缘"：加息压不住战争，压不住 AI 花钱，只有第三条能被间接打断。**美联储手里的锤子，只能敲通胀这台机器的一个齿轮。**

item.title: [a16z] Why Investors Are Rethinking Everything for the AI Era
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、资本从"毒药"变"催化剂"——一次悄然的相变

DG 这段话值得反复咀嚼：过去毁掉一家 startup 的最好方法，是给它太多钱——它会去雇一千个人，然后被协调成本和优先级冲突撕碎。但今天你可以把钱直接扔给算力，算力自己会去把产品和业务变好。

这不是"AI 让创业更容易"那种口水话。这是资本形态本身发生的相变：从"资本 → 人 → 协作 → 产出"这条充满摩擦的链条，变成了"资本 → 算力 → 产出"这条几乎无摩擦的直线。历史上只有一次类似的转折——从手工作坊过渡到蒸汽/电力驱动的工厂时，资本第一次可以"线性买到产能"。今天 AI 让脑力劳动第一次拥有了这种线性性质。这也解释了为什么幂律突然如此极端：当资本的边际收益不再被组织熵吃掉，赢家就真的会拿走一切。

二、LP 的"卡夫卡困境"——一套注定跑输的激励系统

Jen 讲了一段最刺眼的真相：GP 的错误是"遗漏之罪"（miss the next Uber → 被开除），LP 的错误是"承担之罪"（投错了一支基金 → 被开除）。这两种激励在数学上是完全反向的。

结果就是：LP 系统性地会在幂律最极端的年份最保守——因为此时"承担风险"的心理成本最高。而 3000 家 VC 里只有 20 家能持续做出 3x 净回报，也就是说 LP 只要没接触到那 0.67%，就注定拿平均水平（1–2x，锁十年）。这构成了一个残酷的悖论：LP 越努力"专业地分散、专业地评估"，就越可能远离那 20 家。

这个模式跨领域出现过：科学基金评委倾向于资助"稳妥的增量研究"而错过范式突破；企业里"创新者的窘境"；甚至公务员系统的"多做多错、少做少错"——都是同一种"稳定性筛选机制在变革期反向失灵"。venture 只是它最纯粹、最贵的显影版本。

三、编程是一个"陷阱信号"——为什么老 SaaS 死得没那么快

DG 藏了一个几乎没被听众抓住的、极重要的观察：Coding 之所以率先被 AI 攻陷，是因为它同时满足三个稀有属性——完美文档化（perfectly documented）、可验证（verifiable）、可仿真（simulatable）。而商业世界里绝大多数知识工作，一个都不占。

这个洞察一旦你意识到，很多现象就重排了： - 为什么 AlphaGo/AlphaFold 先突破？ 围棋和蛋白折叠恰好也同时满足这三条。 - 为什么律师、放射科医生、程序员先被"打到"？ 他们的工作输出可被复核。而销售、管理、心理咨询——你永远不知道那个决策的反事实，AI 就无法快速自我迭代。 - 为什么公开 SaaS 市场没死透？ 因为 AI 向"三属性不全"的领域扩散会慢得多——"coding 被打穿"是个前兆信号，但不是普适速率。

这意味着一个反直觉的投资推论：最先看起来"最危险"的传统软件公司，很可能反而是最后倒下的——因为它们服务的工作流恰恰缺少这三个属性。而市场目前正在用同一把尺子给所有 SaaS 打折，这里面藏着定价错配。

四、被忽视的连接：AI 的瓶颈不是芯片，是"美国的物理速度"

Ron 最后一句几乎是随口带过的："美国不缺发电，缺的是 speed to power——审批、传输、监管。别的国家一年建 10x 的可再生装机容量。"

把这句话和前面所有讨论叠加起来，你会看到一个几乎没人明说的宏观图景：AI 时代第一次让"监管硬化"直接、实时、可测量地转化为国家竞争力损失。过去高铁、核电、住房建不出来，代价是"生活质量慢了 10 年"——温水煮青蛙。但 AI 训练需要电、需要变电站、需要在 18 个月内拉起来——监管延迟的成本从"慢性病"变成了"急性心梗"。

这也解释了为什么 a16z 开始做"美国机器时代"基金：投资的边界从"数字"重新回到"原子"，不是因为原子突然性感了，而是因为原子是数字继续增长的物理前提条件。这是一次典型的"限制转移"——瓶颈换位置时，价值也会跟着换位置。

📝 转录文本

冷开场 / Cold Open

"We've looked at the data of 3,000 venture capital firms in the US. Only 20 have achieved consistent 3x net returns over the last two decades."

"Right now, clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last 10 to 20 years of technology investing. For the first time, you can take capital and throw it at a company and it compounds their advantage."

"AI is attacking every facet of the GDP — transportation, labor, services, capital, coordination. There hasn't been a technology paradigm that hits on 30 trillion in GDP at the same time. Elon has talked publicly about Grockbot; on Sam's side, he's talked about Astra and some of the long-running capabilities that are going to come out soon."

"What do you think is going to be the next hundred-trillion-dollar market cap company?" "It is possible that…"

主持人开场 / Host Intro

Welcome back to the A16Z podcast. Something fundamental has changed in how value gets created.

Power law used to be just a feature of a cottage industry in venture capital, and now it's systemic throughout. And particularly the three frontier model companies — SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic — represent somewhere between three-and-a-half to 5 trillion dollars of potential enterprise value.

And shockingly, before SpaceX went public, a lot of our LPs and also the broader institutional allocator community didn't have a lot of exposure to it. And so we'll talk about today why potentially portfolio construction and asset allocation may have changed, why power law is not just only in the venture capital industry, and then particularly where and how value actually compounds today.

David George, Ron, Verdian — thank you for joining me.

"Great to be here. Thanks for hanging out." "Thank you for having us here."

一、幂律为何前所未有地极端 / Why the Power Law Is More Extreme Than Ever

Okay, so DG — if you add up every venture-backed IPO for the last six years, all of them together, where does it go from here?

DG: Right now clearly the power law is more extreme than it has been in the last, you know, 10 to 20 years of technology investing — probably going back to the emergence of the network-effect-driven consumer companies. There are many reasons why that's the case.

Increasing returns to scale have always been a dynamic in our business. Obviously it's well covered how a network-effect business can have increasing returns to scale, but so can software businesses — right? And they can take different forms, but brand, reputation in the market, the accumulation of resources, all provide competitive advantages. That all still is the case.

But right now, especially with the labs, for the first time in my career you can take capital and throw it at a company and it compounds their advantage.

And this is a thing — like, how do you screw up a startup? Well, you know, throw too much money at it and have them hire a thousand people, and then you create all these coordination issues and overhead issues and dueling priorities and it sort of gets messed up, because you can't hire enough people to do enough things fast enough.

Now that's not the case. You can throw dollars at compute, and compute can make products and the businesses better. And so to me, it's not terribly surprising that the power law is more extreme. Right now, economies of scale are a very real thing in the AI market, and I think will continue to be the case.

二、十年之礼 & 资产配置的重估 / Ten-Year Gift & Rethinking Allocation

Host: So, Ron — you're not just one of our longtime LPs at accolade, but incidentally, it's been exactly 10 years since you were actually an employee of A16Z. And so for your 10-year anniversary, I've brought this gem back.

"Oh my god. Oh my gosh. This is amazing. Why do you still have this?"

So we dug in the catacombs, and we made this extra-large version just for posterity. I can't believe that I got this from the catacombs.

But incidentally, during the last 10 years, a lot has changed in the world. And if you remember, at that point in time, people were belly-aching about fund sizes being too large back then.

"And you had one at a billion." "The first one at a billion. First venture fund. Exactly."

A lot has happened since then. How do you think about your venture portfolio juxtaposed against your private equity one? And then just also generally, asset allocation. If you were to start from a blank sheet of paper again knowing what you know now, how would you have constructed differently?

Ron: Yeah, let's take venture today. We've reached 100 billion in revenue in AI. It took SaaS 15 years to get to the same point. AI did that in four years — and we're not even close to anywhere in terms of the penetration of demand.

The reason DG is saying you can throw capital at it — that's a function of unlimited demand for inference. And we are at a point where AI is attacking every facet of the GDP: transportation, labor, services, capital, coordination. There hasn't been a technology paradigm that hits on 30 trillion in GDP at the same time.

So you have the fastest-growing technology, it's hitting on all parts of the GDP. As an allocator, it's hard not to make the case that it's not a satellite position — you should be core or a super-core in some shape or form.

DG: I'm very biased, but if you just think about the shape of the markets and how they've changed since I started my career — you know, in private equity and growth equity, that was I guess 18 years ago — this was a cottage industry, and now it's not. Our asset class is 5-to-6 trillion dollars of value. And the dynamics around companies staying private longer, they're not going to reverse.

"You had that insight in 2019 when you left G. It's venture-like outcomes in late stage, which is now happening." "So it's no longer just early stage and you IPO when you have 100 million in revenues."

DG: The top-decile outcomes, I think, used to be 10 billion and now they're like 40 billion.

"Or soon to be probably 100 billion by the time Anthropic and then OpenAI come out."

Yeah. And look, this makes sense, right? The last cycle created 25 trillion of market cap — new market cap — and a bunch of that went to the incumbents. But a lot of it went to the new startups. And each one of these subsequent waves gets bigger than the prior one. So our expectation is: take the 25 trillion, and it's going to be a larger number.

三、AI 的 TAM 究竟有多大 / What Is the Real TAM of AI

Host: I'm constantly confused about the TAM of AI. Would love your thoughts.

Take healthcare. Healthcare spends like 60 to 100 billion on healthcare IT per year. But AI is hitting on actual labor and the value of tasks being performed in healthcare — claims, billing, administration. That's a trillion-dollar industry.

So the TAM of AI can be 10x-plus bigger than traditional SaaS or healthcare IT. What is that value? Well, what's the economic value of a task being performed — that's the TAM you're looking at. And then there's some capture rate that the AI company will take.

But we have no idea how big the TAM can get. Every wave, the incumbents are 10x smaller over time. So it's hard to estimate — but I can tell this for myself: I've been chronically wrong about how big these outcomes can get.

DG: Same here. Yeah, labor. If you just look at how much dollars are spent in the US economy on labor versus software — it's something like 40 times more. Now, that doesn't mean, importantly, that labor is going to go away. Labor is just going to get reinvented, and so we'll end up with a reimagination of the tasks that humans do.

But I think that's actually the whole point of AI — you're going after this different thing. And so to equate it to software and say "oh, it's the next evolution of software" is far too limiting.

Host: Our legal counsel says to us often, "I love Harvey. All my clients think they're lawyers now and they can actually spar with me on topics where they would have probably been like, 'I don't really understand this, I'm just going to defer to you.' So my billable hours have only gone up with the advent of the usage of AI."

All those use cases are massively, massively probably underappreciated — and we still don't even know.

"They're expansionary. That's the whole point."

四、"每一层都会赢"——反零和思维 / Everything Might Work

And then there was this whole thesis where "well, Frontier Labs are going to cannibalize the apps — which layer is going to win?" Turns out everyone is sort of growing.

DG: A friend of mine did a podcast where he described it like "everything is going to work" kind of thing. I describe it slightly differently, but we get questions all the time from LPs: "Which layer in the stack is going to work?" And I'm kind of like, I don't know — the market is going to be so big. I think everything might work.

Now, there's going to be a lot of companies that don't work, and there may be idiosyncratic categories that don't work. But by and large, it's far too limiting to think, "oh, if open source does a good job, it's bad for the labs" and vice versa. So we try to remove ourselves from thinking in a zero-sum way like that.

Host: Why do people think it's going to be winner-take-all? The last era of technology, it was probably winner-take-all in a lot of categories, but this feels categorically different because we're re-underwriting a lot of the fundamentals.

DG: Winner-take-all is an interesting way to describe it. If you look at the market-cap growth of all the leading technology companies — there are many that were successful. It wasn't winner-take-all.

There's an important distinction: we very much are believers in the power law within a given category. The winners will capture the vast majority of the market share and market cap, and second place is playing for scraps. But I think we'll see a massive expansion of the number of categories that we have.

Go back 20 years — CRM was not really a category. I mean, it was small — Siebel Systems and things like that. Now it's a massive category. The same thing will happen.

Our approach: we can tolerate loss. If we're not losing money in a given fund on a given amount of investments, we're not taking enough risk. If you look at our best-performing venture funds over time, I think the loss rate is 60%.

"Or so." "On early stage."

At the growth stage, the loss rate will be lower — probably in the 10 to 20% range. And that's appropriate, because with that you'll get investments that 10x or more. So if we're doing a good job, we're backing the leading company in every category that is a credible category.

五、20/3000 —— 一致性的残酷数学 / The Brutal Math of Consistency

Host: A lot of folks often think that things are overheated in the moment, and then you look back in retrospect and it turns out everything was actually quite cheap. You advise a lot of your LPs on the importance of consistency in venture capital — probably even more than any other asset class.

Ron: The extremeness of the power law that DG talked about — if you as an allocator have not had access to the top 5 to 10 companies over the last 5 to 10 years, you're significantly behind in terms of returns.

Let's take a step back. We've looked at the data of 3,000 venture capital firms in the US. Only 20 have achieved consistent 3x net returns over the last two decades.

"Sorry, say that one more." "20 — less than 1%. Consistent 3x net returns." "That's incredible."

And it's actually — you don't need seven, eight funds in those 20 years. It was: do you have three-to-four 3x-net-TVPI funds over a 20-year period? We found only 20 firms that have done that. Consistency in venture is really, really hard.

What's interesting is the consistent ones consistently had access to the category-defining companies every vintage. Now, there are exceptions, and just having the logo is not sufficient. If you're early stage and you have a large fund, you need to own enough of it. If you're late stage — DJ, I'm curious if you agree — sizing is really critical.

Venture-like returns are possible in late stage, but your best company should be 5-10%-plus of your fund. That way you can actually return the fund on a single company. Fund-returning math in late stage didn't exist before. It now does.

So the ones that consistently have gotten access are in that top 20 out of 3,000. If you don't have them, there's a huge dispersion. The average venture return over the last 10 years, per Cambridge data, is 1 to 2x. You'll do better in private equity. You'll definitely do better in the public markets — and you don't need to lock up your money for 10 years.

六、"中间地带的死亡" / Death of the Middle

I just pulled up a tweet from our friend Eddie who posted this morning:

"Interest in big VC funds has been driven by founders, not LPs. Founders more often than not want the brand that can scale, be a lifecycle investor, and help land customers/hires. LPs have slowly followed along, but most are still dragging their heels — because it actually is counter to conventional wisdom."

Ron: And the outcomes are larger, so funds can be larger. There are some exceptions in those 20 — some small firms focused on niche vertical markets, or playing at a stage so much earlier than the bigger firms. The problem with that strategy: you have to stay consistent in terms of fund size and strategy. If you start getting bigger, you bump into the big firms and it becomes really hard to stay consistent.

"Death of the middle." "Death of the middle. We said we were going to drink every time we said death of the middle."

DG: I'm very complimentary of many of our peers in the venture ecosystem. But this "death of the middle" thing — how do you define it? What's the middle?

The highly specialized funds — some of the ones that were very early to AI with deep, deep domain experts — have done a pretty good job. Sometimes they can move fast, get into things, or take shares of deals that we want to do.

Then there's the large-scale venture — in the sense that we have many product lines and we can scale all the way from a seed to when you go public. We have some peers who employ a similar strategy.

Everything else in between that, I think, struggles to compete a little bit — for the reasons Eddie said. What does the founder care about? The founder cares about taking capital from a partner that they think can de-risk the outcome for themselves. That is the simplest way to describe what the founder really cares about.

Now they care about the partner — the government person. So you have to be a good actor. But there's a reason we build up a tremendous amount of resources. That's why we have 700 employees. That's why we take the management fees on our funds and invest them in operating resources — because we think it will (1) bend the curve on the outcome, and (2) help us to win deals.

Our business is a flywheel. It starts with: are we deep domain experts? Do we have the right point of view? Can we demonstrate to the founder that we are the right partner? If so, we win the deal. If we can help make the outcome better — great. Two things happen: (1) our business has persistence of returns partially because the new founder wants to be around the winners; (2) by being part of the winners, we create killer references, and founders tell other founders, "you should work with these folks." That's the way the flywheel works.

七、种子基金与大厂能否共存 / Can Seed Firms and Mega-Funds Coexist?

Host: One theory — curious to get both your takes: pre-seed / seed. Sub $20-40M valuation, sub-$100M funds. They can coexist with the big firms, because at inception stage there might be seven AI companies doing the same thing. A large firm like a16z would want to wait a round or two until there's more relative certainty — you have to be in the category winner, so you'd rather wait, double down, and lead the A or the B.

So the small firms can carve out a niche a clip or two earlier than the big firms. Do you agree?

DG: Yeah. We have very healthy relationships with seed funds across the ecosystem. We also do seed ourselves. But pre-seed for sure — earlier than we typically do.

"The seed you would do is like chunkier, bigger seed — a serial entrepreneur." "That definitely is our — but we have our Speedrun program, which we just came from earlier this morning."

Host: The market is evolving. Because founders have such a preferential attachment to the brands, we get to look at everything, and sometimes it makes sense for us to do pre-seed and seed. You want that flex of capability. For the founder, they don't really care where your focus is — they just want to be in that orbit.

Our business is principally an early-stage business. We have to be first to the pole. We may not actually do the investment, but we have to at least understand the landscape and market to be able to make informed decisions later on.

I spoke to a few founders at Speedrun today, and they very much are hoping to stay in the orbit long-term. It's virtually impossible to have a mid-stage business effectively without having the early stage and also the late stage behind it.

DG: I'm very biased, but I think the reason we've been successful as a growth fund is because of our early-stage business. Our business starts and ends with early stage. That provides tremendous advantages at growth stage — access, information, knowledge, relationships. And our early-stage partners would probably say the growth business provides them benefits too, because it allows us to scale up and deepen partnerships with founders over time.

Ron: We're big believers that the strongest late-stage franchises have a huge early-stage franchise attached to them. The ability to win is multiplied when you have an early-stage franchise. It's really hard to come in as a de novo late-stage firm and write a $500 million check.

八、AI 让 VC 的工作更难 / AI Is Making Venture Harder Than Ever

Host: How do you think about, from the LP seat, how venture is fundamentally perhaps a structurally different job than when you started your career?

Ron: In a very simplistic way, there's in our mind four ways to do venture: 1. Pre-seed / seed — sub-$150M funds. Close to 2,000 today in the US alone. 2. The messy middle — hundreds of firms. 3. The big firms. 4. Dedicated late stage.

We've done the larger firms for decades. We've done the seed firms. We've selectively done a few in the messy middle. And we haven't done dedicated late stage for the reasons we talked about.

How is it changing? AI is actually making our jobs harder than ever before. Rounds are larger. They're faster. The traction happening in the industry is confusing. Here's why:

A company comes out of pick-your-accelerator. "I went from zero to five million ARR in a month." There's no renewal cycle yet. They're raising off of that traction at huge multiples. A lot of times they're selling to each other in a cohort. And it's not even ARR — they're multiplying by 12.

But for every nine companies like that, there's one really special one doing a couple of million in ARR — actual ARR — that has a huge valuation, that will go on to be the next Cursor. So it is really, really tough today to parse out what's real traction and what's not.

Valuations are really high. This is why the big firms do well. They can wait, or they have enough relative certainty in the next round to lead it. But even then there isn't a lot of certainty. When you guys did Cursor, I don't think there was a lot of certainty. And for how many months were people saying Cursor is dead?

"Even the morning of the acquisition announcement, people were still saying Cursor is dead. I'm like, they just announced they were going to be acquired by SpaceX for 60."

"Tell me if I'm wrong — 3 million ARR, $400 million round, or somewhere around there." "Yeah, something like that."

A lot of people would say, "that's crazy, why did they do that deal?"

九、如何识别真需求 / How to Tell Real Traction from Noise

DG: Founder judgment is a very important thing. Getting to know founders over time, spending a lot of time with them, seeing how they think — I'd like to think my early-stage partners are pretty good at that.

Secondly, it is hard to parse out real versus misleading traction — misleading in the sense that you can't take market signal from it. Not that anybody's doing any misleading.

"There's probably some of that too." "Yeah, there's probably some of that too."

"I love every now and then people are like helping to redefine what ARR actually means." "This is always helpful."

I don't know — come back to: is the market demanding more of your product? That is always the question. That's a Post-It note on my computer screen.

How do you know that when the company's only been operating or selling for a couple of months? You're not going to be able to do it with financial analysis. You'll have to do it by really understanding the customers, talking to the customers.

Take Harvey. They did a really good job commercially early days — smart, research-plus-lawyer combo. They got some high-profile law firms to sign up early. But usage was not very good. If you looked at actual deployment, it looked mediocre compared to other software firms.

"From a retention standpoint?" "Not retention — no, usage of it."

Fast forward, post-reasoning models — that totally flipped. You could see absolute takeoff of adoption. A bunch of different things happened at the same time. Lawyers got way more value out of the product. You could see it in usage and engagement. It became — because it was high-utility usage and engagement — it almost flipped from "we're scared of things like hallucinations" to "no, no, no, every client is actually demanding the law firms use the product."

We look for markets like that. We try to catch them earlier than we did at Harvey. But that's the kind of signal we look for. Everyone can do cohort analysis. Everyone can look at renewal data. But understanding the texture of the market — what the customers actually want, need, and their alternatives — that's how you make the decision. That's why it's so important to have the early-stage business. They're the deepest in the technology and the products.

十、LP 的最大顾虑 / What LPs Are Pushing Back On

Host: Jen, you're the most prolific fundraiser I know. What's the biggest push-back you're getting from LPs on the state of AI, the state of venture?

"You could be very gainfully employed at this firm." "I agree that you are a prolific fundraiser."

A lot of it is worries around: are we catching a falling knife here? Just the timing of the market, are things overheated?

But I do get a lot of sentiment from the LPs that their job is also about to fundamentally change. One aspect: AI making it more challenging to evaluate opportunities and funds. The other aspect: the LP historically has not been incentivized to actually embrace change. This is a job where the end goal is somewhat diametrically opposed with the risk tolerance of the GP.

I often say: a GP can get fired for missing out on the next Facebook, the next Uber. That is the error of omission — that is fireable.

But LPs on the flip side only get fired if you invest into a manager. In some respects the incentive outcomes are actually completely opposite.

"You don't get fired for investing in IBM if you're an LP."

Exactly. And in fact, you don't potentially even get fired for not investing at all. If you miss the frontier models, but you kind of are along the benchmark — maybe slightly below the benchmark — you're keeping your job.

And for a lot of folks, the upside actually is not that interesting to them. So the pitch of "hey, you're going to miss out on the next generation" — the incentive misalignment is actually quite direct.

So where do we go from here in terms of the LP role? I think we also have an important role and function. We often talk about our job as a leader of the venture capital industry: we have to help folks understand where the future is going. And part of that is understanding how to infiltrate not just within their venture capital allocation but across their entire portfolio.

十一、准入、选择、组合规模 / Access, Selection, Sizing

Ron: Access, selection, sizing is what LPs do.

  • Access — you could argue you have the data to figure out who has done well historically out of those 20 firms out of 3,000. Like, you are going to see consistency — right? Maybe half of them are consistent. But the LP's job is also to find the next-gen firms as well as continue accessing that.
  • Selection.
  • Portfolio construction / sizing — critical from an LP standpoint.

Because if you have an asset class where 20 firms out of 3,000 do well, you should concentrate in those 15-20 firms pretty consistently. When I see a portfolio with 50, 60, 70 venture capital firms, it's very hard for me to imagine the overall portfolio can generate better than the average.

And going back to the average in venture — that's just not compelling enough for the liquidity, relative to public markets or private equity. Private equity can probably get you 1.5 to 2x net without the lockup, without the risk. You talked about 60% loss ratio — PE doesn't have that.

PE has other problems we can talk about today when it comes to AI software. But portfolio construction sizing for an LP is critical. I've seen too many times an LP find an interesting fund, actually get it right, and put 1% of their fund into it. Great — you 10x'd it. It returns 10% of your fund. It does not move the needle at all.

十二、公开市场的信号：AI 弹性 / Public Markets Signal: AI Resilience

Host: Where do you all think we are in that evolution — the appropriate percentage of overall capital allocated to venture and growth compared to private equity, public markets, real assets, credit?

DG: This is hard for me to answer because all I do is venture growth. I would be biased to say it should be supersized.

"We like that answer though."

Ron: Look at the public markets today. We vibe-coded something that created a great way for us to assess AI resiliency of public companies. And now we're doing that on the private side — it's helping us hugely in our growth equity portfolio.

In the SaaS public markets, there are only like 15 to 20 companies max trading above 10 times revenues — which is by an insane number, because it used to be dozens and dozens a few years ago. And every one of those companies for the most part is showing acceleration of growth from AI — you're either in monitoring, security, deployment of agents, etc.

So the same principle: if you are in some shape or form tied to AI — which is the fastest-growing facet of all the elements of the GDP — then you should supersize it in your portfolio.

Even private equity today, when doing a new investment, is looking for something AI-native. They're not looking to buy a workflow software company growing 10% that's seed-based. They're looking for the system of record that can show acceleration with an AI-native management team.

That connective tissue of AI is actually across every asset class today. And the strongest way to play it is probably through venture. But that's where selection, access, and portfolio construction is really critical.

十三、退出与流动性 / Exits and Liquidity

Even the exits — we were talking about Silver Lake potentially buying Workday, doing more provocative things in private equity land when you have the capabilities to infuse and bring them into the future.

The other version: exits in venture now way exceed private equity. I was looking this up last night. Private equity this year — the biggest exits are the buyout of EA (~$50 billion) and Medline (~$50 billion). Cursor — let's exclude the IPOs. The Cursor M&A sale to SpaceX was way bigger than that.

You look at the pre-ChatGPT vintages in private equity. You would have paid, I don't know, 15 to 20 times EBITDA for a software asset growing 10-20% max. If you look at the public markets today, that asset is trading at two times revenue.

The problem is not just the valuation — there might not be a buyer for that company. If you're looking at a software company today, the first thing you think about is: what is the terminal value? Is it resilient from AI?

The best way to show that is organic growth acceleration. Our data shows 1 percentage of growth in the public markets is equivalent to 3 percentages of EBITDA.

"By the way — it's funny, because in COVID, everyone was like, 'we need to be profitable.'" "In '21 it was the inverse. Post-, it's basically fully aligned with risk. Correlated with risk in the public."

Unfortunately, a lot of those private equity deals — they're not growing fast enough, not showing acceleration, and may not have the management teams to revamp the business. What Intercom did is a great example. Bring the founder back, revamp the whole business, create an AI-native product, scale it, and then sell. It's almost like you're suiciding your existing business — which in private equity is really hard to do.

"I just spent a little time with the founder. I went up to him at an event and gave him a big high five and said, 'You did it, man. This is the thing that is really really hard to do.'"

It's an n-of-one right now. But there's a bunch of really good founders who are capable, with businesses in public and private markets, who I think are going to take a crack at it.

十四、旧 SaaS 公司的命运 / What Happens to Legacy SaaS

DG (to Host): Let me ask you a question. Pick a 2016-2021 pre-ChatGPT vintage software company. Fine, but doesn't have AI-native features. Not accelerating. Growing like 30%. On the venture books it's at 10-20x revenue. Can't go public anymore — no one cares to take it public. Silver Lake has no interest in that company anymore. They would have a year ago. They don't. What happens to that company?

Host: We have a lot of exposure to those companies too. It's very TBD. I was with one of our CEO founders this weekend, and he said, "Give me the straight scoop. Don't give me a podcast answer" — which is ironic.

Both things can be true: AI is the biggest generational change we've ever seen and will transform industries, and there will be some enduring value of software companies that are able to adapt.

Part of what we're monitoring — which makes us extremely bullish about AI — is actual diffusion into the real economy.

Coding: if you were to paint the bullish scenario for regular software and for slower pace of change, you'd say coding hit — but that's kind of a head fake. Coding is perfectly documented — perfect data, verifiable, simulatable. Most tasks in business do not share those three attributes. So maybe the diffusion into other knowledge work beyond coding will take a lot longer. That would be the case for software companies. Some will evolve and have AI solutions and change their business models. That's a must.

But all that makes me super, super bullish on AI. Look at our portfolio — we have some of those companies, but about 95% of our NAV is not in those companies. It's in the companies growing very fast, accelerating, etc.

The median company in the US is spending $12 per employee on AI per month. The top 1% of the data set we've seen is spending $7,000 per employee per month.

So not only have we had limited diffusion beyond coding — if you just look at the shape of who is consuming tokens and actually getting real value out of AI today, we're super early. Banks — the most cutting-edge banks are probably doing 1% of headcount cost on AI tools.

These are the fastest-growing companies we've ever seen, of all time. They're adding more revenue per month than the mega-cap tech companies. And yet it's probably on the back of adoption of like 10 million users, maybe 20, maybe 30 max. There are one-and-a-half billion knowledge workers in the US. And I think it's going to transform the way we do a lot of work.

Host: CalPERS famously lost out on billions of gains by not investing in VC. They're making up for lost time now — they've converted their portfolio from 91% [PE] to 58%, and venture and growth from 9% to 43%. There's probably some balance in between.

Outside of the fact that — I was joking around about Bending — that was probably a great outcome for Airtable. They're going to spin off the hyper-agent piece of the business and do really interesting things with that. But in the scheme of things, there's going to be a lot of homes for a lot of things. And this zero-sum thinking is probably the pitfall we would advise against.

十五、私募信贷的隐藏风险 / Hidden Risk in Private Credit

We talked about venture growth, private equity, public markets. The composition of all of those has radically changed over the last 10 years. We've also had the emergence of entirely new categories in the private markets — like private credit. Do you have a view on their outlook on a relative basis, in software in particular?

Ron: In technology — the vantage point we have is looking at private credit, which resides in a lot of private equity software portfolios, which is hundreds of billions.

One statistic: 2021-2022, about $200-300 billion in LBO software transactions happened, with over $200 billion in debt taken out. The average valuation for those software deals: 25 to 32 times EBITDA. Those companies today are worth probably half that.

The reason you're seeing redemptions in the credit markets in private credit is exactly that. They're looking at the public markets — you've had the CS apocalypse, it's been a massive correction in software — and you can see a contraction in valuations, which means the leverage ratios have gone up dramatically. If you are a software company that is not resilient to AI, I think you're challenged both in terms of equity position and credit as well.

Host: By the way, even the AI version of private equity is not completely insulated. Just because you put Sears on a website didn't make it Amazon. You have to have the benefit of building Amazon from the studs, logistically.

We've seen it in some of our companies as well. The peer competitor is like, "oh, the first thing I'll do is of course hire AI customer service agents — that's easy, low-hanging fruit." Turns out if you don't actually build in the workflow, you start to churn customers very quickly if they're used to talking to a human. And every drop in NPS is a direct correlation with drop in revenue — then you start to spiral, especially if you have debt laden on top.

So sometimes we hear, "I'll just do the AI version of private equity." It's not a panacea for generating returns — especially when it's so categorically different from a technological perspective to actually infuse that throughout the company.

"You can't just throw an operating partner at the company and say, 'let's put AI on it.' It just doesn't work. If you do have a founder mentality at the management team, it is possible — but the board has to be aligned, the investors have to be aligned. And you do have to make really hard decisions the way Intercom did."

十六、反方论证 / The Case Against

Host: Obviously this is a group that is very pro venture and growth. Let's talk about the legitimate opposition. What is the case for why maybe the risk doesn't justify it?

Ron: The push-back we get a lot is timeline to liquidity. The average unicorn is private for 10-plus years typically, and then you have all these follow-on rounds happening pretty quickly. You see maybe the same logo in five, six different firms. The question is: how do you get out of it?

And an IPO isn't actually a distribution. It could take 12-24-plus months before you actually get liquidity out of an IPO. Especially if you own 10-15% at IPO, it's going to take a long time if you're in the generational company.

Host: What's the counter?

Ron: Counter: 3,000 firms, 20 do well consistently. If you're in the top 1% and you have a category winner, you want to make sure that compounds actually.

Would you have wanted to sell Stripe, Databricks, or any of those companies three, four years ago? The answer is unanimously no. Could some of these companies go public earlier? Sure. Anthropic was really first funded in 2021 — it's about to go public 5 years later. Cursor, from first financing to acquisition, is short. So the best venture firms actually have fund-returning liquidity pretty quickly — maybe even quicker than private equity. But that subset of firms is tiny.

Host: Very famously, a year and a half ago or so, we went to our Fund I LPs. At that point, Fund I was 16 years old, and we had this position in Stripe that we invested in at the seed stage. We asked all our LPs: "Do you want liquidity out on this?" We recognized the job we came to do is now done, 16 years in.

Every single one of those LPs said, "No, we'd rather let this continue to compound." Ultimately, a year later, we decided to make that exit — 17 years in, we've got to get this liquidity out, wrap up the fund.

So many LPs — it's very specific to certain categories. Endowments would prefer to let it run. Family offices, quite frankly, don't want the money back because they don't want to pay taxes on it. They'd rather have it continue to compound. There's specific nuance with each LP group — it's very hard to paint a broad brush stroke.

But also, the very best GPs have manufactured liquidity along the way — particularly in 2021 when a lot of folks didn't take money off the table. That was a good sign of the first indicator. And now in this next cycle: can you actually get some early liquidity out through M&A, and then let the winners IPO over time with the fullness of compounding?

十七、下一个 100 万亿市值的公司在哪里 / The Next $100T Market Cap

Host: I'll end on this note. You and Gavin were tossing back and forth — DG, he didn't want to answer the question on what will be the next $10 trillion company, but he had certainty around what will be the next $20 trillion market cap company. So I'm going to ask both of you: what do you think will be the next $100 trillion market cap?

"Oh my gosh, here we go. I can't even think in those things."

DG: That's probably two tech cycles away, not just one. It is possible that we have entirely new companies that get created. A lot of the market-cap creation that would drive a $10 trillion outcome or more is in new product areas that haven't yet been touched.

Like what I talked about — the diffusion of technology into the enterprise: we're nowhere.

A year ago everyone talked about consumer all the time. No one even talks about consumer AI anymore. But the end use case for consumers is not going to be a chatbot interface. That's the skeuomorphic version. We're going to have a native version — proactive, doing work on our behalf, creating a ton of value for consumers. We're kind of nowhere on that. Yeah, there's a billion chat users, but we're just scratching the surface.

Robotics — we are nowhere on robotics, but I think robotics is going to be bigger than the language stuff. And I think it's going to happen in the next 10 years.

Autonomy — we are almost nowhere on autonomy. There are fewer than 10,000 Waymos live in the US, way fewer robotaxis. A lot of open space for others to build.

Healthcare is 18% of GDP — we've done nothing to scratch the surface either on care delivery or on drug discovery. There are some companies working on it, showing early signs of progress, but the progress we'll make there in the next 10 years is going to be massive.

And then we're in this interesting era of reimagining all things physical world — from defense to manufacturing to data centers. I look at the confluence of all these trends and I'm like — yeah, it may feel like we've done a lot with AI already, but 10 years from now we're going to look back and say, "oh my gosh, those other major areas created a ton of value."

So I'm excited that the next SpaceX, AI, or OpenAI are probably going to get created — and they'll probably be in those kinds of domains.

Ron: I'll add one category that to me is both a concern but a huge opportunity. It's a plug for your new fund — on the opportunities fund you did.

Think very simplistically about the bottleneck in AI today. It's not demand — it's on the supply side. You've got energy, the grid, the data center. Then you've got chips. Then you've got frontier models and apps.

The US is amazing at the right side of that — chips and onwards. The VC ecosystem supports that well. I think the new fund you have is really going to help on the left side as well.

Because the US doesn't have a problem with energy generation. It has a problem with speed to power — permissioning, transmission, regulatory. Other countries are putting out 10x more renewable capacity a year. That is a real bottleneck. And that means reimagining the data center. You talked about the density being 10x-plus — well, you can't just repurpose an old data center for a new AI facility.

So this is where the new fund you have can create not $10 billion, not $50 billion, but $100 billion-plus opportunities that can really solve the bottleneck.

A lot of LPs say, "this is like the dotcom" or "this is COVID." It's not — because the traction is real, and it's not ephemeral revenue like COVID. The bottleneck could be supply. But if you have the right inputs — the fund you're now backing, next-generation chip companies, memory, etc. — that's a huge opportunity.

"It's time for the machine age. Let's bring the machines." "I love it."

Host: All right, let's close on that. Thank you both so much. It was super fun.

"Thank you for having us." "Awesome. See you."
