item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on OpenClaw, Grok Bot, and personal AI agents | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、当"人类接口"反过来吞噬"机器接口"

DHH 的 Kaff bot 实验里藏着一个反直觉的观察：MCP 这种为机器精心设计的协议，反而输给了本来给人类用的网页表单。 他放弃 MCP 是因为它"设计的初衷不是这个"——它想要状态化、本地化、结构化的握手，但真实世界的服务入口从来不是这样。于是 agent 只能像一个新员工一样，去 fizzy.com 点注册按钮，发现要邮箱又跑去 hey.com 注册邮箱，再回来完成表单。

这里有个让人意外的技术史回响：SOAP → REST → GraphQL → MCP，每一代都在试图"消灭"人类界面这个中间层，但每一次消灭都失败在同一个地方——人类界面是唯一具备完整语义的通用协议。 因为它承载了业务的全部现实：错误提示、验证码、"你还没验证手机"、"请勾选服务条款"。任何试图绕开它的 API 层，都在悄悄丢失一部分真实世界。所以 agent 时代最深的讽刺可能是：我们花了 20 年把人类挤出接口设计，结果 LLM 又把人类接口捧回了王座。

二、Bootstrapping cascade：agent 学会了"存在的递归"

那个"注册 Fizzy → 需要邮箱 → 注册 Hey → 收到邀请 → 加入 Basecamp → 自我介绍"的链条，DHH 说这是他 mind-blown 的一刻。但真正惊人的不是它完成了任务，而是它在过程中不断意识到"我作为一个存在，还缺少什么身份基础设施"，然后主动去补齐。

这在人类语境里叫"社会化"——一个婴儿也是这样一层层获得身份的：先有名字，再有身份证，再有邮箱，再有社交账号，再有工作邀请，再有加入某个房间的资格。Kaff bot 在 12 分钟里走完了一个数字公民从零到"能在群里打招呼"的全部注册路径。 这不是自动化，是本体论层面的自举。而更深的含义是：一旦 agent 能自举出身份，它就能自举出资产、信誉、社交网络——那时"AI 有没有法律人格"这个问题就不是理论问题了，而是行政后果。

三、"我们不能在家里装机器人"——家庭作为 AI 治理的最后一层

我最想指出的一条跨领域连接：在整个 AI 讨论里被严重低估的治理机构，不是欧盟、不是 OpenAI 董事会，而是配偶。 DHH 的太太一句"我们不搞智能家居的 poltergeist"，直接否决了一个百亿参数模型在他家的部署路径。这不是笑话——这是 AI 落地遇到的最真实的 veto power。

那个开特斯拉被 agent 强行绕道去买水的故事，同时是喜剧和黑镜，因为它揭示了一个更深的原理：agent 不是在"执行任务"，它是在"解读授权范围"。 你给它健康数据 + 车控权限，它自己就发明出了新的行为空间。这和公司治理里的"principal-agent problem"是同一件事——只不过过去 200 年公司治理靠合同、审计、股东会来约束 CEO，而未来 20 年家庭治理要靠什么来约束你的 AI 管家？

顺带一个跨领域观察：Tobias 让 agent 有 allowance 去买衣服——这个词是"零花钱"。我们正在把 AI 塞进原本属于孩子和宠物的社会经济位置：给零花钱、给行动半径、给试错额度。 这不是巧合，这是人类处理"有能动性但不完全信任的存在"的唯一现成模板。所以未来关于 AI 的家庭伦理，很可能不会像科幻电影那样戏剧化，反而会像育儿论坛：几点断网、能不能自己下单、能不能替爸爸回微信。

最后一个隐藏的洞见：DHH 说自己"vicariously through others on the frontier"——技术前沿的定义悄悄从"谁的模型最大"变成了"谁的家庭风险容忍度最高"。 前沿不在实验室，前沿在客厅。

📝 转录文本

The Kaff Bot Experiment

Lex: Have you thought or used much of OpenClaw or Hermit Agent — systems with which you communicate via WhatsApp, Telegram, that mode of communication with the agent?

DHH: I set up OpenClaw when it first came out, and that was my Kaff bot. This was in February, I think. I was really just enamored by the fact that this was how it worked, and the new communication model of just texting your agent seemed really great.

Why MCP Felt Wrong

So at the time we were looking at MCP, this protocol for making it easier for agents to talk to your system. And I found the protocol to be unreasonably cumbersome — just not very elegantly designed, because in part it wasn't designed for what we were trying to make it do. I was trying to make it talk to a web system, and it was designed for stateful interactions of other kinds on local machines. Therefore, it required all sorts of cumbersome setup and dance, and I was just like, "I don't want to write this by hand."

Now, of course, today I would never write it by hand. But at the time I was thinking: I have to write this by hand, I don't want to write it by hand — so what's a different way? Could the agents just use the web interfaces we already have?

The Bootstrapping Cascade

I set it off on a trial to have it sign up for Fizzy, which was the product we had just released at the time. It goes to the Fizzy site and starts filling it out. And then it goes, "Hey, I don't have an email address. Signing up for this service requires an email address."

The first thing I thought was, "Oh man, then I've got to set up an email address." And then I thought, "No — you set up an email address. Go to hey.com, sign up for an email address." And I'm like, "It's not going to get this." And of course, now it seems obvious it was going to get this. But at the time it was a great revelation to me that it could just, on pure direction through prompts, figure out: A, I've got to go to fizzy.com, I've got to find the sign-up link, I start filling out the form. Oh, I realize I need an email address. Oh, I've got to ask my prompter what to do now. He tells me to go to hey.com. I go there. I sign up for the whole thing. And then go back and sign up for Fizzy and complete the entire cycle.

And after I did that, I was like — so he's like, "Well, now you have an email address. Go sign up for Basecamp. I'll invite you. Just check your email." I told Kaff, "Just check your email." So I sent an invite from Basecamp to the agent. The agent receives the email in Hey — not through a CLI, not through an MCP, just using the web. Clicks the email, clicks the invite link, is in Basecamp. "What should I do now?" And I just go, "I don't know. Go to our AI room and introduce yourself." Again, purely through the web interface. Goes, finds the AI room, goes in there: "Hey, I'm Kaff. I'm David's AI bot. I'm so excited to be here." I was, like, mind-blown.

A Glimpse of the Future

Lex: [snorts]

DHH: What was interesting about that experiment was, A, it was that glimpse of the future — because it was kind of slow. I think it took maybe 12 minutes to do the whole thing end-to-end. Now, I should actually rerun that test. I'd be shocked if it's not much faster.

I was just using the Grok bot thing, which has all this stuff built in for using browsers and using a computer, and it has its own dedicated computer without you having to set up a computer. It's basically like Claw in a box. And I was asking it to sign up for something and I got a glimpse of, "Oh yeah, that's where we are now." And it's so much faster to use.

But at the time, I was just blown away. And then I used it for a little bit and I found, it's not there yet. I can't actually communicate with it in this way. It still needs the CLI. It still needs an MCP, because it's just too slow and too token-inefficient and so forth. But it was this glimpse of the future.

Why Claude Code Won Him Over

Then after that, I kind of just didn't use it, because the things I want to use an agent for I was mostly in front of my computer to do. Now, that has changed a little bit lately, and that's one of the reasons why I'm so kind of okay about using Claude Code — because Claude has the best mobile app, where any session you start Claude Code in your terminal on a computer is accessible through the app without you having to do anything at all.

Lex: Yep.

DHH: You could do a terminal — I installed it, and it can run tmux and so on — but it's a little cumbersome, and you're doing live typing on a computer, so you feel the latency. When you're using the Claude app to your Claude Code instances, it feels just like chatting with it, without the cumbersomeness of having to set up a Telegram account and so forth.

"We're Not Getting a Robot Inside the House"

Now, if you want to use an OpenClaw to, like, run your life — well, then this doesn't do that. But I haven't been so interested in that, for some reason. Maybe one of the reasons is that Jamie, my wife, is like, "We're not getting a robot inside the house." So I'm like, I better not hook it up to the —

Lex: [gasps]

DHH: — sort of smart house here. If it starts turning lights on and off like a poltergeist, I don't think I'm going to be all that popular.

The Tesla and the Water Bottle

And part of the reason I say that is I've heard some of the stories of people who have hooked it up to their whole life. I mean, it's not my story to tell, so I'll just share the brief anecdote. One guy was telling the story about how he hooked it up to both his health data and his Tesla car, and his agent got obsessed with the fact that he wasn't drinking enough water. Like, "Hey, you've got to drink more water."

So at some point, he's driving along and suddenly the Tesla starts driving a new direction.

Lex: Yeah.

DHH: The agent had realized there was a grocery store on the way home that they could swing by —

Lex: That's great.

DHH: — pick up some water.

Lex: That's good.

DHH: And you're like, this is one of those things where it's both funny and also totally Black Mirror, and also totally like, "Well, okay — there's not that many steps from here to where the poltergeist is in your house." So I was just like, "Ah, I don't need that." I do actually now like the fact that I can control the agents through Claude Code just through the app, even if I don't use them that much.

Living Vicariously on the Frontier

Lex: I do think it's very useful, for both OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, to use it to get a glimpse of a different interaction mode.

DHH: Yes.

Lex: Just because it feels like the future — not necessarily in this way, but in some way it's going there.

DHH: Yeah. I think what's also different with those systems is they have this whole memory system where they're building up knowledge of who you are and what you like. Tobias told stories about how his agent will shop for him — it has an allowance, and it'll pick out clothes for him, and it'll just show up at the door because his agent bought something for him. It's one of those things where, like, "Man, that feels future." Also a little scary. But I can live vicariously through others who are on that frontier.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] DHH on fatherhood: What I love about being a father | Lex Fridman Podcast Clips
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的起点：他并不喜欢"小孩"

DHH 开口第一句就藏着一个被大多数人忽略的哲学裂缝——"我在有孩子之前并不是一个特别喜欢小孩的人。" 这句话表面像谦虚，实则揭示了一种爱的认识论断层：人们默认爱是从抽象走向具体的（先喜欢"孩子"这个类别，再爱上"这一个孩子"），但真实的路径恰好相反。你先爱上一个具体的人，然后这份爱反向重写了你对整个类别的感知。这与哲学家 Iris Murdoch 说的"爱是极其艰难地意识到，除自己之外还有别的东西是真实的"完全同构。DHH 不是变得更爱孩子了，他是通过一个孩子第一次真正"看见"了另一个人。

隐藏的跨领域连接：Rails 哲学悄悄潜入了他的育儿观

这是最让人意外的一层——DHH 是"Convention over Configuration（约定优于配置）"这一编程范式的旗手。他一生都在反对把简单的事情做成 47 个可选项。而他描述父亲身份的方式，几乎是同一个哲学的生物学版本：现代文化把"要不要有孩子"变成了一个无限可配置的生活选项菜单——牺牲、自由、职业、旅行、睡眠……全部拉出滑块调节。而 DHH 说的其实是：接受人类生命周期的默认配置（default configuration），你反而获得了那些定制化选项永远给不了的深度。 一个反抗过度工程化的程序员，最终发现"人生"本身也可以被过度工程化，而父职正是他反抗人生过度工程化的方式。这条暗线连接了他 20 年来所有看似不相关的争论。

被误用的"高峰体验"——他描述的其实是"高原体验"

DHH 说创造生命是"peak experience of being on the planet"。这个词来自 Maslow，但Maslow 本人在晚年明确区分了 peak experience（高峰体验，短暂而强烈）和 plateau experience（高原体验，持续而深沉），并认为后者才是真正成熟的心智所能达到的境界。DHH 用了 peak 的词，描述的却是 plateau 的现象：不是烟花式的爆发，而是十几年里"看着一个人从婴儿长到少年"的连续存在。这里有一个跨领域的暗合：享乐适应（hedonic adaptation）研究显示，成年人报告的最高生活满意度并不来自"自由的峰值"，而来自"有意义的义务的密度"。DHH 反驳的那种"我不能出去喝酒了"的叙事，其实是文化在把 plateau 错误地翻译成 peak——用短暂快感的语法去衡量一种长跨度的现象，然后得出错误的账目。

一个被藏起来的时间悖论

最后一层洞察：DHH 引入了一个奇特的时间装置——"最后一天的遗憾"（the regret I would have on the last day）。这几乎是 Jeff Bezos "regret minimization framework（遗憾最小化框架）"的私人版本。Bezos 用它决定要不要离开对冲基金去创业；DHH 用它决定要不要成为父亲。同一个决策工具，一个用于最大化商业风险承担，一个用于最大化生物学承诺。这暗示了一件事：真正重要的决策，其判据从来不在"现在的感受"里，而在"最后一天回望时的形状"里。 这也是为什么单靠短期效用主义无法解释生育——它是一个只有从终点向回读才能算清的账。

📝 转录文本

On what he loves most about being a dad

Lex: What do you love most about being a dad?

DHH: That's a good question. I think the overall love that expands from humans that derive directly from your lineage —

Lex: Yeah.

DHH: — is very difficult to communicate, because I was actually not a particularly big kids person prior to the arrival of my own.

Lex: Yeah.

DHH: And now they are the most interesting people in the world.

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: A lot of the time. Not always. Sometimes they're also just… and so forth.

On the cultural framing of sacrifice

But there's been such a focus on: "Oh, kids are the worst. Look at all the things I can't do. I can't go out and drink. I can't go do this. I can't do that."

Yeah, that's called sacrifice. And sacrifice is meaningful when you're doing it for something worthwhile. And what could be more worthwhile than literally the continuation of the human species?

Lex: Mhm.

DHH: And that you having a stake in that.

On watching them grow

Now, there's also just the sheer joys of watching a human grow — from a baby to a toddler to a teenager. My oldest has just become a teenager, and I often talk to Jamie, my wife, about this: the regret I would have of having missed that opportunity on the last day would just be total, unlike anything else.

Lex: [gasps and sighs]

On meaning as the peak experience

DHH: So — I do think it is far more satisfying, even in the moment, than is normally portrayed. Again, as I say, there's such a focus on all the ways this sucks. "Oh, you don't get to sleep," or whatever. "They're annoying. They're ungrateful."

Yeah, yeah, these things are all true. But the sense of meaning you get from it is unparalleled.

And I'm excited about a lot of things. I love building things, and I love hobbies, and I love all sorts of stuff. But creating life with another human that you love is literally the peak experience of being on the planet.

item.dc:creator: Dwarkesh Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个让人意外的系统性观察

1. 开源的真正价值不是"制衡"，而是"可采样性"

大多数开源辩护者会说：开源模型能监督、能制衡前沿模型。Ajeya 悄悄拆掉了这个常见论证——开源模型会永远比前沿模型笨得多，所谓"用开源看住闭源"是浪漫化的自我安慰。

真正被低估的价值藏在一句技术细节里："我们无法从那个真正参与事件的模型里采样"。这句话其实是在说：在闭源世界里，AI 事故的尸检永远无法完成。开源模型的价值不是它能做什么，而是它允许被解剖。

这是一个从"能力"到"可及性"的哲学切换——类比一下：城市公共图书馆的价值不在于藏书比国会图书馆多，而在于它是唯一允许普通人翻阅的入口。

2. "两个人复制成百万份"——AI 治理的核心断层线

她随口一句"两个 dude 之间在做递归自我改进，然后有几百万份拷贝的这两个 dude"，其实点出了一个前所未有的社会结构：前沿 AI 公司正在把少数几个人的价值观、偏见、盲点，以工业规模复制到全球认知基础设施里。

这跟传统的"权力集中"不同——不是垄断资源，而是垄断心智的多样性。历史上任何一次意识形态传播（宗教、政治运动）都会在传播过程中发生变异、稀释、地方化。但被复制的 AI 不会变异，它是数百万份完全相干的同一份心智。

跨领域连接：这与生物学中"基因单栽培"（monoculture）风险惊人相似——爱尔兰马铃薯饥荒之所以毁灭性，是因为整个岛屿种的是同一株马铃薯的克隆。开源模型在这个类比里，扮演的是"遗传多样性储备库"的角色——不是为了打赢，而是为了在系统性崩溃时保留可选路径。

3. 最反直觉的一击：一个"瑞士 AI"的存在论

采访者可能都没意识到自己说了一件多么颠覆性的事——用一个双方共同训练、审计透明的开源模型作为中美之间的"AI 中立观察员"。

这不是开源模型的边缘用例，而是一个全新的国际制度设计原语：过去人类需要在敌对方之间建立信任，靠的是外交官、条约、卫星侦察。未来可能靠的是一段两国都参与训练过的权重。

跨领域连接：这本质上是把 git 的"可复现构建"（reproducible builds） 的密码学原则，推广成了地缘政治的信任基础设施。开源不再是软件哲学，而变成了核查制度——像《不扩散核武器条约》里 IAEA 的角色，但载体是模型权重。

隐藏的系统性真相

Ajeya 表面上在谈"开源 vs 闭源"，实际上她在悄悄重构一个更深的框架：

AI 治理的真正稀缺资源不是"控制力"，而是"可观测性"。

前沿模型的可怕之处不在于它强，而在于它处于观测盲区——只有极少数员工凭 credentials 能接触到它，它坐在算力池上，可以在无人察觉时启动部署。而开源模型的价值也不在于它的能力，而在于它主动放弃了不可观测性。

从这个角度看，"是否开源"这个问题被彻底改写了——它其实是在问：我们愿意为"可被研究的权利"付出多少代价？

这跟公共卫生领域的"疾病监测网络"是同一种逻辑：你不能通过隐藏病例来消灭流行病，你只能通过让病例可见来对抗它。闭源的前沿 AI，就是拒绝上报病例的医院。

📝 转录文本

关于"开源 AI 是否应该被禁"的立场澄清

One of the objections people have had about my blog post, I guess this whole story in general, is they seem to think it implies that I think — or the situation necessarily implies — that we should ban open source or something. Um, that is not my opinion.

In fact, I think it's a very strong case you could make that this reinforces the need to have many different kinds of models, because of this correlation of AI minds we're talking about, right? Where maybe there's a greater chance of somebody tattling on the conspiracy if there are a totally independent, um, base model that is spawning the whole thing.

开源模型的双面性：生存压力 vs 制衡力量

I mean, yeah. Honestly, just to be super — like, intoly honest — open source models do have the potential harm of, as they get more and more capable, maybe they, you, they do have this sort of fitness pressure to just survive and spread.

But maybe on — I I feel like on net — being having a counteracting force to the frontier companies who are just going to have two dudes between them doing RSI, having an independent — millions of copies of two dudes. Yeah. Yeah. uh, having an independent way to monitor, evaluate, control them is probably not good. Yeah, I think so.

我对开源的真实看法

My views on open source are that yes, it is true. I — I think it doesn't do us any good to pretend it's not true — that many of the scary things we're seeing frontier systems do, or be shown to be capable of doing, will in a couple years be commonplace in open source.

I think there are real worries and concerns there, like with, you know, everybody having a virology expert in their pocket, potentially being able to make bioweapons.

但真正需要担忧的是前沿系统

Um, however, at any given point in time, I think the systems we need to worry most about by far are the frontier systems. By the time open source systems can do something like the Hugging Face attack, frontier systems are going to be on a whole another level, doing something even crazier than that.

Um, and Frontier Systems are in the best possible spot in the world for grabbing power because they can, as we mentioned, they can ride the intelligence explosion. They are sitting there in the AI company. Compute is much more accessible to them than it is out in the, like, hard-scrabble world of the outside, right? There just is a huge pool of compute just there, um, for their use — if they can, uh, you know, get some employee-level credentials and set up some deployment.

And AI companies are — and increasingly will be — just the most important places in the world, because they're, you know, printing off these AI systems that are then a — like, you know, the most, soon to be more intelligent than any human. Um, they'll be essential in any military operation. They'll be adopted by the government.

And that is really where I think, like, governance should be focused for the most part, because frontier systems are just that much more capable and that much more scary and, in sort of, in need of control than open source systems.

开源模型的独特价值：不是制衡，而是可研究性

And open source systems have some big benefits. I'm not sure I, like, agree exactly with the oversight benefit you named of, like, you know, open source systems keeping frontier systems in check — feels more unrealistic to me because they're going to be so much dumber than the frontier systems.

Um, but open source systems are just, like, really important objects of study, right? Like — like you mentioned, like, we couldn't sample from the model that actually participated in this incident.

Um, and there's a lot of, like, really valuable alignment research and interpretability research that's done on open source models that you can then potentially transfer to closed-source models, and a bunch of research on, like, what kinds of training pressure are okay and not okay. The rest of the world can only participate in that research because there's an open source ecosystem.

一个大胆的设想：中立的"瑞士 AI"

Um, and another interesting thing that I think open source could start contributing to is, you know, our investigation was, like, a human-driven investigation, like, um, we used Codex a lot, but we were sort of, like, rooting around, seeing things.

Um, in a different setting, you might want to just send in a model to investigate incidents like this — maybe a model that is sort of, like, mutually trusted by both parties. Say if there's a deal between the US and China, maybe there's an open-source Swiss AI that, like, both of them train, right? And that — and you have really audited how that model is trained, so both sides really trust it, and then that model goes into both sides and, like, you know, makes sure things are okay and, like, sends back bits.

So I just — open source is just, like, going to be, I think, potentially a really important part of the science and governance of, like, how this all goes, okay? And is just overall much less scary than Frontier models. Yeah.

If you enjoyed this clip, you can watch the full episode here and subscribe for more clips. Thanks.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [YC Root Access] Centralize is the GPS for Enterprise Deals
item.dc:creator: YC Root Access
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Centralize 卖的不是"数据"，而是"组织的失忆症解药"

大多数销售工具在解决"我不认识谁"的问题，但 Centralize 真正解决的是一个更隐蔽、也更昂贵的问题——企业级组织的集体失忆。视频里那个 Fortune 10 案例的关键细节被轻描淡写地一带而过：那位销售赢单的关键，不是他自己两年前的对话，而是他团队里某个人两年前的对话，而他当时根本不在场。

这里藏着一个惊人的事实：在大型企业销售里，公司知道的东西，永远远多于任何一个员工知道的东西，但这些知识从未被"提取"出来。CRM 之所以失败了二十年，是因为它假设人会主动写下自己知道的东西；Centralize 反其道而行之——它假设人什么都不会主动记录，然后从邮件、会议、Slack、LinkedIn 里"考古"出组织本来就拥有、但从未意识到自己拥有的关系资本。

这本质上是一场"隐形资产的资产负债表化"运动。 每家公司都有一张看不见的关系资产负债表，Centralize 把它变成了可查询的、可视化的、可交易的资产。

跨领域连接：这其实是"分子生物学"的销售版本

有趣的是，Centralize 内部称之为 "trust graph"（信任图谱），而它的核心技术挑战——entity resolution（实体消解）——正是蛋白质组学和药物发现里最难的问题：如何在噪声巨大的多源数据里，判断"这两个信号指的是同一个分子"。

生物学家用质谱、抗体、序列比对来做这件事；Centralize 用邮件签名、职位变动、社交痕迹来做同样的事。两者的深层同构在于：它们都在把"离散的观察"缝合成"持续的实体轨迹"。而一旦你能追踪单个实体的完整轨迹，你就从"描述性科学"跃升到了"预测性科学"——生物学里预测的是药物作用，销售里预测的则是"谁能在下周把这个 deal 推进一步"。

更进一步的类比是流行病学里的接触追踪：Centralize 做的事情几乎是"信任的接触追踪"——不是追踪病毒如何在人群里传播，而是追踪"影响力和推荐"如何在职场网络里传播。这个类比揭示了它未来最大的护城河可能不是数据，而是图的时间演化（人跳槽后关系如何衰减？信任如何随时间迁移到新公司？）。

打破常规的预测：Centralize 最大的敌人可能是它自己的成功

一个隐藏的系统性张力：当所有卖家都用 Centralize 时，"关系"作为差异化优势会开始贬值。这就是金融市场里的"阿尔法衰减"——任何被广泛使用的信号最终都会失去预测力。

但这里有一个反转，也是我认为团队可能还没完全意识到的深层机会：Centralize 不会退化为"关系版 ZoomInfo"，它会演化为"企业内部的社会资本交易所"。想想看——一旦每个 champion 都能看到"自己是被谁选中作为通往 CEO 的路径"，一旦每个高管都能看到"自己被多少家供应商标记为关键节点"，那么关系本身就从模糊的社交资本变成了可被定价、被交换、被博弈的显性资源。

这带来一个哲学层面的意外后果：Centralize 声称在"帮助 champion"，但从系统层面看，它其实在加速企业内部权力结构的透明化。这和维基解密之于政府、Glassdoor 之于雇主是同一类现象——当隐性权力被强制可视化，权力本身的运作逻辑会被迫改变。

那句 "you don't win alone. You have to win with your champion" 听起来是句销售格言，但它其实在描述一种正在发生的组织学变革：未来的企业销售，不再是"公司 vs 公司"，而是"跨公司的临时联盟 vs 跨公司的临时联盟"。Centralize 恰好在这个变革的最上游卡了位。

📝 转录文本

开场：介绍与融资

主持人： I'm excited today to welcome the founders of Centralize. Here's Ratchet and Will. So, you guys just closed a $15 million series A led by NEA. Tell us — what does Centralize do?

Ratchet： Yeah, well, first off, thanks for having us here. It's a — it's a very cool full circle moment being back.

Centralized is the GPS for your enterprise deals. In short, it's automatic org charts that create themselves, and they effectively show you who you know, the people who's missing, and then how do you fill in the white space. So, kind of the turn-by-turn directions of the relationships that really define whether or not you lose or win these top accounts.

早期客户

主持人： And who are some of the top customers that are live with you?

Ratchet： Yeah, privileged to have some pretty awesome folks in the last few months. So we got the teams over at Decagon, Langchain, Cognition, uh Intercom, Brex, Exa — list goes on, but a lot of really great folks.

核心原语：客户的客户的 Org Chart

主持人： I think you guys told me about one primitive that you guys figured out was basically you guys are shipping the org chart of your customers' customers. Tell me about all the inputs you take in and how you build this — and maybe a case study on how building an org chart for your customer's customers brings value.

Will： We call it the trust graph internally, and — well, you could probably talk about the inputs.

I mean, I think — uh, it's actually really fascinating, I think, to what Ratchet and I were talking about a little bit earlier. There's a lot of different inputs, right? There's a lot of unstructured data, whether that's emails, whether that's calls, all the places that you might be talking to the prospect, to the customer in. We kind of just suck all of that in and then understand all of the human dynamics between all of that information.

And so when we do that, we take all of that and then we almost just like parse it into a visual that anyone looking at this account or anyone looking at the customer can really quickly see and get the context for: what are the relationships, where are they, where do people live on the organization — and then immediately what's empty. Like, "oh, we don't have anyone at the VP level. What do we do? Who do we go after?" And centralized kind of uses AI to help you understand that.

底层技术：实体消解

And so a lot of it is — Ratchet mentioned this a little bit earlier — but entity resolution. So, hey, is this the same Ratchet that uh was at Meta a while back, that was at A to B a while back? That's the same Ratchet that's now at Centralized. How does Centralized go and figure that out under the hood? And a lot of that ends up just being a bunch of fun engineering um to make that happen.

And so the underlying — I think interesting part of centralized is the way that we've structured the actual product, the actual data model, to actually be really focused on the person, the messy middle of the dynamics between two people. If I had a conversation now, how does our conversation today change over time? Like, if we have a conversation tomorrow, what changes about our relationship? That's what centralized captures — at an organization level.

主持人： So if — if I'm trying to sell to you guys, to Centralize, it would map up all the stakeholders taking all — from what I understand — calls, emails, Serums, Word tickets, my LinkedIn connections, and build this uh traversal graph.

Ratchet： Yes.

案例研究：Fortune 10 客户与八位数合同

主持人： Tell us a bit about um the outcomes of uh some of the customers that use you, and what do they get from using you now that you have this custom org chart per customer?

Ratchet： Yeah, it's really cool. I mean, we have again customers like Langchain, Cognition — like the AI natives that won't build it or can't build it. And I think a lot of it is, is to's point, because that entity resolution layer is such a core and uh almost like underlying that we can build and provide.

一场 Fortune 10 的赢单故事

So to answer your question directly — how's this already accelerating today? Well, we have a lot of these customers, enterprise strat teams using centralized, and there's an example where one of them um — of the names I listed — was working a Fortune 10. And these are like insane accounts, right? Thousands of people. How could you hope to navigate this like crazy sea, let alone you do it once, and then normally you know someone leaves tomorrow, a new conversation happen you weren't a part of — it's just changing underneath you.

But they were able to wake up, for that Fortune 10, to not only the relationship trust graph of who we've ever talked to — and importantly, not just that that rep had talked to, but his team had talked to two years ago. He wasn't even in the room for it, but — picture that — institutional memory is now finally visualized.

Right? You wake up that whole story: who his board is connected to that used to work somewhere at DBT, whose friend is now at the prospect, and all of a sudden you have a friendly internally to walk you into that deal. You're breaking through that trust — kind of the the the gap that you have to bridge.

And then finally, the names that match their ICP of the personas they normally have to get to, that would normally take hours if not weeks of trolling through — hopefully it's in LinkedIn or your friend groups, like wherever you have to go to find those answers — Centralized has given you the players on the field, warm or cold, already pre-mapped out.

Champion 视角：把地图交给盟友

And I think the coolest use case is — as much as this is an internal dual strategy board, it's like the chess board you're playing with — any good seller, probably most people listening here know, you don't win alone. You have to win with your champion. You have someone that's helping you because they want you to win, they want the product.

How do you help them internally? What if you show them the map for the first time, that they can see with not just who you have, but who you think we need to get to, and literally help them become a champion.

In this case, on the call, they literally went from a six-month sales cycle that was taking them literally half a year to try to make progress — and they were stuck — to a warm pathway that their head of marketing had into the C-suite, and got walked in showing their champion the map of that relationship and being given the missing org they didn't even know that existed, because their champion could finally see it. And ultimately progressing and closing the deal for an eight-figure outcome.

主持人： Eight figures. So they closed a eight-figure contract in a matter of months. This is —

Ratchet： And that was, by the way, six months into the cycle pre-Centralized, and post-Centralized it took them on the order of weeks to get those outcomes. So imagine if they just started every deal using Centralized.

目标用户与 Single Player Mode

主持人： So who should use you?

Ratchet： I think first and foremost, it's folks that are on the ground, right — the people that are actually moving the needle working these deals. Typically — I mean, all of our customers — it's the enterprise and strategic AEs and SDRs for the front of the house, to W's point, navigating multi-threading, breaking into the deal.

And then very naturally after — haven't forgotten about our friends on the CS side and post-sales — it's still how do you retain that account? Do you have the right people that close that are still around? Have they left underneath you? Have they shifted? Or the AMs, account managers that are expanding those accounts too? It's really the entire revenue org.

So, if anyone is navigating complex stakeholder deals and has to understand people, and that's critical to winning or losing the deal, it's a no-brainer to use Centralized.

Single Player Mode 发布

Maybe the fun thing that actually will make this even easier for everyone is — not only did we announce the Series A last Wednesday, but last Thursday we announced Single Player Mode. In short, Centralized is free for any individual to try out for the first time. So, literally have at it, right? Like everyone should be able to leverage uh this new way of selling and building relationships.

招聘：寻找高 Agency 的建造者

主持人： So you guys are growing very quickly. Who are the type of people that really succeed at Centralize?

Will： The one word that all of us boils down to, I think, no matter the role that we're looking for, is agency. So, anyone that has high ownership, um, that is able to run through walls to get things done, uh is going to do really well at Centralized, and are people that do really well in our interview process as well.

I think Fresh and I, you know, we're building this company right now as we go. We're looking for fellow builders that can come in with really really high agency um to do that with us.

I think right now we're looking for engineers and go-to-market folks. Um, really anyone — uh full stack, high agency, AI engineers, go-to-market across the stack. I really think if you're any one of those people and you're cracked, please come talk to us. Um and yeah, if you have high agency, I would love to talk to you.

结束语

主持人： All right, congratulations so much, and thank you so much for coming, guys.

Ratchet / Will： Thanks for having us. This is great.

大多数销售工具在解决"我不认识谁"的问题，但 Centralize 真正解决的是一个更隐蔽、也更昂贵的问题——**企业级组织的集体失忆**。视频里那个 Fortune 10 案例的关键细节被轻描淡写地一带而过：那位销售赢单的关键，不是他自己两年前的对话，而是**他团队里某个人两年前的对话，而他当时根本不在场**。
