**这本质上是一场"隐形资产的资产负债表化"运动。** 每家公司都有一张看不见的关系资产负债表，Centralize 把它变成了可查询的、可视化的、可交易的资产。
## 跨领域连接：这其实是"分子生物学"的销售版

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Is Robinhood's Tokenized AMC Stock Actually Illegal?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"反向 ADR"革命：这不是衍生品之争，而是资本主权之争

大多数人把 AMC vs Robinhood 之争看作"合规打架"，但真正被埋没的洞察是：Robinhood 做的是一个"反向 ADR"（Reverse ADR） —— 传统 ADR 是把外国股票包装进美国市场，而 Robinhood 是把美国股票包装出美国、送到全球。这个方向的翻转其实是二战后美元霸权逻辑在链上的镜像延续。

一个让人意外的观察：AMC CEO 骂 Robinhood 骂得越凶，AMC 股价越涨（一夜 21%）。这不是巧合，而是揭示了一个新的市场微观结构规律 —— 在 attention 经济里，被 tokenize 本身就是一种"上市二次 IPO"。链上的 mimetic demand 会反哺链下股价。这与传统金融理论完全相反：传统认为衍生品是从标的派生价值，而在 meme + token 时代，衍生层反过来给标的注入了"社交流动性溢价"。Adam Aron 在骂人的同时，其实在给自己的股票做全球免费营销。

二、跨领域连接：AI 数据中心的政治困局 = 19 世纪铁路+新教伦理的镜像

Chris 提到"数据中心可能成为中期选举的核心议题"，这个观察被大部分人低估了。但真正有趣的类比是：当前 AI Lab 的处境，几乎完美复刻了 19 世纪美国铁路大亨的历史节点。

  • 铁路巨头当年也说"我们要重塑美国"→ 引发平民主义反弹（Populist Movement, 1892）
  • Sam Altman 说"我们要拿走所有工作"→ Bernie Sanders 提议禁止超级智能
  • 铁路 tycoons 也曾被指责"用蒸汽机替代人类"
  • 反对铁路的核心不是技术，而是"谁掌握了未来的定义权"

Austin 说的那句"AI Lab 应该走出硅谷去俄克拉荷马"其实指向一个更深的结构性问题：这一轮 AI 建设是历史上第一次"资本极度密集但劳动力零参与"的基础设施建设。铁路至少雇佣了华工和爱尔兰劳工，电网建设创造了国家电工阶级，互联网创造了程序员中产。而数据中心，只有噪声、耗电、税收，没有一个"我们家孩子在里面上班"的社会锚点。这就是为什么两党会罕见地对齐 —— 政治学家把这称为"无从属性基础设施悖论"。

三、隐藏的系统性真相：三个战场其实是同一个战场

如果你把 AMC/Robinhood、AI 监管、Fed 加息、挪威主权基金减持美债 这四件事分开看，它们是四条新闻。但如果把它们叠加，会浮现一个统一的元结构：

在美国国内合法性衰减的临界点上，一切"边缘、离岸、链上"的替代路径都在同时被激活。

  • Robinhood 把股票送去 Jersey（境外）→ 因为美国监管让 capital formation 变贵
  • 全球用户通过 VPN 买美国资产 → 因为本国监管让财富保全变难
  • Norway 减持美债 → 因为美国政治干预 Fed 让主权风险变大
  • Bernie 提议禁 AI → 因为技术精英对普通人的"存在性焦虑"提供的答案不合格

Ram 说"要拥有能在名义价格上重定价的资产"，这个建议表面是宏观策略，本质上是在说：当制度信用被稀释，物理稀缺性和现金流稀缺性就成了唯一的锚。而这也解释了为什么 meme coin 和数据中心概念股在同一时期同时爆发 —— 它们分别代表了注意力的稀缺性和电力/算力的稀缺性，是同一个通胀防御逻辑的两个极端。

啊哈时刻：Cheesecake Factory 今年跑赢大多数半导体股 —— Austin 一句玩笑话里藏着这一集最深的信号：当高端叙事集体高估，"能被吃、能被摸、能被使用"的真实业务反而在悄悄地重新赢回估值权。这是一个静默的"物质主义反扑"。

📝 转录文本

开场：三条宏观论断

We're not going to see rate hikes. Kevin Warsh is talking like a hawk, but he's a dove.

Two, we got productivity growth bailout coming from AI. That's going to save the day. We are in this disinflationary period with these temporary price shocks due to geopolitical concerns, energy production's a bit higher than ever, and it's going to continue to go up.

Three, the AI buildout itself is inflationary. It's contributing like a point and a half the GDP. So that is part of the cost of this buildout. They're not going to get down to the 2% inflation target for at least a few years. That means that you should be owning assets that reprice in nominal terms, especially equities that are indexed to the data center theme.

欢迎与广告

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. Today is Monday, September 7th, Labor Day here in the United States, and we're still here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro.

So before we begin, a quick commercial break. This episode is brought to you by 1inch Aqua, the shared liquidity layer from 1inch. Back multiple liquidity positions with one wallet balance and keep your tokens in your wallet until a swap fills. See how it works at oneinch.com/Aqua.

All right, everybody, as always, I'm your host, Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I'm here with Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto.

一、AMC vs Robinhood：Tokenized 股票之争

事件背景

And Chris, today we're going to start with a fight. So over the weekend, AMC CEO Adam Aaron went after Robinhood's tokenized AMC shares issued out of Jersey by Robinhood Assets, calling them, quote, "contemptible, outrageous, disgusting, detestable, inexcusable, vile."

He said AMC has no connection to it and does not condone it. Vlad Tenev's entire reply was, "What's the concern?" And Aaron's answer was eight paragraphs and a demand that Robinhood voluntarily cease and — kiss, it was misspelled — desist, with Robinhood CLO Dan Gallagher, notably former SEC, saying, "Send your lawyers and we'll educate them."

Tenev, in the same minute, said, "We stand behind stock tokens." Now, weirdly, AMC stock jumped nearly 21% overnight to $3.07 on this fight, according to The Block.

什么是 Stock Token？

And I think where to start is, what is a stock token? So in this case, tokenized debt securities issued by Robinhood Assets expose people to the share price — not the ownership, not the shareholder rights. They are unregistered in the U.S. They are not offered to U.S. persons.

So the substantive charge that synthetic equity decouples stock token ownership and a company having an ability to control its own capital raising efforts, and that it sows distrust in markets generally. But the flip side is there's 13.4 billion of these things.

And to have some sort of price token like this, you're either creating a derivative, which Robinhood did not really do here, or having the reverse of what is called an ADR. That is to say, you have stocks that are backing this token, which you pass the price reference on for.

So previously, OpenAI had disavowed Robinhood's tokens in July 2025. But this to me is a little bit different. OpenAI is not a public company. These are not publicly tradable. That is private stock. Often you need issuer permission for transfers in private stock in a way you do not with public stock. So while this fight has happened once before, it was not the exact same fight.

Chris 的评论：创新与资本形成的冲突

Chris, you have a lot of thoughts on tokenization. You have been involved in this space for a while. What do you make of this dispute between AMC and Robinhood?

Chris: I mean, there's so much going on right now where you're seeing innovation, creativity. I'm sure we're going to talk about some of the meme coin stuff pairings that are also going on Robinhood chain, which are very hard to discuss at work because of the names involved. But gosh, I haven't seen this type of innovation and creativity for decades, post-global financial crisis.

I totally understand the challenges, but like, you know, you were at Wall Street. I was on Wall Street. Synthetic products are a thing — they're everywhere. And I think the challenge here, did Robinhood do anything illegal? I think it's very clear that they've done their homework if you listen to their general counsel.

The second question is, okay, why is there conflict here? Well, if you're a CEO, you would love for someone to buy your equity rather than... because capital markets — U.S. capital markets are where they are today because it's a place for capital formation if you're a company. And so they're making the principles argument saying, wait a second, this isn't right. This isn't fair because you're undermining the principles of capital formation. And frankly, that's one of the core goals of the SEC to ensure that capital formation is available and thoughtfully takes place here in the United States.

And so that's the conflict. It's like, hey, you're messing with my capital formation. But again, you go to a Delta One desk on Wall Street, there's constantly structures, there's constantly synthetic capabilities.

I'm a little bit surprised that there isn't more coordination. I would think in the future you're going to see companies — like right now it's conflictual, right, where AMC and Robinhood are fighting with each other. I think the next iteration of this are real companies working closely with these mass distributors and really finding ways to distribute true tokenized equities for capital formation. Right now, everyone's like every man for himself, but I think in the future, you're going to see more partnerships being formed, and that's where the real value is going to take place.

Ram 加入：衍生品需要真实用例

Ram: Happy Labor Day. In our family, we call it Happy Capitalism Day. Let's go innovation, let's go American enterprise, let's go productivity growth, technology.

A few things. One, capital formation is critical. Derivatives don't create capital formation — it's risk transfer. Derivatives play an incredibly important role. Like you go back to the original use case of the farmer planning for the harvest — they've got uncertainty on the price when they deliver to the market versus all the cost, time, labor they put into it. And derivatives played a very important role in that risk transfer. That's win-win for everybody. That helps Coca-Cola, helps McDonald's manage cattle prices, sugar inputs, helps the end consumer manage inflation. Same story is true for oil.

Now where we're going now is just too much. Now it's like derivatives for the sake of derivatives. Derivatives properly conceived solve real-world problems, and that's when you stay focused. We had a guest on last week talking about derivative contracts on Polymarket and ice cream sellers hedging their risk. That's not going to happen. It's just too much.

So that's one upstairs. The second, on the mechanics, Robinhood can pull this off. The other read-through behind this is that the SPV and the venture markets are just so massive. It's a capital market unto itself. And if you have an SPV and it's fully collateralized, you can enable liquidity in these securities. But derivatives for the sake of derivatives, it's like a hammer trying to find a solution.

VC 的"闪亮物综合症"

Austin: But when you say too much, Ron, what do you mean? You're not putting the genie back in the bottle anytime soon. What do you think is going to happen? And you're right, lack of an obvious principled use case — like derivatives like the mortgage-backed securities market and the creation of principle-only strips and interest rate strips, phenomenal innovations, and you can identify the commercial hedger, the creator of the risk, and you can see how that risk transfer unlocks value and expands the efficient frontier through these transactions.

Ram: We're talking now about just derivatives on these very niche use cases where it's an intellectual stretch, not obvious in the case of the farmer who can't control cattle prices, much less the weather. They're trying to lock in their input costs and the sale costs so they can fix on their margin, and they've got a sound business that's not at risk if there's a bad season. All that makes a lot of sense. It's good sense.

But I think one of the issues we've seen in the digital asset market more generally is VCs have had shiny object syndrome. Now VCs always have shiny object syndrome. It was 3D printing at one time. It was cannabis another time. It was this and it was that. And sometimes those shiny objects go on to be really powerful things, like the transformation we're seeing with AI or DeFi like we've talked about. But I think in some of these cases, derivatives more generally and just speculative use cases that aren't addressing problems...

Chris: VCs have nothing to do with this, right? This is between AMC, which is a public company, and Robinhood, is a public company.

Ram: I think the general zeitgeist though, Chris — does Robinhood build another Layer 1? They built it because Stripe Tempo had it. It was a need to copycat, quick follow-on, fast follow response.

Chris: The legitimate innovation Robinhood was zero-dollar trades. Have you looked at the financials of Robinhood chain? They're printing money right now. It was probably the best financial decision they could have ever made. Now yes it's full of meme coins, we can talk about that, but if you look at the financials, I don't have it in front of me, I'm sure it's great.

Ram: Look, I'm an indirect exposure and pump.fun through Six Man Ventures. So you can make one statement around, hey, will this business make good P&L? You can make another statement around, is this just healthy and sensible for markets, consumers, and investors? Do our finest minds need to focus their time and energy on "let me create scalable meme coin infrastructure" when we know these meme coins 99.99% are going to go to zero? Or do we get back to expanding small business lending, access to credit, transparency in our financial system, transparency in the ABS securitization market where you get a win-win on both sides.

Austin 的市场微观结构分析

Austin: Totally hear you. We're already at meme coins and we haven't even got through AMC yet. Speaking of meme coins, a couple of observations here.

My starting one is that I think this reveals how little people understand about markets microstructure in general. So AMC, if you'll remember, is a movie theater company that burst onto the scene, kind of riding the coattails of GME and thus becoming an investing darling in that same time frame. And they've always had a sort of like "fuck the man," like outsider type vibe to them. I get why they would be arguing here.

But you really need to descend into what's going on to make some of these critiques, and I think they largely reveal somebody who does not understand how markets work — which hypothetically, maybe some other things have also revealed in this case in the past.

A good example is this: if we look at what Coinbase is doing, Chris, you alluded to this earlier, which is perpetual futures for tokenized U.S. stocks versus, call it, an actual stock-backed like deposit token that doesn't pass on governance rights or maybe even not dividends and can be traded by people. Those have two different effects on markets, right?

The futures are a funding trade. Maybe they can be used for hedging, but without a party to stand between the futures and the actual price token, to Ram's point, this is largely speculation. And what it's revealing to me is unfulfilled demand for U.S. stocks by non-U.S. investors.

On the other hand, doing the reverse of an ADR is actual demand for capital. You need the underlying AMC shares to do the — lock the shares in a box and create a thing off the box. So in that case, the critiques of "hey, we lose control of our fundraising" is like, no, that's strictly wrong. This actually gives you more people to fundraise from, not less, and expands the audience of people who want to buy your stock.

So again, I think the microstructure is really important here. And everybody just blitzed past this in the debate in very Twitter fashion to start screaming at each other without defining their terms. And that sort of stuff is why these debates are so filled with screaming idiots on Twitter.

关于投票权和资本形成的辩论

Chris: Yeah, so you're not buying AMC equities with voting rights through this program, right? I guess, Mike and Rob.

Austin: Well, hold on. Let me pause you. Depending on how you structure it, that depends. It may be that Robinhood is buying those, not passing on the voting rights, and that matters.

Chris: That's right. But the purchaser of the token, AMC token, under this regime does not have voting rights. They are not buying equities. We're agreeing with that. But if these were true tokenized equities, maybe you can make a case that, yes, that's wonderful, because now it's capital formation. And I got to push back — the chain gives you that global TAM, that global reach.

And I think we just need to separate the two things. Is it the alchemy that's frustrating you? Is it the fact that maybe it's not clear? I don't know if it is. I'm not a buyer, but I'm not overseas. What is it that's challenging you on this one? I think you're on mute, buddy.

Ram: It's really the focus of the spirit of innovation. Where is this focus of innovation? There's some problems to solve on enabling international investors to access U.S. markets. Great. That's a one-and-done. Enabling AMC to get shares traded — that won't actually create capital. That's just secondary market liquidity. As we all know, it's primary offerings that create capital still — IPOs, venture capital investments, private equity investments. Those are things and innovation that I get excited about.

It's the intellectual fascination with the complex. Like when Sequoia invested in Citadel, I looked at that. It's the same reason why I invested in FTX. I remember, you know, I had a former life doing market making and all this stuff, and it's like these businesses, they have low-up risk. Like Knight Capital, when they had fat finger risk. I don't think VCs truly understand the risks of these businesses. There's a reason why Virtu trades at 10 times earnings and it's a comp for Citadel, for example.

That's what I mean by like, what are this capital going after? Exactly what problem are we solving and is it really that big a deal? These synthetic structures, they're all over Wall Street.

全球投资者与美国市场的普及

Chris: So is the concern then, oh, these are not accredited, they don't understand what they're doing? Is that the issue? Because they go to any Delta One desk.

Ram: It's the focus of our brightest talent and entrepreneurs and corporate executives. Are we solving real problems? Yeah, the rules are all over Wall Street. Wall Street, as you know, they've got netting. They're solving real problems, right? If you are generating a lot of offshore non-dollar revenue, you need a dollar swap to manage your income volatility. That's like a bona fide problem. These corporate CFOs, they're not winging it, unless you're the blue whale at JP Morgan — that's different, right?

But I'm talking about synthetic equity exposure.

Chris: Yeah, this is a case of synthetic equity exposure. Where do you draw the lines? Because one guy's a retail guy and he can't — he's not sophisticated enough to know about it. Like that's a specific example here — it's synthetic equity exposure.

Ram: I think the opportunity set of innovation and the return on that innovation for consumers, small businesses, and market business would be a lot higher. Folks in that talent are there. This is like a one-and-done innovation for someone. It's like, go build it, move on, great. You enabled international access to U.S. markets. Okay, this is not the transformational concepts that I think got us all excited.

Like, for example, DeFi with an intermediary, or the intermediary — that's a really interesting concept, creating transparency on chain without underwriting counterparty risk or settlement risk. Well, that's really interesting. Now, let's have those kinds of conversations. Developing the first agency mortgage-backed security so community banks could lend in their community and not be constrained by their balance sheet — instead, they're constrained by the quality of credit-worthy opportunities. That's legitimate transformation. Internet money — Bitcoin — that's a transformational concept, right? This is not at that level.

Austin 反驳：全球化访问是真正的转型

Austin: I'll be honest, I'm not sure I agree with Rob on this. I think in the specific case where we're taking U.S. stocks and finally making them easily available to average people internationally, which is not a thing that was easy for people to do before, that is transformational, right? A little bit like the process of creating U.S. dollar stablecoins and distributing them globally.

If the average person in India or Thailand or Russia or Nigeria or Argentina can now buy the S&P 500 in a way that they couldn't get their hands on before and actually have it be, if not the thing, a decent approximation of the thing — because I concede the SEC's points on voting rights here — I do think that's transformative.

Ram: Let me ask you this. So are these tokens going to be investable in those markets? Or are these issuers of these tokens required to register in India under the same regulatory framework? If they're required to register, then it doesn't matter, there's nothing incremental here. If it's the former, then you're right, because one of the best things you can do in an emerging market is invest in the United States. You want to store value with growth.

Austin: So the way it's currently working, if you look at how these things are starting to be distributed, is somebody's got to register in the United States to have a broker-dealer here. People are buying, at least in the form that's good — we'll talk about the bad one next, which is some of these meme coin paired things — but let's talk about the good one. People are buying the stock, that's right, I said it, Chris. Are buying the stock, locking the stock in a box, and then using a reference on the box as an actual token that can then be traded on chain.

So now you're moving into the decentralized ecosystem is the way you're talking about, Ram. So if I'm just a random person in like Argentina, I can actually go buy the token. I may not get dividends, I may not get voting rights, but I get the price exposure to say Apple in a way that I could not invest in locally. And because they're doing it in DeFi, it's very hard to find an intermediary.

Ram: Local regulator — we'll see what happens. You do raise a great point. There's two things: as good as investing in American business, and if you can broaden that access, it's a very good thing for people. Right now, those local regulators will call it a security and say it must be filed and registered. That's what's going to happen.

Austin: So now what's going to happen is you got to say to those individuals in those countries, "Hey, here's a token, do it anonymously on chain through a VPN and do not report it to a regulator, and you must violate your tax reporting." Which is — it is a good legitimate investment. And fundamentally, it's about bad laws in those emerging markets that constrain the investment opportunity set of individuals trying to create a better life for themselves.

Ram: Correct.

Austin: This is, by the way, the same existential problem that stablecoins are creating for them. Because what do you need to buy these things? You need the internet and something of value to trade for them. So all of these regimes based around capital controls and locking their people in to expropriate them are now facing the possibility that most people globally, even if imperfect, are about to have access to the U.S. dollar and investment in U.S. capital markets.

为 Robinhood Chain 辩护

Chris: I want to defend Robinhood Chain here for a second because I thought it was an incredible unlock. They are printing money. I was in London when they launched it and announced it. And it's like, wow, finally, you have a company with tens of millions of global distribution that has this chain. There is safety and soundness as you come in. It's backed by insurance. And look what it's doing. It's providing that global access.

Now, we're going to get into meme coins, I think. And one of the things about blockchains and permissionless systems is that people can do what people feel like doing. And maybe it's a tell of humanity. And we can't control that. That's part of the things of running a decentralized chain. But the way that they engineered scalable DeFi, I thought was very, very impressive. It was the DeFi mullet in action.

广告插播

Austin: So before we drag ourselves to the meme coin part of this and then give Rom his once-per-episode ability to take a shot at Sam Altman, we're going to pause here for a moment and take a quick commercial break.

$540 million — that's how much concentrated liquidity sat idle in a given week in the first half of this year. About 30% of the DeFi TVL, if you're wondering. That's according to Dune Research commissioned by 1inch. But there's a solution. 1inch Aqua is the new shared liquidity platform. It lets LPs back multiple positions with the same token balance and keep their tokens in their wallet till a swap comes. Why does that help? Because LPs don't have to split their tokens across positions. They can cover more market conditions and pairs with their full balance. That means more activity across deeper liquidity. See how it works at oneinch.com/Aqua. Remember that providing liquidity carries risk and fees aren't guaranteed.

二、Meme Coins 与股票的怪异配对

FAMI 与 STONK 案例

All right, everybody, welcome back. Now let's talk about some absolute deranged weirdness, which is, as always, meme coins.

So FAMI, a NASDAQ-listed Chinese dried mushroom seller with 15 employees, ran 350% to $0.50 on Wednesday, 720 million shares traded, 90 times its daily average. It is because, of course, of a meme coin on Robinhood chain paired against a token using FAMI's ticker. At the peak, the meme coin implied the valuation was about $60 million, 10 times that of the listed company. The Defiant found the tokenized FAMI was not a Robinhood stock token at all — it just looked like a meme coin with a deployer keeping 38% and no issuer.

STONK ran 250% to $140 million cap after StonkFun integrated like Raydium's launchpad. STONK itself is paired against SPY, so hopefully it's a function of the ETF. But again, holders have no claim on the fund. Hard to see what's going on inside this box.

So to me, going back to Ram's earlier critique, and in fact the AMC CEO's critique, these sorts of things do strike me as a little bit weird, right? Like capitalizing on thinly traded names at off-hours to push price is exactly the sort of behavior you used to see from things like bucket shops.

Chris：Meme Coin 是游戏，不是投资

Chris: I think it's a game and it's not an investment. Even Gary Gensler didn't try to regulate memes because he couldn't. There's no value. No one's trying to make sure that there's value. And so it's a game. Try to catch the runner. And people continue to innovate.

Now this linkage with equities is novel. It's GameStop 2.0. If you're playing the game, you're probably going to lose money. Should there be warnings out there? Probably.

But is manipulation regulated by the CFTC? Absolutely it is. So if you're manipulating these markets, do so at your own risk because it's illegal at their commodities. Are also regulated by the states. So generally, if you're manipulating things, probably shouldn't do that. If you're playing, buyer beware.

But look, there's an entire industry in New Jersey and Las Vegas — casinos — where you go in there and you play the game and it's wonderful entertainment value. And you're probably going to lose money. You do it anyway because you know you're going to, but it's fun. So it is what it is.

I don't think it's what we should be focusing on to build the next generation of finance. However, there is one good thing that comes out of this. And the one thing that meme coins have been particularly amazing at — they trade so violently — is that they're incredible stress tests for blockchains. ETH had it with Pepe, Solana had it. When these things trade with this volume, there's no utility for the buyer. There's actually a lot of utility for the blockchain because it has to handle the throughput. So my hope is that all this activity and craziness paves the way for scalable real-world assets that hopefully follow when the institutions show up. My two cents.

Ram：机会成本论

Ram: I agree with what Chris said. What's the motivation if someone's buying a meme coin? Now, you're right, it's a kind of a modern lottery system where maybe it's not even positive EV. It isn't. Look, semiconductor stocks are up a couple hundred percent the last year. They've sold off 40-50%. Why are you wasting your time with meme coins? These things have earnings growth. They're indexed to big secular trends. Folks, there's a real opportunity. Your opportunity cost is quite high if you're spending time with meme coins.

Austin: I completely agree with that take. Something about the fun absurdity of markets is that Cheesecake Factory has outperformed most of the semiconductors year to date. But the common thing underlying all of these is there is a productive business in there, right? There is somebody doing something with their hands, be that making silicon chips or literal cheesecake. But if you can't find the activity, I think you're always vulnerable to the Warren Buffett critique of "what does this thing do? Where does the money come from?" And that's something I think really is a clear line between utility and non-utility here.

三、AI Frontier 模型更新

新模型发布

All right, so Rom, let's move on to your favorite topic of things that have utility, which is in fact AI. So we've had a couple of pieces of news here.

One, we saw Frontier releases. Anthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 on September 1. It's the same underlying model, different safeguards. Cached reads cost 75% less, 25 cents per million tokens, cutting typical workload costs by about a quarter and highly agentic ones close to 50%.

Some of the benchmarks jumped significantly. We're seeing fewer cyber safeguard interventions per session, and we're starting to see some weird things. Mythos 5.1 designed protein binders with a 50% hit rate across 12 targets. The industry norm in that space is 10 to 15%. Pretty good. Now, is that going to replicate? We'll see. But early on, it's showing interesting stuff.

So OpenAI, GPT-6 Astra, September 3rd, basically is crushing benchmarks. ARC-AGI 3 at 99.9%, Frontier Math Tier 4 at 97.6%. It's the same token pricing as Fable 5.1. It's also improving theoretical math problems that have existed for more than 80 years, in this case, the prime gap bound. So this is starting to get a little bit punchy here.

网络安全能力门槛

I'm going to start with the cyber part and then we'll talk about this before we get to Bernie Sanders, which is Astra is the first OpenAI model to meet the critical cybersecurity threshold under its preparedness framework. The exploit bench was 100%. It discovered and used two previously unknown zero-days, both now disclosed, and both labs now gate their strongest cyber capability rather than just throwing it immediately to the market.

Anthropic built one with the U.S. government. OpenAI is running Daybreak. And Anthropic said it's found no evidence of a critical severity jailbreak of Fable's safeguards. OpenAI saying Astra's written reasoning is harder to monitor and calls that a research priority.

So I want to start here. These things continue to improve. The frontier labs continue to all leapfrog each other. We've seen Anthropic and OpenAI, and then the Chinese models, and now Anthropic and OpenAI again. It just seems like a game of frogs chaining against each other.

Ram：AI 竞争与价值捕获

Ram, I want to start with two questions. What does this say about the capabilities of AI as they're going to be integrated for people? And two, what does it say about where value capture is going to end up in this space?

Ram: One, the pace of innovation is extraordinary. If you're not aligned and linking your human financial capital to AI, you're missing out. I spent most of this weekend spinning up agents on GrokBot. Like, I had breakfast with my kids, we played in the park for a bit, and I was spinning up 35 agents. And it's extraordinary. I had GrokBot and Claude and Astra with GPT's latest model, which is truly impressive, in a Slack channel coordinating different current actions.

Like we're entering this new phase whereas in the rearview mirror is infrastructure build-on that will keep happening in parallel. Now you're seeing genuine innovation at the agent layer, the consumer application layer, startups like Instinct and Granola. The future is coming out fast. It's an incredible time.

We're not at the AGI stage yet. I know Jensen said that because Jensen had to say that because OpenAI is one of his biggest customers. And just the last week, NVIDIA CEO Jensen invested in Hugging Face or wants to make a big investment there and also Poolside, which are U.S. open-weight models, which I think is actually the bigger news story. And those models are designed to be competitive with the Frontier Labs.

So the value leakage is likely to increase and spread out. Jensen, for the last few years, has been investing in firms like CoreWeave and Nebius and others — kind of almost anyone would take a check — Marvell, securing his supply chain and distribution to hedge against these hyperscalers. Now he's doing it at the LLM level.

So all this is really good for consumers. It's great for innovation. It's a tremendous amount of competitive ferocity we're seeing from very, very talented players. But we're not yet at Astra, I use these models all the time, okay, it's not there yet. We're not at AGI. Yeah, I'll be the first to let you know. And the other big gap is AI doesn't yet demonstrate leadership. There's no vision, there's no agency. It's not telling you what it should be telling you, even there and asked to.

Austin：Ram 说 AI 的好话了

Austin: Did you hear that, Austin? I did, yes. Rom said something nice about AI. I was going to say, I'm trying to remain calm right now. No, but like, joking aside, what I respect about Rom is he's willing to change his opinions when facts on the ground change. And I think, you know, as somebody who uses all of the models myself, OpenAI's products have gotten a lot better over the last few releases, not just in terms of the core models, but also tooling around them.

And I think that relates to something that if you're working at one of the AI labs, you have probably underfixated on, which is to say one of the core problems in emerging technologies is engineers building cool products for engineers because they think like engineers and assume all of the other stuff is easy slash will be solved. But as we all know, the best technology does not win. RIP Betamax. Yes. And what will actually win is making it usable in the hands of normal people.

So actually what Rom said that was most interesting to me and what I am keeping an eye very closely on is GrokBots. If you can create agentic AI that is easy to use in a no-code way for normal people and deploy that at scale, you were going to win. Because like my mom could probably, with enough time, figure out how to use GrokBots. I don't think she's ever going to use OpenClaw.

竞争与去监管

Ram: Before, like, there's a difference between technology, the company, and the leadership. I'm an AI bull, have been consistently so. This is where you should be focused in your financial capital and your human capital. You should be attaching yourself to those trends. Is OpenAI the great leading model? Yes. Is it a great investment versus like owning a semis? Probably not.

Chris: What I really like about the phase of the market that we're in is that you're seeing real competition, right? Everyone thought Anthropic was going to take the prize and run away with it. OpenAI comes back. Then Grok comes out of nowhere and you're seeing real competition. And all of a sudden Jensen shows up with Hugging Face, goes long on the open-source models. You get the Chinese out there. This is what happens when you don't have regulation forcing consolidation.

And that's exactly what regulation does. Eventually, regulation will come in, maybe. There'll be a common fixed layer of costs. And that forces consolidation, which you hate to see. I love this phase where these companies are pushing each other. They're accelerating. And the breakthroughs are real. The ability for breakthrough is incredible. So excited about that.

数据中心的政治风险

But we're going into a cycle. And as much as the innovation is exciting, people are really freaking out about it. They're freaking out about data centers. I'm very, very concerned.

You know, as I start talking to people on the ground in Pennsylvania and other places, data centers are going to be probably one of the top issues going into midterms. And it's not often you see Democrats and Republicans align. They're aligning. And when they align, it's very powerful because they don't align on very much. And if data centers are in the crosshairs, we could see a pretty quick change to how this country perceives the innovation that's possible. So throwing it out there.

Austin: The interesting part about the data center debate to me is how little facts are actually relevant to the debate, right? If you look at most of the claims that people start with when they're talking about data centers, they are just factually wrong. Like they do not use massively disproportionate amounts of water. They are not often responsible for massive increases in electricity prices. They do often bring a lot of taxes to the local area. I actually think noise and nuisance is like the number one complaint for people very local to them. Get it. Totally fair, legitimate point.

But when you look at what people talk about, it's not those things. And so the fact that both sides are aligning to this really seems to me more about social commentary. Because, Ram, to your earlier point about the leadership not being the technology, you've had the leaders of some of these AI companies basically on the road being like, "So here's what's going to happen. Our machines are going to take all of your jobs, like 100% of the jobs. We're going to take all of the jobs. You will have no jobs. We will have all the jobs. And then on top of that, we're going to start using AI to run the government and control you. And we're essentially summoning God or like some form of moral authority. And so we're going to control everything. Hey, wait, why are you opposed to us building data centers?"

Right? To me, this seems more like a marketing and trust issue than it is like a core facts issue, because if people were building data centers so that Netflix could serve like shows faster, everybody would be behind that in the United States. If you look at the revealed preference of American consumers, it's not less internet.

And so I think when you look at the opposition, you have to drill through sort of that first layer that's imperfect paint on it and get to the core of like, why are people agitated about this?

Bernie Sanders 反 AI 法案

Because to leg into the second part, you had Bernie Sanders out there trying to create a bill to ban artificial superintelligence. And I want to be very clear, they have defined none of these things. But what he basically says is there should be a pause on advanced development until a regulator writes rules and a directive to pursue a global ban. Good luck with that, Bernie. Where the penalties are benchmarked to unlawful nuclear weapons development with the idea of stopping, quote, "AI oligarchs from building machines that humans cannot control."

And ignoring the fact that none of the terms are defined in here, like Bernie Sanders has been a cipher for like incoherent concerns by the American electorate for a long time. I view this as signal about people being mad that he is proposing this. Like, Ron, what do you think?

Ram: Yeah, no, I agree. I mean, he also proposed a regulation saying that AI can't be smarter than a human. What is that about? Computers could do math faster than humans right now. We need a panel to determine which human that is, I guess. Yeah, Austin, I'm okay with it, or Chris, I'm okay with it. But like, I'm kidding.

Like, it's like Harrison Bergeron, right, from Kurt Vonnegut. Everyone's equally dumb so we can achieve equality. That's where it smacks up. The bigger issue you have for the center — it's just populism. So they're all trying to run to the left of one another. The political genius of Trump was adopting populism. I'm not a populist, to be clear. I'm a capitalist. I believe in free markets, technology, innovation, entrepreneurship, accountability. Let's go. Let's build.

But what they've done is they're running to the left of one another. That's what it is, right? So selling fear. That's what populism does. Let's sell fear. Let's not sell the future. Anti-trade, anti-technology. That's what this is about. It's not a winning issue.

Chris: It's not a winning issue because people are going to and are deriving joy and satisfaction from AI. It sells itself. If you want to learn how to use a GrokBot, you just say, "Hey, GrokBot, ask me some questions so I can use you." And it will show you. That's it. There's no complex onboarding process. You can mainline AI by asking it.

I think this is a wake-up call for the AI industry. They're making plenty of money. They're making incredible breakthroughs. The potential is immense. But they've got to — not stop building, but they have to focus on education. And they have to get the message out. And if they don't, you're right, Ram, it's a populist issue, but the world is becoming more populist, and we can have some real policy issues that really hurt the ability to innovate and align with all those capitalist ideas that you and I both support. If they don't start deploying, they got to up their game in DC. They have to really get their message out.

And look, no technology is perfect. It can be used for good or evil. But there's a lot of potential with this technology that needs to be explained.

Austin：AI 与美国人的对齐

Austin: I think if you want to talk about alignment, which is a favorite word of a lot of the labs, they need to start thinking about alignment with the American people if they don't want to have even more of a backlash. Right? If you're building technology that could be greatly enhancing productivity, you can't be running around saying "we're going to take all the jobs." Right? That is rightly seen by people as a pretty aggressive and, to be blunt, anti-American in some ways stance. You need to be talking about all the benefits it's going to bring.

And on top of that, you need to be making sure that people actually get those benefits, right? Solving theoretical math problems, while it's cool on Twitter as a former theoretical mathematician, let me tell you, many of those are of highly questionable value for long periods of time. On the other hand, sequencing cancer, right, like solving very specific problems in coding to improve information security and deploying all these sorts of things faster are concrete things.

And I think the AI labs are making a mistake, spending all of their time in a circle jerk in Silicon Valley, like talking about AI safety, instead of just being out there trying to cure as much cancer as humanly possible and then demonstrate that loudly to people.

And in some ways, the fact that they don't already see this tells you how incredibly out of touch they are. So my number one advice to these people, if you want to stop the data center backlash, is get out of Silicon Valley. Go to places like Idaho. Go to Texas. Go to Oklahoma City. Go to Nebraska. Go to North Carolina. Go meet actual people. Go to those communities. Find out what's important. Find out what they care about, and then demonstrate value for them. Because otherwise, they're rightly going to be pissed, right, that you're essentially just ignoring them. And it's incredible for people who are allegedly so smart to be so incredibly tone-deaf about politics. Get ready to talk about data centers during Thanksgiving. Oh my god.

四、Warsh、加息与利率之争

Warsh 与 Waller 表态

All right, well, let's close here on one other thing that people will definitely unfortunately be talking about at Thanksgiving, which is Warsh and hikes.

So Chair Kevin Warsh put September on the table at Jackson Hole on August 28th, saying the Fed has work to do on inflation. Traders now think there's a 58% chance of a hike in September. Hilariously, Warsh, understanding a little bit about how algorithms work, also used the word "hike," literally meaning going for a hike, repeatedly at the start of his speech, knowing what it would do to algos. I just want to say as a former volatility trader, next time, buddy, get "hike" and "cut" in there at least three times each, and you're really going to cause things to go crazy.

But that aside, Waller came out on Thursday and said he'd support a hold if disinflation holds up. But if it, quote, "if inflation comes in hot, I would consider a rate hike." He judges policy currently only slightly restricting aggregate demand. Waller was talking about core being 3.3% and three-month core has come down. But again, future data seems to be what's driving this.

Crypto took this as a dovish read. Bitcoin ran up. Spot Bitcoin ETFs continue to take money in. And then Friday showed up and payrolls came in at plus 162k against a 56k consensus. And interestingly, July was revised up to plus 21k from a previous decline of 23k. This is reversing a trend where payrolls have consistently been revised down over and over for a while here.

政治覆盖层与美联储

So essentially what we're looking at here is the political overlay is becoming real. Trump is saying, "Lower the rate or I'll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit," calling this an embargo better than tariffs, and telling the Fed board to, quote, "be patriots for a change." But on the other hand, we have all these people at the Fed essentially expressing caution.

So Ram, I want to start with you. I know you've been watching rates markets as a driver for equities here. What are you taking from the chaos around this whole debate?

Ram: We're not going to see rate hikes. Kevin Warsh is talking like a hawk but he's a dove. Two, we got productivity growth bailout coming from AI. That's going to save the day. We are in this disinflationary period with these temporary price shocks due to geopolitical concerns. Energy productions are a bit higher than ever, and it's going to continue to go up. Three, the AI buildout itself is inflationary. It's contributing like a point and a half of the GDP. So that is part of the cost of this buildout. They're not going to get down to the 2% inflation target for at least a few years. That means that you should be owning assets that reprice in nominal terms, especially equities that are indexed to the data center theme.

Chris：柴油价格与中期选举

Austin: Chris, what do you think? Are we getting a hike in September?

Chris: I agree with Rob, speaking for myself, but a couple of things that I'm watching is diesel. Diesel is hitting record shattering prices, I think averaging like $5.85 a gallon. That hits real America, that hits the truck drivers. And so it's no surprise, off goes Kushner and Wyckoff to Russia and Ukraine, because a lot of that's hurting supply.

And so if you're Trump right now, your eyes on midterm elections, you don't want to go through impeachment after impeachment if the Congress turns. So you need to keep as many seats as possible. How do you do that? You got to attack inflation. There are some things hopefully he can do to help control that vis-a-vis the Middle East. He's been trying to do that. It's been difficult. Bessent needs rates down, which is another challenge.

And so to me, I don't think anyone's in a position to raise rates under this environment, whether they're independent or not, we can decide. But what can he do to bring inflation down? Is there anything within his control? Because he has to perform well in midterms. Inflation will hurt midterms. And people are watching markets as well. So it's all about that from my perspective, and he's going to try to do whatever it takes.

Austin：口炮 Fed 反而推高长端利率

Austin: One of the interesting things to me about Trump is I feel like he's very much clearly a real estate and equities guy with the way he talks about markets. Because jawboning the Fed as the president will cause rates to go up. Let me say that as a former rates trader. Because people will look at this and say, "Ah, what is going to happen on a long enough timeline is the central bank will be captured by political interests, which means I should trust this country less, which means that I should demand more for the bonds."

To be clear, every time Trump shit talks the Fed, add a basis point to the 30-year, kind of what's going on in my head, right? Like he's actually moving rates up with this behavior, not down. So the constant political threats seem not to work the way he thinks in rates markets.

The other part of it is, Chris, you were just alluding to this, and I think you're correct. If this is a supply shock, there's not much the Fed is going to be able to do to address this thing just by moving rates around, because the level of interest rates does not create atoms, right? What we need is more fuel physically to do this.

Now, is there some level where the Fed could get rates high enough that we've destroyed demand? Yes. Is anybody going to enjoy that outcome when we cause a massive recession as Volcker did in the early 80s? Absolutely not.

国会才是问题所在

And so I look at all of this and I see Bessent talking about it. I see the Fed talking about it. I see Trump talking about it. And the great irony is over here who needs to talk about it and is not talking about it is Congress. Because fundamentally, I think all of these three guys are like pushing on a string until Congress stops spending so much money. Do you think I'm wrong about that? What do you think?

Chris: Yeah, where I am — you're totally wrong. There's no way Congress is going to stop spending money. Like how is that a viable outcome? Seriously?

Austin: I mean, okay, one, I think in the current framework they're not, but I would tell people in general you should probably expect inflation to continue if Congress is not going to stop spending money, right? Like the balance of payments thing is real, and eventually the pain will become severe enough that they're going to have to change their behavior. But Chris, you're right, it's usually got to get a lot worse than where we are now before people start actually reacting to it. Maybe we should wait till after midterms.

I mean, in fairness to the poor guy, Paul Ryan started talking about this what, close to 10 years ago, and they immediately kicked him out of Congress. So I guess there's precedent for not doing that.

Rom, what do you think? Do you think I'm wrong on just like it's a raw balance of payments issue in the end?

Ram: Inflation will be sticky for a while. I think for all the reasons that we've talked about. So the main thing you should just do is position your portfolio accordingly. Own real assets that have earnings growth, where you're a beneficiary of inflation.

挪威主权财富基金减持美债

Austin: I don't think that's wrong. And to that end, we're starting to see other people reacting in this way in the market. Like Norway is a good example. So Norway, I think it's the world's largest sovereign wealth fund at $2.3 trillion — certainly the world's largest sovereign wealth fund, if not — it's close if it's not the largest — recommended that the government bond share for U.S. bonds fall from 70% to 50% with treasuries taking the largest cut. So that's $80 billion off $215 billion of treasuries held at the end of June, and the slice going from 34.1 to 21.9%.

So you're starting to see people who are professional money managers, long-term focus, not captured by U.S. local interests, starting to bail out on U.S. debt, especially long-dated U.S. debt. Like, do you guys think that's signal or do you think something else is going on here?

Ram: No, those are headlines you see when rates are topping out. That's it. I'm waiting for the viral Ray Dalio Economic Machine thing to go out. That'll be the top. That's when you go — that'll be the time you actually buy bonds. You want that. That's when you buy the bonds. Yeah, this is just what you expect to see during moments like this.

1994 类比与利率顶部

Austin: Yeah, I mean, so where I'm finding it harder to interpret this than usual is, Ram, my gut is to agree with you. You look at these things and you say to people, well, when people complain like this and when all the usual talking heads are on and when you're getting front page articles about this — like when the Time cover saying U.S. Treasuries are dead comes out, you buy Treasuries, right? Like classic signal.

The flip side though, and Chris, we've seen this in Asia in the 90s — sometimes when you lose hold of the rope, it can go a lot further than you thought before you get your hands back on it. Yeah, I agree. We saw — god, I can't remember what it was, I'm seeing if I can look it up — that there was, yeah, it's HSBC, noting parallels to 1997. So this was Frederick Newman — surging U.S. yields, weak yen, unbridled tech optimism. And there the ten-year climbed from 5% in '93 to nearly 8% by October 1994.

Now obviously, had you bought it at 8%, you made a killing. But, Ram, I guess I'll ask you, are you saying you think the top is near here in rates terms, or are you just saying watch for the signals and maybe it's got room to run?

Ram: Yeah, no, I think you're in the 8th or 9th inning around rates. There's an outside shot that runs to 5%, but if that happens, that's the top. You should be a better buyer of rate-sensitive securities. I see in the equity market too, it's not just the bond market. You have all sorts of rate-sensitive stocks that are cheap. Like solar names, surprisingly, are rate-sensitive. Building supply material names and homebuilders are rate-sensitive. These companies have lots of debt. So I think you should be looking at opportunities in those areas.

保险板块的角度

Chris: How are you feeling about the insurance sector, if this is your view on rates?

Ram: That's a really good question. Because as you know, insurance companies are balance sheets that are publicly traded. They've taken premiums and deployed, and they go buy bonds and equities and longer-duration assets. So when rates go up, the fair value of their balance sheet declines. So when rates go down, that could be bullish. Now, the trade-off is are they originating quickly on the front book versus the back book? So that matters too. And the front book is like new policies and what rates are coming in at and to what extent they've hedged their existing book of business with rates. So it depends, is the short summary. What we say — I was gonna say, get us a one-handed economist.

结束语

All right, so on that note, I hope that everybody enjoyed us on this Labor Day episode of Bits and Bips. So thank you as always. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. Until then, everyone.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits and Bips. Just remember nothing we say here is investment advice, and please check UnchainedCrypto.com/BitsAndBips for more disclosures. We'll be right back.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"反向 ADR"革命：这不是衍生品之争，而是资本主权之争
大多数人把 AMC vs Robinhood 之争看作"合规打架"，但真正被埋没的洞察是：**Robinhood 做的是一个"反向 ADR"（Reverse ADR）** —— 传统 ADR 是把外国股票包装进美国市场，而 Robinhood 是把美国股票包装出美国、送到全球。这个方向的翻转其实是二战后美元霸权逻辑在链上的镜像延续。
**一个让人意外的观察**：AMC CEO 骂 Robinhood 骂得越凶，AMC 股价越涨（一夜 21%）。这不是巧合，而是揭示了一个新的市场微观结构规律 —— **在 attention 经济里，被 tokenize 本身就是一种"上市二次 IPO"**。链上的 mimetic demand 会反哺链下股价。这与传统金融理论完全相反：传统认为衍生品是从标的派生价值，而在 meme + token 时代，**衍生层反过来给标的注入了"社交流动性溢价"**。Adam Aron 在骂人的同时，其实在给自己的股票做全球免费营销。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 数据中心的政治困局

item.title: [Lex Clips] How agents are perfect for Linux | DHH and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"缺陷"的相变：Linux 悖论的反转时刻

DHH 提到的这个洞察其实是一场哲学级的反转：Linux 那些"过度具体、极度晦涩的错误信息"——过去二十年被视为它对普通用户最不友好的地方——在 AI 到来的瞬间从最大劣势变成了最大优势。

这里发生的不是"AI 帮我们读懂 Linux"，而是一次受众的悄然置换：错误信息的目标读者从人类变成了模型。当读者变了，同一段文本的"质量"评价就完全颠倒——对人越晦涩、对模型越具体、越能定位。Windows/macOS 那种"抱歉，出错了"式的友好错误，反而在 AI 时代变成了信息稀薄的负资产。

这让我想起一个跨领域的对照：基因组测序数据也曾是"垃圾"。ACGT 的四字母长串对人类完全不可读，被嘲笑为"没有信息的信息"。直到算力和模型追上来，这堆"乱码"才突然成了医学最珍贵的诊断金矿。Linux 的 stack trace 正在经历同样的相变——从噪声到信号的临界点，不在数据本身，而在读者的认知带宽。

二、多智能体的"意外副作用"：并发即混沌工程

DHH 顺口提了一句极其关键但没展开的话："当你同时跑多个 agent，它们会揪出你底层基础设施里所有那些人类手动操作从未触发过的竞态条件。"

这句话背后藏着一个反直觉的系统性真相：多智能体开发的最大价值可能根本不是"更快写代码"，而是意外成了一个永久在线的分布式压力测试。竞态条件是软件工程中最狡猾的一类 bug——它们只在特定并发时序下浮现，人类工程师几乎不可能靠手工重现。而 agent 群在正常工作时天然就是并发调用者，等于免费把 Netflix 的 Chaos Monkey 内嵌进了每一次日常开发。

跨领域连接：这与生态系统入侵物种的意外收益同构。一个物种进入新环境的"目的"从来不是暴露原生态位的脆弱性，但它的存在本身就是一场自然选择的实时体检。多智能体之于软件基础设施，等价于外来物种之于生态系统——不是它们要找 bug，是它们的存在方式就在找 bug。

三、被 GitHub 封禁的 bot：人类带宽校准的社会性基础设施正在崩溃

那个"12 秒提交 28 个 issue 被 GitHub 判为垃圾"的插曲，看似是小笑话，其实是一个时代级信号。

GitHub 的反垃圾阈值、API 速率限制、issue 模板规范——这些"社会性协议"全部按人类的思考与打字速度校准。当 agent 的产出速率把这些校准值撑爆，我们看到的不只是"技术摩擦"，而是整套围绕人类带宽建立的数字社会契约正在集体失灵。

这与 2010 年 5 月 6 日"闪崩"惊人相似：高频交易的速度撞碎了为人类交易员设计的市场微结构。市场并没有变得"更坏"，只是原来那些默默维持秩序的隐性假设——"下单速度大致等于人的反应速度"——被瞬间证伪。GitHub 的 spam filter 就是软件世界的 NYSE circuit breaker，它下一个必须被重新设计的假设是："issue 提交者是人"这条隐性前提。

四、最出人意料的一击：预发行 bug 报告与"未来时态"的软件工程

DHH 讲的那个 Mise 故事——bug 报告在软件还没发布之前就到了作者邮箱——是整段访谈里最容易被忽略但最颠覆的时刻。

传统软件工程的因果链是：发布 → 用户遇到问题 → 提交 issue → 修复。这个链条的时间箭头一直朝前。而 agent 能够去读未发行代码、模拟运行、预判问题——它把因果链倒过来了：问题在成为问题之前就被报告。

这在物理学上有个精确的对应：从被动观测宇宙 → 主动做粒子对撞实验。前者只能等宇宙自己产生现象，后者主动制造现象。Agent 让每一个开发者都从"等用户报 bug 的观测者"升级为"主动对撞未来场景的实验者"。而 Shopify 的那个研究更是钉死了这件事——agent 审查过的 PR 在生产环境里造成的问题更少——这已经不是"AI 能不能调试"的问题了，而是人类审查员正在从最后防线变成质量的瓶颈。

一个更让人心里一震的推论：如果 agent 能在软件"存在"之前就报告它的 bug，那么"软件版本"这个概念本身可能正在失效。版本号是为人类的记忆和沟通设计的，不是为持续演化的代码库设计的。Mise 需要一天更新七次这件事，只是这个更深变化的第一声回响。

📝 转录文本

Linux + Agents: A Perfect Match

I think this, by the way, is one of the other breakthroughs that is going to lead to the total domination of Linux.

The agents have taken all of the hardship out of diagnosing Linux systems and turned the fact that Linux produces these overly specific, totally arcane error messages into its greatest advantage.

When Linux has an issue, the agent can take that very specific error message that makes no sense to a normal human and correlate it with the fact that the agent was pre-trained on 40 million lines of Linux code, so it knows exactly where to look and dial it down.

I have not had a single problem on my Linux machine since the beginning of this year that an agent could not diagnose. That was not true a year and a half ago. A year and a half ago, I was still searching on forums to find answers to esoteric questions.

Now, the agents know the source code of not just the Linux operating system, but every single piece of software I have on that box. The agent has access to the source code of all of it.

The Crash Watcher in Omakub Quattro

In fact, this was one thing I built in just before we shipped. So, once you set up your default agent, Omakub Quattro has a crash watcher. If any app on your machine crashes, it'll pop up a little thing, ask you whether you want your AI to diagnose the problem.

Yeah. That's amazing. Unbelievable.

I've seen things where there's an error in some subsystem — some not even Linux, just some app I installed — the agent starts digging through the logs and looks up systemd log, then it checks out the damn source code of the application that crashed, pins down that it's in this Rust file line 472 that there's an unbounded, unwrapped variable that overflowed or whatever it is. Then, offers you whether you want to file a bug report with all this detail.

The Mise Story: An Amazing Anecdote

I'll give you one amazing anecdote.

So, I was working with um this guy JDX who's working on Mise. This is this package manager for uh fast-moving development tools. This is how we manage all the agent software and so forth. Normal package managers are not built to be updated seven times a day.

[snorts]

And all of these agent harnesses are updated about seven times a day. So, we needed an out-of-band uh package manager, and Mise just turns out to be perfect for this.

Anyway, it had a small bug. There was some uh race condition — which agents are very good at finding, because when you start running multiple agents at the same time, they will suss out all these race conditions you have in your underlying infrastructure that was never triggered by a human trying to do manual thing.

Banned by GitHub for Spam

So, it finds this issue, right? I tell um I tell the agent, "Hey, um can you post this as a bug report to JDX's uh GitHub?"

And unfortunately, right before that, I had had to do a QA run on Omakub itself with eight different agents. It had found 28 real issues that it needed to file. Well, it went to GitHub and tried to file all 28 issues at the same time, which it did in about uh I don't know, 12 seconds.

GitHub, not unreasonably, marked that as probable spam and banned my Omakub bot. And then I couldn't do that. So, I was blocked from the bot having access to GitHub.

So, I just told it, "Hey, you know what? Just email JDX. Here's his email address." I had already set it up with hey.com, an email address. We have a CLI that's in beta right now. So, I set it up with that so it can send the email. That's how it gives me reports about outstanding issues and PRs.

A Bug Report Before the Release

So, it sends JDX this email about the bug it found. And he was like, "Wait, this is the first time I've gotten a bug report in unreleased software." Because it had downloaded the source code to Mise, saw that he had already fixed a bug but that it would not fix the problem entirely in software that had not shipped yet.

Yeah.

Pinpointed the problem. And he was like, "Damn it, I got a bug report before we even cut a release."

Unbelievable — AGI levels of mind-blowing stuff.

Can Agents Actually Debug? The Shopify Study

And that was actually — if you remember — that was an open question, whether AI assistants could debug well. That was kind of the thought that, yeah sure, they can write code, but can they find issues?

They are so incredibly good at this. And this is actually interesting, because I was on the perhaps same side of that — a little skeptical about, can it reason about all these things?

And Mikhail, who's the CTO at Shopify, ran a scientific study on this. They had — and this was I think late last year or early this year — where he had agents go back through all the incidents, both outages and other problems that Shopify had had in production, trace that back to the PR that was merged, and find out whether the PRs that had been reviewed by human or PRs that had been reviewed by agents were of higher quality.

Well, lo and surprise, the —

[clears throat]

— the PRs that had been reviewed by agents caused fewer issues in production. And this was with models we had 6 months ago.

At this point, 100%, in the majority of domains we work in today, agents are better at finding bugs.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、"缺陷"的相变：Linux 悖论的反转时刻
DHH 提到的这个洞察其实是一场哲学级的反转：**Linux 那些"过度具体、极度晦涩的错误信息"——过去二十年被视为它对普通用户最不友好的地方——在 AI 到来的瞬间从最大劣势变成了最大优势**。
这里发生的不是"AI 帮我们读懂 Linux"，而是一次**受众的悄然置换**：错误信息的目标读者从人类变成了模型。当读者变了，同一段文本的"质量"评价就完全颠倒——对人越晦涩、对模型越具体、越能定位。Windows/macOS 那种"抱歉，出错了"式的友好错误，反而在 AI 时代变成了**信息稀薄的负资产**。
这让我想起一个跨领域的对照：**基因组测序数据也曾是"垃圾"**。ACGT 的四字母长串对人类完全不可读，被嘲笑为"没有信息的信息"。直到算力和模型追上来，这堆"乱码"才突然成了医学最珍贵的诊断金矿。Linux 的 stack trace 正在经历同样的相变——**从噪声到信号的临界点，不在数据本身，而在读者的认知带宽**。

item.title: [Business of Sport] Does the British Media Hate Successful People | James Haskell
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Haskell 其实是"英国媒体逻辑"最完美的产物，而不是受害者

他花大量时间抱怨英国媒体如何"捧杀"名人、如何嫉妒成功者。但仔细听他的叙述会发现一个悖论——他的所有商业成功（书籍、播客、代言、DJ 事业）恰恰是建立在"被误解"这一情感杠杆上的。他自己说了："我一周会收到三四次'我以前觉得你是个混蛋，现在改观了'的私信。"

这意味着："先被讨厌"是他商业模式的入口漏斗。如果英国媒体真的像美国媒体那样对成功者友好，Haskell 就没有那个"人格反转"的戏剧曲线可以卖了。他愤怒地抱怨的那个系统，正是他所有非橄榄球收入的定价机制。这就像鱼在抱怨水太湿——他把生存环境错认成了敌人。

跨领域连接：橄榄球的溃败 = 传统媒体的溃败 = 同一种"业余治理精英主义"的病

他讲的那个 RFU（英格兰橄榄球联盟）故事有一个让人震惊的细节：理事会成员被要求投票决定是否解散自己的职位。他们当然否决了。 这不是橄榄球的问题，这是一个跨越所有百年机构的通用病理：

  • BBC、《卫报》等传统媒体也是被"业余治理者"（60 岁以上、不理解社交媒体、以"传统"为身份认同）把持
  • 大学的终身教职委员会
  • 大多数国家的中央银行治理结构
  • 医学专业协会

Haskell 无意间描述的是"自我延续型精英治理"的通用溃败模式：一个组织当它的治理层由"以'守护传统'为身份"的业余者组成时，这个组织无法进行任何威胁到治理层身份的改革。你看到的不是橄榄球病了，你看到的是任何以"业余精神"为道德优越性的机构，在专业化经济中都必然崩溃。 Full Contact 被 Netflix 砍掉这件事之所以成为完美的隐喻，是因为它揭示了：这些机构宁愿死，也不愿被看见真实的自己。

隐藏的系统性真相：Haskell 的整个人生哲学是一个"疼痛货币化"引擎

注意他讲话的节奏和主题的隐藏结构： - 身体（10 万英镑修复、睾酮从 3 恢复到 25） - 童年（父亲的操纵、17 岁开始的治疗） - 职业（受骗签约、被低薪、诉讼 68 万英镑） - 关系（离婚、父亲留下的财务烂摊子）

大多数运动员在退役后会尽力掩藏这些伤口。Haskell 做的完全相反——他把每一次疼痛都转化成了一个内容产品：书、演讲、播客话题、纪录片素材。

这里有个惊人的洞察：他其实是英国最早期的"创伤经济"从业者之一，只是他自己没意识到。他反复说的那句"你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己"——这不仅是他父亲的教诲，这是内容经济时代的核心资产。在一个"真实性 = 稀缺性"的注意力市场里，愿意公开承认自己被父亲坑了 10 万英镑的前橄榄球国脚，比一百个完美的品牌大使更有价值。

他抱怨自己"没坐过私人飞机"——但真正的问题不是他赚得不够多，而是他还没有意识到自己已经从"橄榄球运动员"进化成了一个"人格 IP 运营者"，而后者的定价模型完全不同。 他还在用运动员的账本算内容创业者的收入。这就是他"下一个突破"的所在位置。

📝 转录文本

开场：关于金钱、诚实与英国媒体的自白

I'm not one of these bitter old rugby players that doesn't want people to earn. I'm mercenary in lots of areas. I love money. I love working hard. I work very hard. Do I think players should earn more money? Yes. Is there more money in the game? No. And that's the biggest problem.

My dad taught me a very valuable lesson when I was younger, which was: you can lie to everyone else, but you can't lie to yourself. There was lots of things probably that I didn't get right to start with.

I was tragically underpaid at Wasps for five years that I was there. I was the lowest paid player in the England squad. And what they used to trade off was the fact that great culture, unbelievable players would win everything. But they never invested in the squads, they didn't have the money, they underpaid people, people took pay cuts to come and win stuff.

Rugby turned the greatest opportunity and balls it up to the point where they cancelled it before the second season even came out. And that is all you ever need to know about rugby, because they don't know what they're doing.

We're actually not that happy for people to do well over here. Our media is the worst media in the world. Every celeb or every sportsman says it, because they'll build you up and then they will go out of their way to **** you over.

Business is fun. Fascinating.

见面寒暄：礼服、领带与训练后的身体

主持人：James, I'm so excited for this. My favourite thing is someone who has an opinion and stands behind it. Not that common, I find, today, but I think we'll do just fine here.

Haskell：My pleasure. I mean, I'd like to say I dressed up for the occasion to appear more corporate, but I'm actually going to the Gentleman TV series premiere this evening, and I realised, as per my diary management, that I didn't have enough time to get home. So I showered, spruced myself up, come in. So I'm killing two birds with one stone.

主持人：I just love the fact that you actually put the tie on for the show as well.

Haskell：Also, yeah, I didn't need to, but then I don't know why, I just finally did my top button up. And that one itself was quite hard because I trained this morning. I did some boxing training which was pretty intense, and being a slightly sort of muscle-bound individual trying to access your own tie in a tailored shirt while trying to put your… my hands don't physically get around there. So once I did it, I was like, I'm into it now, I'm not going to around.

身体的代价：伤病、手术与 10 万英镑的自费维修

主持人：Can I ask, how broken is your body?

Haskell：Pretty broken, yeah. From my perspective, I'm not one of these rugby players that at this point in time — touch wood — that I have any sort of cerebral issues or mental issues. I played a very physical position and my approach to my training and the way I worked was very, very intense. A lot of my teammates and coaches would say I was one of the most professional players they'd seen in terms of nutrition, training, working with other people, accessing other sports, talking to different individuals.

I reinvested a lot in myself, so I never accepted what the club offered me wherever I was. I'd always get my own physio, own nutritionist. I would do what they wanted me to do, but I would always think there was a better answer.

Because if you look at the NFL, for example — if you're paying Patrick Mahomes 450 million over 10 years, if he breaks down, that is a massive issue, and they have high level quality of staff and people to look after. If the best rugby player in your squad is paid — I mean today it's slightly different — but say paid 350, 400 grand a year, the budgets of a medical and everything else like that are not the highest. So you're not going to get access to the best people. Sometimes you do have amazing people, but often you'll get some average care.

And so having finished playing, I've had probably four or five operations since I retired. I had a discectomy on my back, I had a screw taken out my wrist, I had my bicep reattached, I had my ankle cleaned out, and then I ultimately had my ankle fused about a year ago. I'll get no insurance to pay for it — all myself. I reckon I've done probably 100 grand on injections, physio, medical fees, pilates. I've tried Ayurveda, Reiki — I've tried everything. Even when I went to Fiji, I saw something about my ankle, like a witch doctor. He wrapped my foot in leaves. I'll do anything to feel better.

But I've always — I see a wellness doctor, I work with a testosterone company. I had my testosterone test the other day: it was three. It starts at a healthy level about 12. So I was really low. I'd obviously shot myself to pieces with kind of training and tiredness. So I've got that back up to about 25.

I've always looked to get my bloods done. So everything I do is science-based information. It's not gym wisdom where a meathead says, oh, you want to take this. Because like anything in life, the cheque's always in the post. If you drink and smash it up now, it's not now you're going to worry about — it's when you're older. When you smoke now, it's not a problem, it's when you're older.

So my body's pretty wrecked, and sometimes having a low level of pain in my back, my neck, my ankles, my feet — waking up, feel like you've been hit or been put through a tumble dryer. But I do look after myself.

唯一的遗憾：42 场比赛与麻醉针

I have no regrets. The only thing that I would have done differently in my career was I would have taken more rest. We shouldn't have played as many games as we played. And I wouldn't have played injured. Well, I was injecting anaesthetic into my ankle — not me doing it, but the doctor was doing it in bits, trying to get through games. There's just no need to do that.

主持人：How many games are you playing a year?

Haskell：Oh well, at my peak, I played 42 games a year. Yeah, and I used to play 80 minutes as a back row player. And I would then practice my tackling every day.

So at some point, would I say that I am someone that would be in a place that could potentially have dementia or Alzheimer's? I've had a brain scan as part of a medical with a company called One World Beck, and there was some stuff on there, but nothing that you would think.

Actually, because bizarrely, my dad, who's passed away — I think he wasn't completely… I want to say English, but he wasn't. There was something going on with his genetics because he had bigger cast than Trevor Leota. His two of my fingers would be like one of his fingers. Massive joints, big lips. So I don't know what my grandma was up to, but he had some genetics. When I've had DEXA scans, which does your bone density, my bone density is massive. So I think I've got pretty hard bones, pretty hard head — but obviously your brain still rattles around, so I would be susceptible for that.

关于 Sam Warburton、法国联赛与"活在当下"

主持人：Can I just ask on the number of games? We had Sam Warburton in a few years ago. He was talking about when he got to play in Wales domestically and then when he got offers in France. The big challenge with France was: yes, fine, good money, but the demand to play would be more, he would have then had to compromise what he then did for Wales. So did you have to make choices between where you would put that focus? Because 42 games a year for the intensity that you had to play at your full potential for England and Wasps — is that virtually impossible?

Haskell：I mean look, I love Sam. As an aside, I think he's become a brilliant commentator. If you'd said to me Sam Warburton was going to be one of the most accomplished commentators and sort of orators around our game, I wouldn't have said so, because personality-wise he's quite quiet — great leader, unbelievable player, but I didn't know he had that kind of media stuff in him. So I'm always supremely impressed by him.

I never thought of it like he thought of it. I never came into question. I live very presently. I got therapy from the age of 17 to last week around — to start with — consistent performance, addressing criticism, bits and pieces. And through that journey you obviously find out you've maybe got some blind spots you need to work on. I didn't have any sort of conditions per se, so I live very much in the moment. If you can't control it, I wouldn't worry about it. So I never thought about that.

I played, I would be professional — sleep, train, not drink, rest, recover, and put my best out there. Would 42 games — would I have underperformed for England? I don't think so. It never crossed my mind. It was never considered. I never had to make any compromises. It made me a better player going to Stade Français, playing with Sergio Parisse, Dimitri Szarzewski, Pierre Rabadan, Juan Hernández — some of the best players in the world.

I'd come back to England camp, you're looked after. In those days when I was in France, I never missed an England game. I was playing under the coaching staff, Martin Johnson and John Wells — great guys, great coaches, but not like Eddie Jones. Eddie Jones' environment was light years ahead and better. I had five England coaches in my career; Eddie Jones was a million miles away from that.

Sometimes those sessions under those guys are draconian and long and purposeless and really a bit like, what the hell are we doing here? So maybe some of our performance did — but actually, no, I never did that.

Travis Allen 的教训：训练太多，比赛太少

I would say my biggest thing about my performance was doing too much off the field by extra training. So I was doing, not necessarily in France, but when I was in England, I was doing wrestling at London Shoot Fighters to help with tackling, takedowns. I was doing extra conditioning. I was seeing Margot Wells, a sprint coach. I was doing extra weights to help rehab injuries. And I was then trying to pursue a career and hustling in business and entrepreneurial spirit.

To the point where one of my friends, a guy called Travis Allen, who's a Kiwi — he's a specialist in certain training techniques and treatments — he sat me down and was like, "I don't understand why you're setting records in training and lifting all these weights, doing all this extra fitness when no one gives a shit. It's all about the performance on the weekend."

I remember it quite clearly. We had this meeting at High Road House in London. He said, "I want to sit through and go through a game with you." He sat and went through a game with me and he's like, "Look, you're playing inside yourself. You look like you're scared of the ball. You don't want to make mistakes. You turn up to training tired."

And I sat there and I thought, "What the fuck are you talking about? I know you're a Kiwi, so you immediately think you know more about rugby than everybody else." But he was a mate of mine. I've always been very good at listening to feedback. I don't necessarily like it at the time, but I have very much a level of self-awareness in terms of how I am as a person, what I say, how people view me. I watch people's body language all the time. I'm very in the moment. I never get too down. I don't look backwards.

And so I went away from that meeting going, he's right.

父亲的教诲：你可以骗所有人，但骗不了自己

And my dad taught me a very valuable lesson when I was younger, which was: you can lie to everyone else, but you can't lie to yourself. And when someone says, for example, you've got a drink problem, or you're late, or you're lazy, or you're tired, or you don't behave, or you're not a good parent — you can listen to it and you can have all the excuses. But that moment when perhaps when you go to bed, when you switch your phone off just before you close your eyes, everything hits you. And then you're like, maybe there's a bit of truth in this.

And that happened twice in my career at that point. And also, the day before my first day at Wasps, my dad said to me, "I know you don't like tackling. You're a bit of a fucking pussy. But what people want or don't want — the fact they're commenting is brilliant, because you want now to create interaction.

And every time I do something, I want people — because that's what life's like — to equally like or dislike me. If people have no reaction to you, what are you doing in life? It's creating conversation. Negative or positive is brilliant.

We're actually not that happy for people to do well over here at all.

America, American dream society, is built on people doing well and wanting to support you. Our media is built on criticism and destruction. People love to gossip over here and go, "Fucking hell, so-and-so thinks he's better than he is." And that all bubbles away in the corner.

Now, so you have to back it up with performances. You look at guys like Mayweather. The problem with sportsmen in the UK is if you do well and you put your head above the parapet, that's fine, but you better fucking back it up. How many people were so keen to see Conor McGregor get filled in? Because he made other people uncomfortable.

It makes people uncomfortable, because a lot of people like to be average. Some people were born, will be born, get a job, and it won't be a career, it's a job. They will have a family and that's all they'll ever do. And they're very happy with that.

When someone goes, "I am almost like a polyglot. I've got a million things under my belt. I deal with this kind of stuff. I've got a personality. You're good-looking. You're funny. You're gregarious" — people want to see you fail.

And our media is the worst media in the world. Every celeb or every sportsman says it, because they'll build you up and then they will go out of their way to fuck you over and crush you. And then we like to raise you up again and then we crush you again. America is a very different ballgame. Now, with the advent of social media and TMZ and all that kind of stuff, it is going a bit more that way. But I do think sports — having a personality is important.

  1. How you treat people
  2. How hard you work
  3. How you treat your body
  4. How you treat your mind

Because once it's broken and you have treated it badly, there's no fixing it again. And I think the last thing is how hard you work. You've got a choice. You've got one life. You never know when it's going to finish, when it's going to end. Life is difficult. It doesn't matter how successful you are. The great leveller is: if you are in the celebrity spotlight and are in sport and are in business, you're still human. You still have all the same issues.
